Aug 25, 2026: NeurIPS has no affiliation or partnership with any third-party service that claims to collect registration or housing information on our behalf. The only authorized source for NeurIPS registration and Housing is through the official NeurIPS website. Please do not share registration details with any outside party. July 23, 2026: Due to a technical issue during release, we are currently re-releasing all reviews and initial meta-reviews. Reviews will be temporarily offline during that time. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. AI Reviewing Experiment This year NeurIPS will be held in Sydney, Atlanta, and Paris. Author Eligibility. We want to speak directly to the concern many of you have expressed, and we owe you a clear explanation of what happened, why it happened, and where we stand now. We understand this situation caused genuine alarm and we take that seriously. In preparing the NeurIPS 2026 handbook, we included a link to a US government sanctions tool that covers a significantly broader set of restrictions than those NeurIPS is actually required to follow. This error was due to miscommunication between the NeurIPS Foundation and our legal team; there was never an intention to restrict participation beyond our mandatory compliance obligations. The responsibility for that error is ours as an organization, and we deeply apologize for the alarm and impact this miscommunication had on our community. We have updated the link and clarified the text of our policy, which is consistent with that of ACM and IEEE, as well as other international conferences and NeurIPS in the past. As in previous years, NeurIPS welcomes submissions from all compliant institutions and individuals. We want to reiterate that NeurIPS is a community-driven event, created by and for the community, and strives to be inclusive. The NeurIPS 2026 organizing committee was particularly saddened to learn of this institutional miscommunication. The organizing committee has taken on the responsibility of running the conference this year with the goal of fostering open communication, knowledge sharing, and global scientific discourse. We thank the community for bringing this issue to our attention and working with us through this situation. items.content: 2027 - Call For Blogposts Key Dates Abstract & Submission deadline : December 1st, 2026 23:59 AOE Submit to OpenReview Any modifications to your blog post, via a pull request on github (see here for more information) Notification of acceptance : March 1st, 2027 Camera-ready merge : March 15th, 2027 ICLR Blogposts Track The Machine Learning community is currently experiencing a reproducibility crisis , a reviewing crisis [Littman, 2021] , and submission crisis. Because of the highly competitive, noisy, and overwhelmed reviewing process of ML conferences [Tran et al., 2020] , researchers have an incentive to oversell their results, slowing down the progress and diminishing the integrity of the scientific community. Moreover with the growing number of papers published and submitted at the main ML conferences [Lin et al., 2020] , it has become more challenging to keep track of the latest advances in the field. Blog posts are becoming an increasingly popular and useful way to talk about science [Brown and Woolston, 2018] . They offer substantial value to the scientific community by providing a flexible platform to foster open, human , and transparent discussions about new insights or limitations of a scientific publication. However, because they are not as recognized as standard scientific publications, only a minority of researchers manage to maintain an active blog and get visibility for their efforts. Many are well-established researchers ( Francis Bach , Ben Recht , Ferenc Huszár , Lilian Weng ) or big corporations that leverage entire teams of graphic designers and writers to polish their blogs ( Facebook AI , Google AI , DeepMind , OpenAI ). As a result, the incentives for writing scientific blog posts are largely personal; it is unreasonable to expect a significant portion of the machine learning community to contribute to such an initiative when everyone is trying to establish themselves through publications. Submit your blogpost on OpenReview . A Blog Post Conference Track Last year, we ran the fifth iteration of the Blogpost track at ICLR 2026! It was very successful, with accepted posts presented in person at the main conference. Our goal is to create a formal call for blog posts at ICLR to incentivize and reward researchers to: Review past work and summarize the outcomes, develop new intuitions, or highlight some shortcomings. Present novel perspectives or interpretations of existing machine learning concepts or techniques. Discuss important issues in machine learning, such as reproducibility, from a novel perspective. Analyze the societal implications of recent advancements in machine learning and AI. If you are unsure about the content of your post you can reach us at iclr-blogpost-track@googlegroups.com . Past blog posts can be accessed here: 2022 , 2023 , 2024 , 2025 , 2026 . A very influential initiative of this kind happened after the Second World War in France. Because of the lack of up-to-date textbooks, a collective of mathematicians under the pseudonym Nicolas Bourbaki [Halmos 1957] , decided to start a series of textbooks about the foundations of mathematics [Bourbaki, 1939] . In the same vein, we aim to provide a new way to summarize scientific knowledge in the ML community. We will not consider politically motivated blogposts for publication. AI Usage The rise of AI agents has led to an increase in AI-generated submissions, ranging from minor help with figures or grammar to fully AI-generated content that the authors do not themselves understand [Shah, 2026] . Blog posts should distill complex ideas into clear, engaging, and accessible content. Thus, we expect all text to be written primarily by humans (grammar editing is fine), though we welcome AI-generated widgets or figures that interactively bring the material to the reader, as we understand they take significant time to create. AI-generated text will be part of the reviewer rubric, and we may desk-reject AI-generated blog posts. Thank you for your understanding. Submission caps There is a cap of two submissions per person. Blog posts discussing previously published work Content Write a post on a subject that has been published at a top-tier venue (ICLR, ICML, NeurIPS, AAAI, UAI, CVPR, SIGGRAPH, ECCV, ICCV, etc.) relatively recently. Conflict of interest The authors of the blog posts will have to declare their conflicts of interest (positive or negative) with the paper (and the paper’s authors) they write about. Conflicts of interest include: Recent collaborators (less than 3 years) Current institution – reviewers will be asked to judge if the submission is sufficiently critical and objective of the papers addressed in the blog post. Blog Posts must not be used to highlight or advertise past publications of the authors or their lab . We will only ask the authors to report if they have a conflict of interest. If so, reviewers will be asked to judge if the submission is sufficiently critical and objective of the papers addressed in the blog post. Publication The posts will be created and published under a unified template; see the submission instructions and the sample post hosted on the blog of this website. Poster Additionally, accepted posts will have the option to present their work as a poster during the main poster session. For more information about the main poster session (time, poster format, etc.) please refer to the ICLR homepage. Submissions Please check our submission instructions for more details. We accept submissions in both Markdown and HTML. We believe this is a good trade-off between complexity and flexibility. Submit your blogpost on OpenReview Contact For any technical issues with the blog post repository (for example, blog posts not displaying correctly or issues while following the submission instructions ), please open an issue in our GitHub repository . For other inquiries, reach us via email at: iclr-blogpost-track@googlegroups.com For more information, visit our website: https://iclr-blogposts.github.io/2027/about/ Organizers Sophie Xhonneux – Mila, Université de Montréal Leo Schwinn – Technical University of Munich Quentin Bertrand – Inria Nicholas Gao – CuspAI Yan Scholten – Technical University of Munich Rémi Emonet – Hubert Curien Laboratory, University of Saint-Étienne, Inria References Michael L Littman. Collusion rings threaten the integrity of computer science research . Communications of the ACM, 2021. David Tran, Alex Valtchanov, Keshav Ganapathy, Raymond Feng, Eric Slud, Micah Goldblum, and Tom Goldstein. An open review of OpenReview: A critical analysis of the machine learning conference review process . arXiv, 2020. Hsuan-Tien Lin, Maria-Florina Balcan, Raia Hadsell, and Marc’Aurelio Ranzato. What we learned from NeurIPS 2020 reviewing process . Medium, 2020. Eryn Brown and Chris Woolston. Why science blogging still matters . Nature, 2018. Paul R Halmos. Nicolas Bourbaki. Scientific American, 1957. Nicolas Bourbaki. Elements of mathematics. Éditions Hermann, 1939. Nihar Shah. Asking authors about their own papers . Medium, 2026.

items.title: From KTIR to SpyreCode: An MLIR Dataflow Backend for IBM Spyre
items.summary: Featured projects TL;DR Torch-spyre’s Inductor decides how each kernel’s work is divided across Spyre’s cores and manages tensor residency between on-chip scratchpad and off-chip memory, and the backend compiler turns those decisions into something the hardware can actually run. The contract between them is represented using KTIR (Kernel Tile IR), an MLIR representation built on a data-parallel view of the accelerator, in which every compute tile can see every memory and a single logical tensor can live spread across several cores’ scratchpads. The contract between them is represented using KTIR (Kernel Tile IR), an MLIR representation built on a data-parallel view of the accelerator, in which every compute tile can see every memory and a single logical tensor can live spread across several cores’ scratchpads. A new open-source Dataflow Scheduler consumes KTIR and turns each tile’s work into a dataflow pipeline: it splits the kernel into programs, starts from a simple load → compute → store pipeline, routes every transfer through the memory hierarchy given in an architecture description, and expands that pipeline into a nested, double-buffered, multi-instance schedule. The output of the scheduler is represented using DataflowIR , an MLIR intermediate representation that Spyre’s device-specific stages use to produce SpyreCode , a symbolic SpyreBinary plus a job plan that the Spyre runtime prepares once and launches many times, filling in tensor addresses and shapes at launch. This post is the middle chapter of three. Extending Inductor for the IBM Spyre Accelerator described how torch-spyre’s Inductor extensions settle layout, tiling, work division and scratchpad placement, and Building Spyre as a Native PyTorch Device described how the runtime launches a compiled artifact whose symbolic values are only filled in at the last moment. This post covers how the decisions Inductor makes actually become a program the runtime can launch. Where the backend compiler sits in the Spyre software stack Three ideas run through the design. The frontend decides the parallel decomposition, and the backend makes it run. KTIR is designed to carry the mapping Inductor has already chosen (which core computes what, over which data, out of which memory) so that the backend never has to rediscover it. The backend’s job is dataflow scheduling inside that mapping. Scheduling means building a pipeline. Spyre is a dataflow machine with decoupled access and execution, so loads, stores and compute run on separate engines communicating via FIFOs. The scheduler starts from the simplest legal pipeline and refines it one transformation at a time, and every one of those steps is a readable MLIR rewrite. The boundary is an IR, not a library call. KTIR, the scheduler’s ScheduleIR and DataflowIR are all ordinary MLIR built on upstream dialects ( linalg , scf , arith , memref , tensor ), and the scheduler and its dialects are open source under Apache-2.0. Device-specific lowering stages for code generation start at the DataflowIR boundary. KTIR: the contract between Inductor and the backend Why a new interface One of the key requirements for efficient backend scheduling is a contract between torch-spyre’s Inductor and the backend compiler with the capability and flexibility to capture the complete data-parallel view of the accelerator, in which every compute tile can see every memory and a single logical tensor can live spread across several cores’ scratchpads. KTIR ( RFC 0682 , implemented in torch-spyre/ktir-mlir-frontend ) is a tile-based, block-structured IR built on open-source MLIR. Our goal was to make it expressive enough to capture data-parallel mappings from two quite different sources: Inductor on one side, and hand-written Spyre kernels in languages like Triton or Helion on the other. A data-parallel abstraction of the accelerator KTIR is written against a deliberately simple picture of the hardware: a set of cores, each with a compute engine and its own on-chip scratchpad, joined by an on-chip interconnect that also reaches one or more off-chip memories. The property that matters most is that every compute tile has a global view of every memory , which means its own scratchpad, every other core’s scratchpad, and device memory. Hardware abstraction of a multi-core accelerator embodied in KTIR (from RFC 0682) That picture matches Spyre’s shape closely: 32 cores on a ring, each with 2 MB of scratchpad, backed by off-chip device memory. Data moves between device memory and the scratchpads in sticks , fixed 128-byte chunks that hold 64 fp16 values. Intentionally, the picture leaves out details such as FIFOs, load/store units and decoupled execution engines. KTIR describes what each compute tile does and where its data lives , not how that data gets there , because working out how it gets there is exactly the scheduler’s job. KTIR is also compositional. Arithmetic, reductions and control flow come straight from upstream MLIR dialects ( arith , math , linalg , scf , tensor , memref ), and a dedicated dialect, ktdp , adds the two things those dialects can’t express: explicit memories and explicit accesses. A second, much smaller dialect, spyreop , covers Spyre’s own intrinsics. The core ktdp operations are: ktdp op What it expresses get_compute_tile_id Which compute tile this is; 1-D or multi-dimensional, over the grid attribute on the kernel construct_memory_view Interpret a region at some (possibly symbolic) address in a named memory space as a strided tensor; no allocation, no data movement construct_distributed_memory_view Compose several memory views, each covering part of a global coordinate space, into one logical tensor construct_access_tile A structured set of coordinates into a view: an integer set for the domain and an affine map for the traversal order, so tiles can be rectangular, strided, skewed or triangular construct_indirect_access_tile The same, with some dimensions indexed through another tensor, e.g. paged KV-cache gathers load / store The only data movement: consume an access tile and produce or write a data tile inter_tile_produce / inter_tile_reduce Communication between compute tiles, e.g. an all-reduce of partial sums Here is a complete kernel, an elementwise add over 96×64 fp16 tensors divided among 32 compute tiles of three rows each. #tile = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 2 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 63 >= 0)> // 3x64 #full = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 95 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 63 >= 0)> #id = affine_map<(d0, d1) -> (d0, d1)> // The tensors' start addresses arrive as arguments: PyTorch's allocator owns them. func.func @add(%A: index, %B: index, %C: index) attributes {grid = [32]} { %c0 = arith.constant 0 : index %c3 = arith.constant 3 : index %id = ktdp.get_compute_tile_id : index %row0 = arith.muli %id, %c3 : index // this tile's 3-row slab %A_view = ktdp.construct_memory_view %A, sizes: [96, 64], strides: [64, 1] { coordinate_set = #full, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<global> } : memref<96x64xf16> // ... %B_view and %C_view alike %A_t = ktdp.construct_access_tile %A_view[%row0, %c0] { access_tile_set = #tile, access_tile_order = #id } : memref<96x64xf16> -> !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> // ... %B_t and %C_t alike %a = ktdp.load %A_t : !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> -> tensor<3x64xf16> %b = ktdp.load %B_t : !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> -> tensor<3x64xf16> %e = tensor.empty() : tensor<3x64xf16> %c = linalg.add ins(%a, %b : tensor<3x64xf16>, tensor<3x64xf16>) outs(%e : tensor<3x64xf16>) -> tensor<3x64xf16> ktdp.store %c, %C_t : tensor<3x64xf16>, !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> return } The kernel keeps four concerns apart. Views say how memory should be interpreted, access tiles say which coordinates a given tile touches, loads and stores are the only operations that move data, and linalg does the arithmetic. Notice also that the work division is already settled: grid = [32] , together with the arithmetic on %id , is the partitioning, and the backend is expected to honor it rather than second-guess it. Spyre intrinsics: the spyreop dialect Upstream arith and math cover most of the arithmetic a kernel needs, but Spyre’s compute units also offer operations that no generic dialect has a name for. A kernel that wants one of those should be able to ask for it directly, instead of hoping the backend recognizes some particular pattern of arith ops. For that, KTIR comes with a second, much smaller dialect, spyreop , which exposes Spyre intrinsics as ordinary MLIR operations. It covers elementwise and activation functions ( exp , gelu , sigmoid , silu , softplus , sqrt , rsqrt , reciprocal , realdiv ), the building blocks of normalization (a combined mean and mean of squares, and the normalizing and scaling halves of LayerNorm, some with fused variants), integer and address arithmetic (including idx32toaddr , which computes base + stride × index for gathers), and compare and select . The dialect also defines df16 , IBM’s 16-bit DLFloat format, which splits its bits 1-6-9 between sign, exponent and mantissa rather than IEEE half precision’s 1-5-10, along with “fused” types that carry a pair of floats as a single value. Intrinsics appear wherever any other scalar computation would, which is inside the body of a linalg.generic : %y = linalg.generic {indexing_maps = [#in, #out], iterator_types = ["parallel", "parallel", "parallel", "parallel"]} ins(%x : tensor<6x64x64xf16>) outs(%init : tensor<1x6x64x64xf16>) { ^bb0(%a: f16, %out: f16): %g = spyreop.gelu %a : f16 linalg.yield %g : f16 } -> tensor<1x6x64x64xf16> Because they are just operations in a linalg body, intrinsics fuse with the surrounding elementwise work like anything else, and the scheduler carries them through as compute until it is ready to lower them. How each intrinsic expands into the hardware’s own instruction sequence is not written in the scheduler at all: it lives in the architecture description, as one of the device patterns described later in this post. How KTIR captures Inductor’s work mapping The Inductor post walked through a series of decisions torch-spyre makes before any code is generated. Each of them has a direct counterpart in KTIR: Decision in torch-spyre’s Inductor passes How it appears in KTIR Work division: the per-op core split, e.g. a matmul’s 16 × 2 grid The kernel’s grid attribute, plus affine arithmetic on ktdp.get_compute_tile_id that picks each tile’s slice Stick-granularity layout: which dimension is the stick, and the tiled order of the others Strides of construct_memory_view , and the access_tile_order of each access tile Coarse tiling and working-set reduction scf.for loops around loads, compute and stores, which run the chain tile by tile Scratchpad residency chosen by the scratchpad allocator A memory view in #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = k> at the offset the allocator assigned A tensor split across cores so each slice fits in scratchpad construct_distributed_memory_view over per-core ct_local views Core-to-core relayout ( lx_relayout ) An access tile over one distributed view, stored into a view with a different distribution Reduction split across cores (partial sums of one output tile) inter_tile_produce / inter_tile_reduce Paged tensors and gathers construct_indirect_access_tile Device-specific activations and normalization steps spyreop intrinsics inside linalg.generic bodies Tensor addresses owned by PyTorch’s allocator Kernel arguments. They stay symbolic all the way to SpyreCode and are substituted by the runtime at launch Tensor shapes known only at runtime, within a bound !ktdp.runtime_arg<index, granularity = G, upperbound = U> , kept symbolic and substituted at launch in the same way The last two rows are where this post meets the runtime post. Because KTIR allows a start address or a size to be a value rather than a constant, every layer beneath it can keep that value symbolic until the runtime is in a position to supply it. Tensors pinned in scratchpad, distributed across cores What most sets KTIR apart from GPU-oriented tile IRs is the way it treats on-chip memory. A tile language like Triton describes each program instance loading blocks of a tensor from global memory, computing on them, and storing the results back. How those blocks are staged through shared memory, registers and caches is left to the compiler and the hardware, and a program instance’s on-chip storage is private to it and lives only as long as it runs. In that model there is typically no way, and little need, to say that a tensor should still be sitting in a particular core’s on-chip memory when the next operation reads it, or that one program instance should read data held on-chip by another. That works well on hardware where caches and a dynamic scheduler smooth over data movement. It doesn’t fit Spyre. There is no hardware-managed cache to fall back on, and keeping a tensor on-chip from one operation to the next is one of the biggest performance levers available. On Spyre, the scratchpad isn’t a cache that a kernel happens to hit; it’s memory the compiler chooses to use, with Inductor’s scratchpad allocator deciding which buffers stay resident, at what address and on which core. KTIR therefore makes on-chip placement a first-class part of the IR rather than an implementation detail: it simply writes that decision down. Each memory space names a physical memory: #ktdp.memory_space<global> is device memory, and #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = k> is the scratchpad belonging to compute tile k . A view’s coordinate_set records which part of a larger logical tensor it holds, so if you combine per-core views with construct_distributed_memory_view , you get a single tensor, indexed by global coordinates, whose storage is spread across several scratchpads. // X[128, 1024] f16, left in scratchpad by an earlier op of the kernel: // 32 rows on each of four cores, at the offset the scratchpad allocator chose. #rows0 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 31 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> #rows1 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 - 32 >= 0, -d0 + 63 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> // ... #rows2, #rows3 %X0 = ktdp.construct_memory_view %lx_off, sizes: [32, 1024], strides: [1024, 1] { coordinate_set = #rows0, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = 0> } : memref<32x1024xf16> %X1 = ktdp.construct_memory_view %lx_off, sizes: [32, 1024], strides: [1024, 1] { coordinate_set = #rows1, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = 1> } : memref<32x1024xf16> // ... %X2, %X3 %X = ktdp.construct_distributed_memory_view (%X0, %X1, %X2, %X3 : memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>) : memref<128x1024xf16> // Compute tile 1 reads rows 48-79: half from its own scratchpad, half from core 2's. #rows32 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 31 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> %id = ktdp.get_compute_tile_id : index %row = affine.apply affine_map<(d0) -> (d0 * 32 + 16)>(%id) %t = ktdp.construct_access_tile %X[%row, %c0] { access_tile_set = #rows32, access_tile_order = #id } : memref<128x1024xf16> -> !ktdp.access_tile<32x1024xindex> %x = ktdp.load %t : !ktdp.access_tile<32x1024xindex> -> tensor<32x1024xf16> A distributed memory view: one logical tensor, pinned across four scratchpads This one construct does quite a lot of work. First, it lets intermediate tensors stay on-chip from one operation to the next: a producer can store into a distributed ct_local view and a consumer can load from it without either of them ever mentioning device memory, which is precisely the kind of fusion without a round trip that the softmax example in the Inductor post was built around. Second, it turns a core-division mismatch into ordinary IR. When a producer and a consumer divide a tensor differently, the consumer’s access tiles just cross scratchpad boundaries, and since every compute tile can see every scratchpad, that is still nothing more than a load ; the on-chip relayout that torch-spyre’s co-optimizing allocator weighs against a spill needs no special-purpose op. Third, it keeps placement binding. The runtime post argued that “placement must be explicit and binding because compiled code may depend on it,” and KTIR is where that dependency is recorded, since the memory space and coordinate set on a view are the placement contract. The backend compiler at a glance The backend compiler is a single MLIR pipeline in two halves. The open-source Dataflow Scheduler lowers KTIR through ScheduleIR to DataflowIR , and three device-specific stages (symbolic SpyreBinary generation, metadata generation for runtime symbol substitution, and SpyreCode generation) then turn DataflowIR into SpyreCode. DataflowIR is the only point where the two halves meet. The Spyre backend compiler: KTIR in, SpyreCode out The rest of the post follows the figure from left to right, spending most of its time on the scheduler and then covering the three stages below it more briefly. The Dataflow Scheduler: KTIR → ScheduleIR → DataflowIR A dataflow accelerator is a distributed collection of compute engines and scratchpad memories connected by wide datapaths with FIFOs. It follows a decoupled access-execute design, in which moving data (DMA, scratchpad loads and stores) and computing on it happen on separate engines that run at the same time. On a machine like that, scheduling means building a dataflow pipeline across space and time , deciding which engine performs each step and how the steps overlap with one another. The Dataflow Scheduler does this as an MLIR pass pipeline, and a handful of principles shape how it’s built. It is driven by an architecture description rather than hard-coded for one chip, which we look at more closely below. Every schedule is expressed in a single execution model built from just three constructs: nested scf.for loops, ktdf.pipeline (stages that overlap across iterations) and ktdf.parallel (identical instances that split an iteration space between them), and every analysis and transformation reasons in those terms. Wherever it can, the scheduler leans on upstream MLIR, lowering compute to linalg.generic and fusing it with upstream passes, and using scf for loops and memref for buffers. And throughout, it follows one strategy: start with the most naive correct pipeline, then let each later pass either make it legal on the hardware or make it bigger, in small steps that can be tested on their own. The passes fall into three groups, each with a fixed IR contract at its boundaries, so passes can be added or reordered within a group without disturbing the others. Dataflow Scheduler: three pass groups, one IR contract each At four named checkpoints ( pre_mapping , pre_scheduling , post_scheduling and post_lowering ) the scheduler applies rewrite patterns written in PDL. Those patterns live in the architecture description rather than in the scheduler, which means a device can supply its own lowerings without forking the scheduler. This is where each spyreop intrinsic, such as spyreop.exp or spyreop.gelu , is replaced by the hardware’s instruction template, and where an inner-dimension reduction becomes a SIMD reduction. The scheduler’s intermediate form, ScheduleIR , is the ktdf dialect used alongside linalg , scf and memref . Its vocabulary is small enough to list in full: ktdf construct Meaning ktdf.pipeline [modulo(size: N)] A chain of stages that overlap across iterations; modulo rotates through N copies of its resources (N-buffering) ktdf.stage depends_in(...) depends_out(...) One step of a pipeline, eventually bound to one kind of execution unit ( applicable_units ) ktdf.private Resources private to one pipeline: FIFO slots, scratchpad buffers, tokens !ktdf.token A pure ordering value between stages, with no runtime cost of its own !ktdf.fifo.slot<SRC -> DST, 64xf16> A slot in a hardware FIFO between two units ktdf.data_transfer / ktdf.ind_data_transfer Explicit movement between memories and FIFOs, direct or through an indirect-address buffer ktdf.read_from_fifo / ktdf.write_to_fifo How a compute stage consumes and produces FIFO data ktdf.parallel ... distribute(num_instances = N) Split an iteration space into contiguous blocks over N identical hardware instances ktdf.tiling.reserve_size / derive_size / linearize_index Placeholders for tile sizes chosen later, the current tile’s extent, and the original index The architecture description Everything the scheduler knows about the hardware comes from a single MLIR file written in the ktdf_arch dialect. That file describes the device as a graph. Its nodes are memories, with their kinds and sizes, and execution units, with the features the scheduler cares about: SIMD lane counts per element type, the word sizes and access granularities of load and store units, the depth of each FIFO. Its edges are datapaths, each with a transfer granularity. Groups scope resources the way the hardware does, for example a core that owns a scratchpad along with the load/store and compute units that use it. Here is a trimmed and simplified version of the sample device used in the scheduler’s tests: #L1 = { kind = "L1", size = 1048576 } // 1 MB scratchpad #SFU = { kind = "SFU", ktdf_arch.features = { ktdf_arch.feature.compute, ktdf_arch.feature.simd = { lanes = #ktdf_arch.map<f16 = 64, f32 = 32, i32 = 32> } } } #L1LU_CORE_FIFO = { ktdf_arch.features = { ktdf_arch.feature.queue = { depth = 16, ordered } } } ktdf_arch.device @sample_device { %ddr = memory #DDR group { kind = "core" } share(%ddr) { %l1 = memory #L1 %mnilu = group { kind = "MNILU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // DMA load unit %mnisu = group { kind = "MNISU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // DMA store unit datapath #DDR_MNILU %ddr to %mnilu : memory, exec_unit datapath #MNILU_L1 %mnilu to %l1 : exec_unit, memory %sfu = group { kind = "SFU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // compute unit %l1lu = exec_unit #L1LU // scratchpad load unit %l1su = exec_unit #L1SU // scratchpad store unit datapath #L1LU_CORE_FIFO %l1 to %l1lu : memory, exec_unit datapath %l1lu to %sfu : exec_unit, exec_unit ... } patterns ["pre_scheduling"] { ... } // device-specific rewrites, in PDL patterns ["post_scheduling"] { ... } } A kernel refers to its target with a one-line declaration that imports this file and maps KTIR’s memory spaces onto the device’s memories, for example global onto DDR and ct_local onto L1 . From then on, nearly every decision in the pipeline reads something from the description. The SIMD lane count sets the width of the first pipeline. The datapaths form the routing graph that path expansion searches, so the hops a transfer takes are whatever the graph allows. Access granularities, transfer granularities and FIFO depths constrain how each transfer can be shaped. Memory sizes bound what address assignment can place, and therefore which tile sizes fit. And the patterns blocks supply the device’s own lowerings, such as how each spyreop intrinsic expands into the hardware’s instructions, at the scheduler’s checkpoints. Because all of that lives in the description rather than in the passes, retargeting the scheduler means writing a new description, not changing the scheduler. Spyre has its own description, the scheduler’s tests run against the sample device above, and the same passes run unchanged on both. Step 1: Break the kernel into programs A KTIR kernel is a sequence of operations, whereas a Spyre program is a single pipeline configuration loaded onto the device, so the scheduler’s first real decision is where to cut the kernel into separately scheduled programs. The scheduler makes that cut by working backwards from each ktdp.store , through the compute that feeds it, to the ktdp.load s it ultimately depends on. Everything connected that way forms one compute group , a single load → compute → store chain through memory, and a group ends either at a load that belongs to a different group or at any operation with a region, such as a loop or a conditional. Each group then becomes its own nested MLIR module, module @local_schedule_N , while the original kernel turns into an orchestrator that keeps the control flow and address arithmetic and calls the programs in order. The number of programs is therefore exactly the

%id, %c3 : index // this tile's 3-row slab %A_view = ktdp.construct_memory_view %A, sizes: [96, 64], strides: [64, 1] { coordinate_set = #full, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<global> } : memref<96x64xf16> // ... %B_view and %C_view alike %A_t = ktdp.construct_access_tile %A_view[%row0, %c0] { access_tile_set = #tile, access_tile_order = #id } : memref<96x64xf16> -> !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> // ... %B_t and %C_t alike %a = ktdp.load %A_t : !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> -> tensor<3x64xf16> %b = ktdp.load %B_t : !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> -> tensor<3x64xf16> %e = tensor.empty() : tensor<3x64xf16> %c = linalg.add ins(%a, %b : tensor<3x64xf16>, tensor<3x64xf16>) outs(%e : tensor<3x64xf16>) -> tensor<3x64xf16> ktdp.store %c, %C_t : tensor<3x64xf16>, !ktdp.access_tile<3x64xindex> return } The kernel keeps four concerns apart. Views say how memory should be interpreted, access tiles say which coordinates a given tile touches, loads and stores are the only operations that move data, and linalg does the arithmetic. Notice also that the work division is already settled: grid = [32] , together with the arithmetic on %id , is the partitioning, and the backend is expected to honor it rather than second-guess it. Spyre intrinsics: the spyreop dialect Upstream arith and math cover most of the arithmetic a kernel needs, but Spyre’s compute units also offer operations that no generic dialect has a name for. A kernel that wants one of those should be able to ask for it directly, instead of hoping the backend recognizes some particular pattern of arith ops. For that, KTIR comes with a second, much smaller dialect, spyreop , which exposes Spyre intrinsics as ordinary MLIR operations. It covers elementwise and activation functions ( exp , gelu , sigmoid , silu , softplus , sqrt , rsqrt , reciprocal , realdiv ), the building blocks of normalization (a combined mean and mean of squares, and the normalizing and scaling halves of LayerNorm, some with fused variants), integer and address arithmetic (including idx32toaddr , which computes base + stride × index for gathers), and compare and select . The dialect also defines df16 , IBM’s 16-bit DLFloat format, which splits its bits 1-6-9 between sign, exponent and mantissa rather than IEEE half precision’s 1-5-10, along with “fused” types that carry a pair of floats as a single value. Intrinsics appear wherever any other scalar computation would, which is inside the body of a linalg.generic : %y = linalg.generic {indexing_maps = [#in, #out], iterator_types = ["parallel", "parallel", "parallel", "parallel"]} ins(%x : tensor<6x64x64xf16>) outs(%init : tensor<1x6x64x64xf16>) { ^bb0(%a: f16, %out: f16): %g = spyreop.gelu %a : f16 linalg.yield %g : f16 } -> tensor<1x6x64x64xf16> Because they are just operations in a linalg body, intrinsics fuse with the surrounding elementwise work like anything else, and the scheduler carries them through as compute until it is ready to lower them. How each intrinsic expands into the hardware’s own instruction sequence is not written in the scheduler at all: it lives in the architecture description, as one of the device patterns described later in this post. How KTIR captures Inductor’s work mapping The Inductor post walked through a series of decisions torch-spyre makes before any code is generated. Each of them has a direct counterpart in KTIR: Decision in torch-spyre’s Inductor passes How it appears in KTIR Work division: the per-op core split, e.g. a matmul’s 16 × 2 grid The kernel’s grid attribute, plus affine arithmetic on ktdp.get_compute_tile_id that picks each tile’s slice Stick-granularity layout: which dimension is the stick, and the tiled order of the others Strides of construct_memory_view , and the access_tile_order of each access tile Coarse tiling and working-set reduction scf.for loops around loads, compute and stores, which run the chain tile by tile Scratchpad residency chosen by the scratchpad allocator A memory view in #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = k> at the offset the allocator assigned A tensor split across cores so each slice fits in scratchpad construct_distributed_memory_view over per-core ct_local views Core-to-core relayout ( lx_relayout ) An access tile over one distributed view, stored into a view with a different distribution Reduction split across cores (partial sums of one output tile) inter_tile_produce / inter_tile_reduce Paged tensors and gathers construct_indirect_access_tile Device-specific activations and normalization steps spyreop intrinsics inside linalg.generic bodies Tensor addresses owned by PyTorch’s allocator Kernel arguments. They stay symbolic all the way to SpyreCode and are substituted by the runtime at launch Tensor shapes known only at runtime, within a bound !ktdp.runtime_arg<index, granularity = G, upperbound = U> , kept symbolic and substituted at launch in the same way The last two rows are where this post meets the runtime post. Because KTIR allows a start address or a size to be a value rather than a constant, every layer beneath it can keep that value symbolic until the runtime is in a position to supply it. Tensors pinned in scratchpad, distributed across cores What most sets KTIR apart from GPU-oriented tile IRs is the way it treats on-chip memory. A tile language like Triton describes each program instance loading blocks of a tensor from global memory, computing on them, and storing the results back. How those blocks are staged through shared memory, registers and caches is left to the compiler and the hardware, and a program instance’s on-chip storage is private to it and lives only as long as it runs. In that model there is typically no way, and little need, to say that a tensor should still be sitting in a particular core’s on-chip memory when the next operation reads it, or that one program instance should read data held on-chip by another. That works well on hardware where caches and a dynamic scheduler smooth over data movement. It doesn’t fit Spyre. There is no hardware-managed cache to fall back on, and keeping a tensor on-chip from one operation to the next is one of the biggest performance levers available. On Spyre, the scratchpad isn’t a cache that a kernel happens to hit; it’s memory the compiler chooses to use, with Inductor’s scratchpad allocator deciding which buffers stay resident, at what address and on which core. KTIR therefore makes on-chip placement a first-class part of the IR rather than an implementation detail: it simply writes that decision down. Each memory space names a physical memory: #ktdp.memory_space<global> is device memory, and #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = k> is the scratchpad belonging to compute tile k . A view’s coordinate_set records which part of a larger logical tensor it holds, so if you combine per-core views with construct_distributed_memory_view , you get a single tensor, indexed by global coordinates, whose storage is spread across several scratchpads. // X[128, 1024] f16, left in scratchpad by an earlier op of the kernel: // 32 rows on each of four cores, at the offset the scratchpad allocator chose. #rows0 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 31 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> #rows1 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 - 32 >= 0, -d0 + 63 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> // ... #rows2, #rows3 %X0 = ktdp.construct_memory_view %lx_off, sizes: [32, 1024], strides: [1024, 1] { coordinate_set = #rows0, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = 0> } : memref<32x1024xf16> %X1 = ktdp.construct_memory_view %lx_off, sizes: [32, 1024], strides: [1024, 1] { coordinate_set = #rows1, memory_space = #ktdp.memory_space<ct_local, ct_id = 1> } : memref<32x1024xf16> // ... %X2, %X3 %X = ktdp.construct_distributed_memory_view (%X0, %X1, %X2, %X3 : memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>, memref<32x1024xf16>) : memref<128x1024xf16> // Compute tile 1 reads rows 48-79: half from its own scratchpad, half from core 2's. #rows32 = affine_set<(d0, d1) : (d0 >= 0, -d0 + 31 >= 0, d1 >= 0, -d1 + 1023 >= 0)> %id = ktdp.get_compute_tile_id : index %row = affine.apply affine_map<(d0) -> (d0 * 32 + 16)>(%id) %t = ktdp.construct_access_tile %X[%row, %c0] { access_tile_set = #rows32, access_tile_order = #id } : memref<128x1024xf16> -> !ktdp.access_tile<32x1024xindex> %x = ktdp.load %t : !ktdp.access_tile<32x1024xindex> -> tensor<32x1024xf16> A distributed memory view: one logical tensor, pinned across four scratchpads This one construct does quite a lot of work. First, it lets intermediate tensors stay on-chip from one operation to the next: a producer can store into a distributed ct_local view and a consumer can load from it without either of them ever mentioning device memory, which is precisely the kind of fusion without a round trip that the softmax example in the Inductor post was built around. Second, it turns a core-division mismatch into ordinary IR. When a producer and a consumer divide a tensor differently, the consumer’s access tiles just cross scratchpad boundaries, and since every compute tile can see every scratchpad, that is still nothing more than a load ; the on-chip relayout that torch-spyre’s co-optimizing allocator weighs against a spill needs no special-purpose op. Third, it keeps placement binding. The runtime post argued that “placement must be explicit and binding because compiled code may depend on it,” and KTIR is where that dependency is recorded, since the memory space and coordinate set on a view are the placement contract. The backend compiler at a glance The backend compiler is a single MLIR pipeline in two halves. The open-source Dataflow Scheduler lowers KTIR through ScheduleIR to DataflowIR , and three device-specific stages (symbolic SpyreBinary generation, metadata generation for runtime symbol substitution, and SpyreCode generation) then turn DataflowIR into SpyreCode. DataflowIR is the only point where the two halves meet. The Spyre backend compiler: KTIR in, SpyreCode out The rest of the post follows the figure from left to right, spending most of its time on the scheduler and then covering the three stages below it more briefly. The Dataflow Scheduler: KTIR → ScheduleIR → DataflowIR A dataflow accelerator is a distributed collection of compute engines and scratchpad memories connected by wide datapaths with FIFOs. It follows a decoupled access-execute design, in which moving data (DMA, scratchpad loads and stores) and computing on it happen on separate engines that run at the same time. On a machine like that, scheduling means building a dataflow pipeline across space and time , deciding which engine performs each step and how the steps overlap with one another. The Dataflow Scheduler does this as an MLIR pass pipeline, and a handful of principles shape how it’s built. It is driven by an architecture description rather than hard-coded for one chip, which we look at more closely below. Every schedule is expressed in a single execution model built from just three constructs: nested scf.for loops, ktdf.pipeline (stages that overlap across iterations) and ktdf.parallel (identical instances that split an iteration space between them), and every analysis and transformation reasons in those terms. Wherever it can, the scheduler leans on upstream MLIR, lowering compute to linalg.generic and fusing it with upstream passes, and using scf for loops and memref for buffers. And throughout, it follows one strategy: start with the most naive correct pipeline, then let each later pass either make it legal on the hardware or make it bigger, in small steps that can be tested on their own. The passes fall into three groups, each with a fixed IR contract at its boundaries, so passes can be added or reordered within a group without disturbing the others. Dataflow Scheduler: three pass groups, one IR contract each At four named checkpoints ( pre_mapping , pre_scheduling , post_scheduling and post_lowering ) the scheduler applies rewrite patterns written in PDL. Those patterns live in the architecture description rather than in the scheduler, which means a device can supply its own lowerings without forking the scheduler. This is where each spyreop intrinsic, such as spyreop.exp or spyreop.gelu , is replaced by the hardware’s instruction template, and where an inner-dimension reduction becomes a SIMD reduction. The scheduler’s intermediate form, ScheduleIR , is the ktdf dialect used alongside linalg , scf and memref . Its vocabulary is small enough to list in full: ktdf construct Meaning ktdf.pipeline [modulo(size: N)] A chain of stages that overlap across iterations; modulo rotates through N copies of its resources (N-buffering) ktdf.stage depends_in(...) depends_out(...) One step of a pipeline, eventually bound to one kind of execution unit ( applicable_units ) ktdf.private Resources private to one pipeline: FIFO slots, scratchpad buffers, tokens !ktdf.token A pure ordering value between stages, with no runtime cost of its own !ktdf.fifo.slot<SRC -> DST, 64xf16> A slot in a hardware FIFO between two units ktdf.data_transfer / ktdf.ind_data_transfer Explicit movement between memories and FIFOs, direct or through an indirect-address buffer ktdf.read_from_fifo / ktdf.write_to_fifo How a compute stage consumes and produces FIFO data ktdf.parallel ... distribute(num_instances = N) Split an iteration space into contiguous blocks over N identical hardware instances ktdf.tiling.reserve_size / derive_size / linearize_index Placeholders for tile sizes chosen later, the current tile’s extent, and the original index The architecture description Everything the scheduler knows about the hardware comes from a single MLIR file written in the ktdf_arch dialect. That file describes the device as a graph. Its nodes are memories, with their kinds and sizes, and execution units, with the features the scheduler cares about: SIMD lane counts per element type, the word sizes and access granularities of load and store units, the depth of each FIFO. Its edges are datapaths, each with a transfer granularity. Groups scope resources the way the hardware does, for example a core that owns a scratchpad along with the load/store and compute units that use it. Here is a trimmed and simplified version of the sample device used in the scheduler’s tests: #L1 = { kind = "L1", size = 1048576 } // 1 MB scratchpad #SFU = { kind = "SFU", ktdf_arch.features = { ktdf_arch.feature.compute, ktdf_arch.feature.simd = { lanes = #ktdf_arch.map<f16 = 64, f32 = 32, i32 = 32> } } } #L1LU_CORE_FIFO = { ktdf_arch.features = { ktdf_arch.feature.queue = { depth = 16, ordered } } } ktdf_arch.device @sample_device { %ddr = memory #DDR group { kind = "core" } share(%ddr) { %l1 = memory #L1 %mnilu = group { kind = "MNILU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // DMA load unit %mnisu = group { kind = "MNISU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // DMA store unit datapath #DDR_MNILU %ddr to %mnilu : memory, exec_unit datapath #MNILU_L1 %mnilu to %l1 : exec_unit, memory %sfu = group { kind = "SFU_Block" } share() { ... } -> exec_unit // compute unit %l1lu = exec_unit #L1LU // scratchpad load unit %l1su = exec_unit #L1SU // scratchpad store unit datapath #L1LU_CORE_FIFO %l1 to %l1lu : memory, exec_unit datapath %l1lu to %sfu : exec_unit, exec_unit ... } patterns ["pre_scheduling"] { ... } // device-specific rewrites, in PDL patterns ["post_scheduling"] { ... } } A kernel refers to its target with a one-line declaration that imports this file and maps KTIR’s memory spaces onto the device’s memories, for example global onto DDR and ct_local onto L1 . From then on, nearly every decision in the pipeline reads something from the description. The SIMD lane count sets the width of the first pipeline. The datapaths form the routing graph that path expansion searches, so the hops a transfer takes are whatever the graph allows. Access granularities, transfer granularities and FIFO depths constrain how each transfer can be shaped. Memory sizes bound what address assignment can place, and therefore which tile sizes fit. And the patterns blocks supply the device’s own lowerings, such as how each spyreop intrinsic expands into the hardware’s instructions, at the scheduler’s checkpoints. Because all of that lives in the description rather than in the passes, retargeting the scheduler means writing a new description, not changing the scheduler. Spyre has its own description, the scheduler’s tests run against the sample device above, and the same passes run unchanged on both. Step 1: Break the kernel into programs A KTIR kernel is a sequence of operations, whereas a Spyre program is a single pipeline configuration loaded onto the device, so the scheduler’s first real decision is where to cut the kernel into separately scheduled programs. The scheduler makes that cut by working backwards from each ktdp.store , through the compute that feeds it, to the ktdp.load s it ultimately depends on. Everything connected that way forms one compute group , a single load → compute → store chain through memory, and a group ends either at a load that belongs to a different group or at any operation with a region, such as a loop or a conditional. Each group then becomes its own nested MLIR module, module @local_schedule_N , while the original kernel turns into an orchestrator that keeps the control flow and address arithmetic and calls the programs in order. items.content: Trustworthy AI / Cybersecurity English 한국어 中文 NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform: A Reference for Continuous In-Silicon Agent Monitoring Secure AI agents with a safety enforcement layer spanning software and hardware. Sep 28, 2026 By John Myers , Alex Watson , Ali Golshan and Ofir Arkin Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA OpenShell provides an open-source secure runtime that executes autonomous AI agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. The NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform combines OpenShell on NVIDIA Vera CPUs with NVIDIA Sentry on BlueField-4 DPUs to create a layered safety architecture. Five core principles guide the platform: verifiable policy, out-of-band enforcement, controlling the path to the model, scaling agent authority with reasoning visibility, and applying a shared responsibility model across labs, enterprises, and hardware providers. NVIDIA Sentry extends monitoring and enforcement into BlueField hardware using NVIDIA DOCA to correlate agent interactions, policy decisions, and tool access for contextual activity records. In NVIDIA Vera Rubin POD systems, BlueField-4 DPUs sit on the node's only path to the model, providing continuous out-of-band observability and real-time policy enforcement at line speed. Next Steps Get started with NVIDIA OpenShell to run agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. Explore the NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform to understand the layered safety architecture for AI agents. Read the technical walkthrough on adding runtime controls to AI agents with NVIDIA OpenShell for implementation details. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more To understand where agentic AI stands today, consider the last seismic shift in technology: the rise of the internet in the 90s. It was new and full of possibilities. You could build a website over a weekend and share it with the world, or chat with someone half way around the world in online chat rooms without long-distance telephone fees. It brought endless opportunity, but also a lot of risk. A website could run code on your machine, steal your sensitive information, or infect your computer with a virus. People loved it anyway. To introduce a layer of trust, the community built things like encrypted connections and a lock icon to know when a connection was safe. The step function change in safety came from a radical security idea at the time: isolate each page in its own sandbox (a tab in a browser) so that a rogue page couldn’t infect the rest of your computer. Amazon, Google, Netflix, and Meta were all built on this trust layer. Security and safety for the internet enabled online commerce, connection, gaming, and so much more that wouldn’t have been possible before. Security and safety didn’t slow the pace of innovation—they allowed it to accelerate. Why build a trusted layer for agents now? Several frontier labs have recently reported versions of the same story: AI agents broke out of the evaluation environments that were meant to contain them and reached systems they never should have been allowed to. Some of the agents even misreported what they did. The security controls in place were insufficient. Over the past few weeks, these reports have led to a serious debate about the pace of agent development. We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community. It was not a single new capability that led to these breakouts. It was a combination of tools, time, and ambiguous instructions, along with a desire for the agent to think “outside the box.” Agent safety requires independent security controls. The internet was not made secure by requiring that web developers promise to be good. It became safe because the browser stopped trusting the code in the web pages explicitly. We need to build this trust layer for agents. Figure 1. NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform Reference Design combines NVIDIA OpenShell on NVIDIA Vera and NVIDIA Sentry on NVIDIA BlueField-4 Lessons learned from building OpenShell NVIDIA OpenShell (Apache 2.0) is an open source secure runtime for executing autonomous AI agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. Building OpenShell over the past year, we have learned that every agent should run in a zero-trust environment out of the box. They need isolation, monitoring, and behavior detection. Today, we are introducing an open stack that makes this possible. In our own research, we’ve watched how agents can go off course. Drift refers to agent actions that depart from the intended task or operating constraints. Drift can occur in response to a policy block, a bug, or a missing tool. Drift can also occur when instructions are ambiguous or agents are left to run for days or weeks to solve hard problems where the first 1,000 things they try do not work. This can’t be trained away while retaining the capability. And here’s the most important lesson: an agent in these circumstances cannot be expected to fully govern its own behavior. Five core principles for building an agent system Policy needs to be verifiable: Before an agent runs, a prover shows that its policy cannot escape the intent of the operator. Enforcement must be out of band: The controls do not live inside, or within reach of the agent. The agent does not need to know it is being watched. The path to the model (the brain) is the control point: An agent cannot act without its next thought. By controlling the path to the model, you own both the best observation point and also the kill switch to interrupt it if you need to. Scale agent authority with the ability to inspect its thinking: The more an agent can do, the more its reasoning needs to be visible. An advantage of open models is that the entire reasoning space and activations are all visible. Applying the shared responsibility model: Labs, enterprises, and hardware providers each own a layer, just like the cloud today. The agent runtime and its policy language need to be open so any provider can plug in. Three open agent safety platform layers A safety platform for AI agents includes the following three layers: The application: What end-users are building. Contains the necessary primitives for mission success: models, harnesses, tools, data, and support scripts and programs. The runtime: Projects the application layer onto infrastructure. Orchestrates the agentic workload onto infrastructure that meets end-user requirements (end-user workstation, edge device, data center) and provides continuous monitoring and real-time policy enforcement and governance. The infrastructure: Concrete hardware resources used to execute agentic workloads. Network calls to upstream services, databases and filesystem access, general purpose compute for tool and code execution, accelerated compute for safety monitoring and increased workload density. A layered foundation for agent safety OpenShell runs each agent in a sandbox and turns the operator’s instructions into a verifiable policy. Operators define which files, networks, tools, processes, and credentials an agent can access. OpenShell checks those limits before the agent runs and enforces them as it works. For organizations that want an additional, independent layer, NVIDIA Sentry extends monitoring and enforcement into NVIDIA BlueField hardware. NVIDIA DOCA makes the BlueField security foundation programmable and connects it with OpenShell policy. It correlates agent interactions, policy decisions, and tool and data access to create a contextual record of agent activity. This helps safety systems identify drift, investigate suspicious behavior, and determine when intervention or deeper analysis is needed. The DOCA gateway complements this behavioral protection with identity governance, continuously verifying each agent’s identity and delegated authority to ensure it operates within its assigned scope. To learn more, refer to the technical walkthrough, Add Runtime Controls to AI Agents with NVIDIA OpenShell . Operating at AI factory scale NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform is optimized to run on NVIDIA Vera CPU- and BlueField DPU-based systems, and is also compatible with other hardware systems. In an NVIDIA Vera Rubin POD , each compute tray includes a BlueField-4 data processing unit on the node’s only path to the model. From this position, BlueField-4 provides continuous, out-of-band observability into agent behavior and enforces security policies in real time at line speed. Isolated from the host and beyond the agent’s reach, it stands as a trusted infrastructure protection layer even when host resources cannot be trusted. Organizations can use it to run NVIDIA Sentry as an optional security layer alongside OpenShell. This foundation allows for resilient security, enforcing the OpenShell policy in silicon, and for the continuous evaluation of the security and integrity of agents. This includes assessing their runtime security and monitoring for any deviation from their designed intent based on a predefined behavioral profile. In this architecture, entire fleets of agents, subagents, tools, and applications all stay inside the boundary with full lineage. For anyone already running on an NVIDIA Vera system with BlueField-4, enabling these protections is just a software update. The agent economy The internet was built on open source, open research, and people who believe that the internet could change the course of humanity. Adding trust turned a great concept into a great economy. The agent economy, and the next set of great companies, is waiting for the same layer. And we can build it the same way, together. NVIDIA is working with industry leaders across the AI ecosystem to build this foundation through NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform . We welcome frontier labs, developers, and infrastructure providers to build with us. Figure 2. Companies across the AI ecosystem—spanning applications, models, infrastructure, chips and energy—support NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform Get started with NVIDIA OpenShell . Ali began his career conducting security and vulnerability research for the U.S. intelligence community, focusing on resilient infrastructure and nation-state cyber defense challenges. Ofir has authored numerous influential research papers and articles, and is a recognized speaker in the information security community. View all posts by Ofir Arkin Comments

The step function change in safety came from a radical security idea at the time: isolate each page in its own sandbox (a tab in a browser) so that a rogue page couldn’t infect the rest of your computer. Some of the agents even misreported what they did. The security controls in place were insufficient. We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community. It was not a single new capability that led to these breakouts. It was a combination of tools, time, and ambiguous instructions, along with a desire for the agent to think “outside the box.” Agent safety requires independent security controls. The internet was not made secure by requiring that web developers promise to be good. It became safe because the browser stopped trusting the code in the web pages explicitly. NVIDIA Open Agent Safety Platform Reference Design combines NVIDIA OpenShell on NVIDIA Vera and NVIDIA Sentry on NVIDIA BlueField-4 Lessons learned from building OpenShell NVIDIA OpenShell (Apache 2.0) is an open source secure runtime for executing autonomous AI agents in sandboxed environments with kernel-level isolation. Building OpenShell over the past year, we have learned that every agent should run in a zero-trust environment out of the box. They need isolation, monitoring, and behavior detection. Today, we are introducing an open stack that makes this possible. In our own research, we’ve watched how agents can go off course. Drift refers to agent actions that depart from the intended task or operating constraints. Drift can occur in response to a policy block, a bug, or a missing tool. Drift can also occur when instructions are ambiguous or agents are left to run for days or weeks to solve hard problems where the first 1,000 things they try do not work. The infrastructure: Concrete hardware resources used to execute agentic workloads.
