items.content: Developer Tools & Techniques Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile Oct 19, 2026 By Sylvain Gugger , Axel Feldmann , Yinuo Liu and Siddharth Samsi Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model that abstracts thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives to automatically target Tensor Cores and other advanced GPU hardware features. Machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented the Mamba-2 state-space model in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize three custom kernels for the forward pass: chunk_cumsum, fwd_pass_state, and compute_out. The chunk_cumsum kernel computes per-token, per-head cumulative sums of the decay term in log-space using ct.cumsum, storing results for reuse by the subsequent kernels. The fwd_pass_state kernel uses ct.mma to execute Tensor Core matrix-multiply operations that advance the hidden state across sequence chunks, applying the jump formula with exponential decay and pre-multiplied operands. The compute_out kernel fuses the carried-state term, the decayed and causally masked interaction matrix, and the skip connection into a single tiled kernel that keeps intermediate matrices in registers and casts to TF32 for Tensor Core execution. Performance optimizations include latency hints for DRAM traffic modeling, operand swapping to route fused operands to Tensor Memory, transposed memory layouts for TMA-friendly access, and an autotuner that searches block size and occupancy parameters for each input shape. Next Steps Get started with cuTile to write high-performance GPU kernels in Python. Explore the cuTile Python documentation for API details and usage guides. Review cuTile Python GitHub repositories for source code and contribution information. Examine sample code to see practical kernel implementations. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them. Overview and prerequisites To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. Sequence modeling computational trade-off Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Mamba-2 architecture The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is: \(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\) y t = c t ⊤ h t + D x t y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t Where: \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\) \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\) \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply: \(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\) This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores. An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just: \(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\) If building a matrix \(B\) of shape ( T, S ) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape ( T, H ) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\): Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula. Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute: \(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\) Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this: Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention). When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection): \(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) With \(M\) the traditional causal mask. Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like: \(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\) Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability. Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe This will translate into three kernels: chunk_cumsum : Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk. fwd_pass_state : Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above. compute_out : Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step. Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk. The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay a and a per-token timestep dt . The effective decay at token t for head h is a[h] * dt[t, h] , and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute exp2 instead of exp , the result is scaled by log2(e) . This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use: ct.bid , ct.load / ct.store , and ct.cumsum . The full kernel is short: @ct.kernel def chunk_cumsum_kernel( a: torch.Tensor, # [num_heads] dt: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] output: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] chunk_size: ct.Constant[int], BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int], ) -> None: chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,), shape=(BLOCK_H,), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype)) The kernel is launched with a grid of (num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size) , the first line determines where you are in the grid using ct.bid . The broadcast product of a_tile (shape [BLOCK_H] ) and dt_tile (shape [1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H] ) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile. ct.cumsum(..., axis=1) then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by fwd_pass_state and compute_out . Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state fwd_pass_state computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that compute_ou t will later project into outputs. At its core, the kernel is a sequential loop over chunks as described earlier. Each kernel launch loads one (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice, hid_tile has a shape [BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE] and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk. head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group hid_tile = ct.load( init_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) In each iteration of the loop, first store the hidden state: num_chunks = ct.cdiv(b.shape[1], chunk_size) for chunk_idx in range(num_chunks): ct.store( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)).astype(hiddens.dtype), ) The rest of the loop loads one chunk of x , b , dt , and decay_cumsum to compute the next chunk’s initial hidden state. As shown previously, the math is: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) ct.extract enables taking the last token from the decay tile loaded (to compute \(G_last\)). Use exp2 instead of exp for performance reasons, as shown previously. ct.mma is the API that will execute the matrix-multiply add while leveraging the Tensor Cores. x_tile = ct.load( x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) dt_tile = ct.load( dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_tile = ct.load( decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_last = ct.extract(d_tile, index=(chunk_size - 1,), shape=(1,)) b_dt_d = b_tile * (dt_tile * ct.exp2(d_last - d_tile))[:, None] hid_tile = ct.exp2(d_last) * hid_tile hid_tile = ct.mma(x_tile.transpose(), b_dt_d.astype(b.dtype), hid_tile) After the final chunk, hid_tile contains the final hidden state, which is stored. During inference this value can be fed back as the next call’s init_state ; during training it is usually discarded. ct.store( final_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)), ) The sequential dependence stays inside a single grid point (program instance), while the independent (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slices run in parallel across the grid. Kernel 3: compute_out compute_out is the final kernel in the forward pass. It takes the per-chunk initial hidden states produced by fwd_pass_state and computes the token outputs, implementing the output equation derived earlier: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) A direct PyTorch implementation would compute these three terms separately, materializing the full [B, n_chunks, chunk_size, chunk_size] interaction matrix C @ B.T in global memory. compute_out fuses them into one tiled kernel and keeps that matrix in registers. Each kernel launch owns one (batch, chunk, head, head_tile) output tile and works in two phases. Phase 1 loops over state tiles, using ct.mma to build the interaction matrix cb_tile = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state term C @ H.T at the same time. chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group cb_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, chunk_size), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) out_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) # Phase 1: build CB = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state output for state_tile_idx in range(state_size // BLOCK_STATE): b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) c_tile = ct.load( c, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) h_tile = ct.load( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) cb_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, b_tile.transpose(), cb_tile) out_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, h_tile.transpose().astype(c_tile.dtype), out_tile) Phase 2 applies the decay and causal mask to cb_tile ( ct.arange and ct.where build the lower-triangular mask M , so no mask tensor is ever materialized) and then adds all of the terms to get the final output tile. Both accumulators start as ct.full register tiles, and the final ct.mma casts to ct.tfloat32 to run through the Tensor Cores at near-FP32 accuracy. # Phase 2: decay + causal mask then final computation d_tile = ct.load(decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) x_tile = ct.load(x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) d_val = ct.load(d, index=(head,), shape=(1,)) cb_tile = cb_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) # pairwise decay idx = ct.arange(chunk_size, dtype=ct.int32) cb_tile = ct.where(idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :], cb_tile, 0.0) # causal mask out_tile = out_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None]) # decay carried state dt_x = dt_tile[:, None] * x_tile out_tile = ct.mma(cb_tile.astype(ct.tfloat32), dt_x.astype(ct.tfloat32), out_tile) out_tile = out_tile + d_val * x_tile # D * x skip ct.store(out, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), tile=out_tile.reshape((1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD)).astype(out.dtype)) As mentioned, while some numerical unstable exponentials are computed in the ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) line (some of those are positive numbers), immediately mask them out so potential overflows don’t end up poisoning the computation. Mamba-2 performance optimization With the Mamba-2 workload defined in the cuTile-Python DSL, several key performance optimizations are introduced: Latency hint: cuTile allows you to annotate ct.load and ct.store operations with latency hints to model DRAM traffic. The compiler leverages these hints to optimize instruction scheduling and pipeline buffer depth. Swap A/B: On the NVIDIA Blackwell fifth-generation Tensor Core, MMA operands are asymmetric: operand A can live in Tensor Memory, but operand B must live in Shared Memory. For an input-fusion pattern like the SIMT-op + Dot-op in fwd_pass_state , the identity \(B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = (AB)^{\mathsf{T}}\) is used to route the fused operand ( b_dt_d ) to operand A, relieving shared-memory contention. GMEM layout: The default strided memory access for decay_cumsum and dt lowers to cache-unfriendly LDG instructions. Transposing to a [batch, head, token] layout ensures contiguous access, enabling the use of TMA. cuTile-Python autotuner: Since performance bottlenecks shift with input shape, no single optimization strategy fits every model configuration. These optimizations are integrated alongside cuTile parameters ( block_size , occupancy) into a unified search space, leveraging cuTile exhaustive_search to automatically find the optimal setup for each input shape. Mamba-2 forward pass performance benchmarks This implementation of the Mamba-2 forward pass kernel is available through TileGym . A complete example is shown below. import torch import tilegym from tests import common from tests.ops.test_mamba2 import Mamba2ProblemSpec tilegym.set_backend("cutile") num_tokens, state_size = 16384, 128 torch.manual_seed(0) spec = Mamba2ProblemSpec(batch_size=4, num_tokens=num_tokens, num_groups=1, num_heads=8, state_size=state_size, head_size=64, chunk_size=128, dtype=torch.bfloat16, state_dtype=torch.float32) fwd_inputs = spec.get_sample_inputs(with_reference=False, with_backward=False) fwd = common.benchmark( lambda: tilegym.ops.mamba2_chunk_forward(**fwd_inputs), use_cupti=True, ) print(f"Forward: {fwd['forward']['median'] * 1000:.2f} us") The performance of the implemented Mamba-2 forward pass was evaluated against an open source implementation of the Mamba-2 kernel written in Triton, under the following software and hardware configurations: Software mamba_ssm 2.3.2.post1 (NVIDIA Dynamo-Triton reference), Triton 3.7.1 cuTile: cuda-tile 1.5.0 TileIR assembler ( tileiras ) 13.4 PyTorch 2.13.0, CUDA 13.3 (Driver and Runtime API, NVCC V13.3.33), Driver 595.58.03 cuda-python / cuda-bindings 13.3.1 Python 3.12.3, Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-107 Hardware Single NVIDIA B300 SXM6, compute capability 10.3 (NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra) 1920 MHz max SM clock, 1100 W power limit, 268 GiB HBM Figure 5. Performance of cuTile Mamba-2 forward pass The results show that the optimized cuTile forward-pass kernels are 1.14x to 1.82x faster, with speedups growing as sequence lengths and state size increases. Note that these are kernel-level speedups only and end-to-end training results will also depend on the backward pass implementations. Learn more NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them. Overview and prerequisites To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. Sequence modeling computational trade-off Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Mamba-2 architecture The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is: \(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\) y t = c t ⊤ h t + D x t y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t Where: \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\) \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\) \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply: \(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\) This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores. An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just: \(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\) If building a matrix \(B\) of shape ( T, S ) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape ( T, H ) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\): Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula. Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute: \(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\) Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this: Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention). When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection): \(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) With \(M\) the traditional causal mask. Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like: \(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\) Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability. Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe This will translate into three kernels: chunk_cumsum : Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk. fwd_pass_state : Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above. compute_out : Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step. Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk. The inputs to this kernel are a per-head scalar decay a and a per-token timestep dt . The effective decay at token t for head h is a[h] * dt[t, h] , and the kernel accumulates that product along the chunk dimension. These cumulative sums are all in log-space and the exponential of them is always taken (or some linear combination of them). Since it’s much cheaper to compute exp2 instead of exp , the result is scaled by log2(e) . This kernel introduces the cuTile primitives that all three kernels use: ct.bid , ct.load / ct.store , and ct.cumsum . The full kernel is short: @ct.kernel def chunk_cumsum_kernel( a: torch.Tensor, # [num_heads] dt: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] output: torch.Tensor, # [batch_size, num_tokens, num_heads] chunk_size: ct.Constant[int], BLOCK_H: ct.Constant[int], ) -> None: chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) a_tile = ct.load(a, index=(head_tile_idx,), shape=(BLOCK_H,), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).astype(ct.float32) d_tile = ct.cumsum(a_tile * dt_tile, axis=1) * LOG2E ct.store(output, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx), tile=d_tile.astype(output.dtype)) The kernel is launched with a grid of (num_chunks, num_head_tiles, batch_size) , the first line determines where you are in the grid using ct.bid . The broadcast product of a_tile (shape [BLOCK_H] ) and dt_tile (shape [1, chunk_size, BLOCK_H] ) gives the effective per-token, per-head decay over the tile. ct.cumsum(..., axis=1) then scans along the intra-chunk token dimension, and the result is stored in the layout expected by fwd_pass_state and compute_out . Kernel 2: fwd_pass_state fwd_pass_state computes the initial hidden state of each chunk and the final hidden state after the last chunk. It does not directly compute the output. Instead, it prepares the carried state that compute_ou t will later project into outputs. At its core, the kernel is a sequential loop over chunks as described earlier. Each kernel launch loads one (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slice of the hidden state, as shown below. Within that slice, hid_tile has a shape [BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE] and will contain a tile of the initial hidden state for each chunk. head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group hid_tile = ct.load( init_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) In each iteration of the loop, first store the hidden state: num_chunks = ct.cdiv(b.shape[1], chunk_size) for chunk_idx in range(num_chunks): ct.store( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)).astype(hiddens.dtype), ) The rest of the loop loads one chunk of x , b , dt , and decay_cumsum to compute the next chunk’s initial hidden state. As shown previously, the math is: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) ct.extract enables taking the last token from the decay tile loaded (to compute \(G_last\)). Use exp2 instead of exp for performance reasons, as shown previously. ct.mma is the API that will execute the matrix-multiply add while leveraging the Tensor Cores. x_tile = ct.load( x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) dt_tile = ct.load( dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_tile = ct.load( decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size,)) d_last = ct.extract(d_tile, index=(chunk_size - 1,), shape=(1,)) b_dt_d = b_tile * (dt_tile * ct.exp2(d_last - d_tile))[:, None] hid_tile = ct.exp2(d_last) * hid_tile hid_tile = ct.mma(x_tile.transpose(), b_dt_d.astype(b.dtype), hid_tile) After the final chunk, hid_tile contains the final hidden state, which is stored. During inference this value can be fed back as the next call’s init_state ; during training it is usually discarded. ct.store( final_state, index=(batch, head, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), tile=hid_tile.reshape((1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)), ) The sequential dependence stays inside a single grid point (program instance), while the independent (batch, head, head_tile, state_tile) slices run in parallel across the grid. Kernel 3: compute_out compute_out is the final kernel in the forward pass. It takes the per-chunk initial hidden states produced by fwd_pass_state and computes the token outputs, implementing the output equation derived earlier: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) A direct PyTorch implementation would compute these three terms separately, materializing the full [B, n_chunks, chunk_size, chunk_size] interaction matrix C @ B.T in global memory. compute_out fuses them into one tiled kernel and keeps that matrix in registers. Each kernel launch owns one (batch, chunk, head, head_tile) output tile and works in two phases. Phase 1 loops over state tiles, using ct.mma to build the interaction matrix cb_tile = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state term C @ H.T at the same time. chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, batch_head = ct.bid(0), ct.bid(1), ct.bid(2) batch = batch_head // x.shape[2] head = batch_head % x.shape[2] group = head // num_heads_per_group cb_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, chunk_size), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) out_tile = ct.full((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD), 0.0, dtype=ct.float32) # Phase 1: build CB = C @ B.T and accumulate the carried-state output for state_tile_idx in range(state_size // BLOCK_STATE): b_tile = ct.load( b, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) c_tile = ct.load( c, index=(batch, chunk_idx, group, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_STATE), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO, ).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_STATE)) h_tile = ct.load( hiddens, index=(batch, head, chunk_idx, head_tile_idx, state_tile_idx), shape=(1, 1, 1, BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE), ).reshape((BLOCK_HEAD, BLOCK_STATE)) cb_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, b_tile.transpose(), cb_tile) out_tile = ct.mma(c_tile, h_tile.transpose().astype(c_tile.dtype), out_tile) Phase 2 applies the decay and causal mask to cb_tile ( ct.arange and ct.where build the lower-triangular mask M , so no mask tensor is ever materialized) and then adds all of the terms to get the final output tile. Both accumulators start as ct.full register tiles, and the final ct.mma casts to ct.tfloat32 to run through the Tensor Cores at near-FP32 accuracy. # Phase 2: decay + causal mask then final computation d_tile = ct.load(decay_cumsum, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) dt_tile = ct.load(dt, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size,)) x_tile = ct.load(x, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), shape=(1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD), padding_mode=ct.PaddingMode.ZERO).reshape((chunk_size, BLOCK_HEAD)) d_val = ct.load(d, index=(head,), shape=(1,)) cb_tile = cb_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) # pairwise decay idx = ct.arange(chunk_size, dtype=ct.int32) cb_tile = ct.where(idx[:, None] >= idx[None, :], cb_tile, 0.0) # causal mask out_tile = out_tile * ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None]) # decay carried state dt_x = dt_tile[:, None] * x_tile out_tile = ct.mma(cb_tile.astype(ct.tfloat32), dt_x.astype(ct.tfloat32), out_tile) out_tile = out_tile + d_val * x_tile # D * x skip ct.store(out, index=(batch, chunk_idx, head, head_tile_idx), tile=out_tile.reshape((1, chunk_size, 1, BLOCK_HEAD)).astype(out.dtype)) As mentioned, while some numerical unstable exponentials are computed in the ct.exp2(d_tile[:, None] - d_tile[None, :]) line (some of those are positive numbers), immediately mask them out so potential overflows don’t end up poisoning the computation. The compiler leverages these hints to optimize instruction scheduling and pipeline buffer depth. For an input-fusion pattern like the SIMT-op + Dot-op in fwd_pass_state , the identity \(B^{\mathsf{T}}A^{\mathsf{T}} = (AB)^{\mathsf{T}}\) is used to route the fused operand ( b_dt_d ) to operand A, relieving shared-memory contention. These optimizations are integrated alongside cuTile parameters ( block_size , occupancy) into a unified search space, leveraging cuTile exhaustive_search to automatically find the optimal setup for each input shape. Mamba-2 forward pass performance benchmarks This implementation of the Mamba-2 forward pass kernel is available through TileGym . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.28601 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Evolving Agent Interfaces Authors: Saaket Agashe , Yuzhe Yang , Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega , Bhuvan Chandra Koduru , Chih-Lun Li , Jiachen Yang , Ang Li , Xin Eric Wang View a PDF of the paper titled Evolving Agent Interfaces, by Saaket Agashe and 7 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents' trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at this https URL . Work done at Simular. eric@simular.ai \uselogo Evolving Agent Interfaces Saaket Agashe Yuzhe Yang Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega Bhuvan Koduru § Chih-Lun Li Jiachen Yang Ang Li Xin Eric Wang Corresponding author: = Abstract Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents’ trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s Figure 1 : Conventional computer-use agents execute tasks through fixed, human-designed interfaces. Agent S4 evolves interfaces as software repositories through experience. A task agent attempts synthetic tasks, and a meta-agent studies its trajectories to construct and refine the repositories. Each repository combines interfaces, such as GUI interactions, file operations and application-specific workflows, with knowledge of when to use them. 1 Introduction We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. — Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson Computer-use agents (CUAs) carry out tasks by observing and acting on digital environments. Their interfaces determine what they can observe and which operations they can request. Current computer-use frameworks focus on GUI interaction, supplemented by dedicated tools ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . These interfaces are designed by humans and fixed before task execution. Even though these interfaces are built specifically for agents, they still depend on human judgments about what those agents need. This practice creates three problems for computer-use. First, it ties progress to manual labor. Computer use is open-ended, and each new family of tasks or model release exposes new failure modes. A human researcher must read trajectories, diagnose failures, and use them to write new primitives, observation formats, or memory mechanisms, and then release the result as a new agent framework with a new preset interface. This loop does not scale with task diversity. Second, a static interface often mismatches the task, and current methods compensate with test-time compute instead of a better interface. For example, an agent may complete a shell task by clicking to open a terminal window, typing commands one character at a time, and reading screenshots of a partly occluded terminal for feedback, when a direct shell interface would be faster and more reliable ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . Additional sampling can raise benchmark scores under such mismatches, but through wasteful and brittle strategies. Third, methods that compose test-time experience into reusable skills or routines inherit the same limit ( Agashe et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Each skill is a composition of the preset observations and actions. Distillation can reorder what the interface allows, but it cannot extend it. These problems arise because the interface is treated as a design decision that humans make before deployment, and not as an object that can be studied and improved from the agent’s own experience. Figure 2 : With Evolving Agent Interfaces built by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 in binary success on the challenging OSWorld V2 benchmark at a small fraction of their cost. Instead, computer-use interfaces should evolve from the agent’s own experience. Therefore, we introduce Agent S4 1 1 1 The name reads as Agent S cientist for (4) Evolving Agent Interfaces an autonomous CUA scientist that studies computer-use agents and builds Evolving Agent Interfaces through population-based evolution. Its output is a repository of mixed interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The task agent’s model and harness remain fixed, with the harness governing model invocation, execution, permissions, and task budgets. The task agent uses candidate repositories of Evolving Agent Interfaces to attempt synthetic tasks, producing trajectories without ground-truth success labels. A meta-agent studies these trajectories and forms hypotheses about how changes to actions, observations, or usage knowledge could help the task agent. It constructs descendants through mutation of one repository or crossover between two. Descendants can add, revise, or remove interfaces and knowledge, and the population retains alternative designs for further development and recombination. To limit specialization to the tasks that motivated these changes, Agent S4 separates the evidence used for construction from that used for selection. The meta-agent receives training trajectories, while validation instructions, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain hidden from it. Validation performance guides parent selection. We evaluate the final selected repository on the full benchmark. The meta-agent never observes any benchmark task while constructing interfaces, and the validation tasks influence only which repositories are selected during evolution. We evaluate Agent S4 on OSWorld V2 ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) and ScienceBoard ( Sun et al., 2025 ) . On the full 108-task OSWorld V2 set, Qwen3.8-27B with the evolved repository reaches 21.3 % 21.3\% binary success, above both GPT-5.5 ( 13.0 % 13.0\% ) and Claude Opus 4.8 ( 20.6 % 20.6\% ) at about 4.3 % 4.3\% and 1.5 % 1.5\% of their respective costs. In a separate evolution run on ScienceBoard, which covers niche scientific applications, the evolved repository reaches a 58.6 % 58.6\% success rate, compared with 41.4 % 41.4\% for the human-designed interface of Qwen CUA. These results show that agents can evolve their own computer-use interfaces from purely synthetic, verifier-free task experience and outperform human-designed interfaces. We compare our setup against evolutionary baselines such as linear evolution and measure the effect of giving the meta-agent a scratch virtual machine to test its evolved interfaces. Finally, we qualitatively compare agents that act through evolved interfaces with agents that use fixed, human-designed interfaces. Our contributions are: • Evolving Agent Interfaces from synthetic, verifier-free experience. We introduce Agent S4, which evolves a repository of interfaces and usage knowledge from synthetic task experience, without success labels or task verifiers, while the task agent’s model and harness stay fixed. Validation tasks the meta-agent never sees decide which repositories to develop further. • Evolving interfaces outperform fixed ones. With a repository of interfaces evolved by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds both GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.8 in binary success on OSWorld V2 at a small fraction of their cost, and improves ScienceBoard success over a fixed-interface agent with the same model. • Analysis of evolved interfaces. Repository and trajectory analyses show that evolved interfaces change both what the agent observes and how it acts, across desktop-wide, application-specific, cross-application and task-specific interfaces. We also compare evolution strategies, with and without a scratch environment for the meta-agent. 2 Problem Formulation We study how the interfaces of a computer-use agent can be evolved from task experience. An agent updating a spreadsheet through screenshots must identify visible cells, enter values, and inspect the display to check the result. A structured interface can expose the relevant rows and formulas, accept a bulk edit, and return the changed values. Both interfaces can achieve the same subgoal ( Coutaz et al., 1995 ) , but they require different decisions and provide different feedback. Their cost and reliability can also differ. Task experience can reveal which operations are missing, which observations are difficult to use, and where a different interface would help. We call reusable interfaces that are constructed and improved from task experience Evolving Agent Interfaces . To make interfaces and knowledge available across tasks, we represent them in a persistent repository R R . It contains executable interfaces and supporting knowledge such as capability descriptions, reusable workflows, configuration, and notes about when and how to use them. Let 𝒟 \mathcal{D} be the target distribution of tasks and A A the agent that uses the repository. Let J ⁡ ( A , R , x ) J(A,R,x) denote the expected task score when A A uses repository R R to attempt task x x . We seek a repository constructed from task experience that maximizes this score across tasks, R ⋆ ∈ arg ⁡ max R ​ 𝔼 x ∼ 𝒟 ​ [ J ⁡ ( A , R , x ) ] . R^{\star}\in\arg\max_{R}\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\!\left[J(A,R,x)\right]. (1) This objective concerns performance beyond the experience used to construct the repository. We next define the agent, interfaces, and interaction process that determine J J . Computer and task. A computer C C has a state s ∈ 𝒮 s\in\mathcal{S} comprising its files, running applications, displays, services, and reachable network endpoints. A task x = ( g , s 0 , V x , B x ) x=(g,s_{0},V_{x},B_{x}) consists of an instruction g g , an initial state s 0 s_{0} , an evaluator V x V_{x} that scores the outcome, and a budget B x B_{x} . Interface. An interface I = ⟨ c I , 𝒜 I , 𝒪 I ⟩ I=\langle c_{I},\mathcal{A}_{I},\mathcal{O}_{I}\rangle connects an agent to one or more parts c I c_{I} of the computer through a language of requests 𝒜 I \mathcal{A}_{I} and a language of observations 𝒪 I \mathcal{O}_{I} . Executing a request can change the state and returns an observation, ( s ′ , o ) ∼ T I ( ⋅ ∣ s , a ) (s^{\prime},o)\sim T_{I}(\cdot\mid s,a) . A GUI interface, for example, accepts clicks and keystrokes and returns screenshots. A shell interface accepts bash commands and returns a string with the requested information, return values or error message. Model, harness, and agent. A model M M is a language model that generates responses and requests conditioned on its input context. A harness H H manages model invocation, request execution, task budgets, permissions P H P_{H} , and preparation of the model’s context, including any context compaction. An agent A = ( M , H ) A=(M,H) is the model operating through this harness. The agent initially has access to a base set of interfaces ℐ \mathcal{I} . The harness executes requests through these interfaces and places the resulting observations in the model’s context. For example, the harness can execute a spreadsheet helper under a time limit and permission boundary. The helper defines the requests for reading or editing cell ranges and the values returned to the agent. The harness governs execution, while the interface specifies the available operations and feedback. Computer use. Computer use is the process through which an agent observes and acts on a computer through available interfaces to accomplish a task. The interaction history h t h_{t} records the interfaces, requests, and observations from earlier steps. At step t t , the agent chooses an interface and a request based on the instruction and this history, with context preparation by H H left implicit, ( I t , a t ) ∼ M ( ⋅ ∣ g , h t , ℐ ) , ( s t + 1 , o t ) ∼ T I t ( ⋅ ∣ s t , a t ) . (I_{t},a_{t})\sim M(\cdot\mid g,h_{t},\mathcal{I}),\qquad(s_{t+1},o_{t})\sim T_{I_{t}}(\cdot\mid s_{t},a_{t}). (2) The available interfaces shape which operations the agent can request and what evidence it receives about their effects. Formally, R = ( ℐ ⁡ ( R ) , K ⁡ ( R ) ) R=(\mathcal{I}(R),K(R)) , where ℐ ⁡ ( R ) \mathcal{I}(R) contains its executable interfaces and K ⁡ ( R ) K(R) its supporting knowledge. The repository supplies interfaces ℐ R = ℐ ∪ ℐ ⁡ ( R ) \mathcal{I}_{R}=\mathcal{I}\cup\mathcal{I}(R) and knowledge that informs the agent’s choices, ( I t , a t ) ∼ M ( ⋅ ∣ g , h t , ℐ R , K ( R ) ) . (I_{t},a_{t})\sim M(\cdot\mid g,h_{t},\mathcal{I}_{R},K(R)). (3) Each attempt is subject to the task budget B x B_{x} and harness permissions P H P_{H} . The score J ⁡ ( A , R , x ) J(A,R,x) averages the evaluator’s score over these interactions. Interface evolution. Interfaces implemented as programs can be revised like any other software. A program can export a material schedule through Blender’s Python API, extract selected rows from a Calc workbook, or return supplier prices gathered through a sequence of browser operations. Each defines its own requests and observations ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2023 ) . Because these interfaces are code, an agent that can read trajectories and write code can redesign them. It can decide which operations to combine, what information to return, and how a result can be checked. We call this process interface evolution . Given a repository R k R_{k} and the trajectories 𝒯 k \mathcal{T}_{k} of the agent using it, an evolution step produces a revised repository, R k + 1 = E ⁡ ( R k , 𝒯 k ) . R_{k+1}=E\!\left(R_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k}\right). (4) Task experience guides each step. Repeated reconstruction of the same calculation across tasks can motivate a reusable operation, and a repeated inability to verify a change can motivate a new observation. Trajectories with the revised repository then provide evidence for further revision. Section 3 instantiates E E with population-based evolution. 3 Agent S4 Figure 3 : Agent S4 turns task experience into an evolving repository of interfaces and knowledge. Starting from parents selected by held-out validation, the meta-agent studies their task trajectories to identify limitations, then revises one repository through mutation or combines ideas from two through crossover. Task agents then use the descendant to produce trajectories on synthetic tasks and a separate score on held-out validation tasks. Each descendant joins the population alongside its parents, allowing earlier designs to be revisited and recombined over successive iterations. Agent S4 builds Evolving Agent Interfaces and usage knowledge through population-based evolution of repositories, keeping the task agent’s model M M and harness H H fixed. Each iteration selects parents from a population, constructs a descendant through mutation or crossover, evaluates it, and adds it to the population while retaining its parents (Figure 3 ). Training experience guides the repository changes, and held-out validation guides subsequent selection. This optimizes Equation 1 for the fixed task agent A A . Algorithm 1 gives the procedure. 3.1 Population and selection The population contains repository variants, each with its own interfaces and knowledge. We initialize ℛ 0 = { R 0 } \mathcal{R}_{0}=\{R_{0}\} from a seed repository (Appendix A.2 ) and evaluate it to obtain training trajectories and a validation score. These records are retained with each candidate as the population grows. At each step, an operator schedule chooses mutation or crossover. Mutation requires one parent, and crossover requires two distinct parents. For each parent, binary tournament selection draws two eligible variants uniformly and chooses the one with the higher validation score. A sole eligible candidate is selected directly. For crossover, the first selected parent is excluded from the second selection. The selected repositories and their saved training trajectories provide the starting point for the next descendant. 3.2 Mutation and crossover The meta-agent A meta = ( M meta , H meta ) A_{\mathrm{meta}}=(M_{\mathrm{meta}},H_{\mathrm{meta}}) constructs descendants using a fixed model and harness. Work done at Simular. eric@simular.ai \uselogo Evolving Agent Interfaces Saaket Agashe Yuzhe Yang Gonzalo Gonzalez-Pumariega Bhuvan Koduru § Chih-Lun Li Jiachen Yang Ang Li Xin Eric Wang Corresponding author: = Abstract Computer-use agents are limited by the interfaces humans give them. An agent may type a spreadsheet cell by cell when a single line of code would do, or print all two thousand lines of a file through a shell to find one function. Both the interfaces and the knowledge of when to use each are built by hand, which cannot keep pace with new applications, workflows, and models. We argue that interface design should itself be an agent capability. We introduce Agent S4, an autonomous computer-use scientist that builds Evolving Agent Interfaces from task experience. A meta-agent examines task agents’ trajectories on synthetic training tasks, without success labels, and constructs and revises interfaces and usage knowledge in a repository. Population-based evolution then selects which repositories to develop further by their performance on validation tasks the meta-agent never sees, favoring changes that generalize beyond the seen tasks. On OSWorld V2, Agent S4, with Qwen3.8-27B and the evolved repository of interfaces, sets a new state of the art in open-source computer-use agents, reaching 21.3% binary score, 3.8 times the same model with fixed interfaces. This is above both GPT-5.5 (13.0%) and Claude Opus 4.8 (20.6%), at about 4.3% and 1.5% of their respective costs. On ScienceBoard, the evolved interfaces improve the success rate from 41.4% to 58.6% with the same model. These results suggest that useful interfaces can be evolved from experience, making autonomous interface design a source of improvement complementary to advances in models and harnesses. We open-source our code at https://github.com/simular-ai/agent-s Figure 1 : Conventional computer-use agents execute tasks through fixed, human-designed interfaces. Agent S4 evolves interfaces as software repositories through experience. A task agent attempts synthetic tasks, and a meta-agent studies its trajectories to construct and refine the repositories. Each repository combines interfaces, such as GUI interactions, file operations and application-specific workflows, with knowledge of when to use them. 1 Introduction We want AI agents that can discover like we can, not which contain what we have discovered. — Richard S. Sutton, The Bitter Lesson Computer-use agents (CUAs) carry out tasks by observing and acting on digital environments. Their interfaces determine what they can observe and which operations they can request. Current computer-use frameworks focus on GUI interaction, supplemented by dedicated tools ( Xie et al., 2024 ; Zhou et al., 2024 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) . These interfaces are designed by humans and fixed before task execution. Even though these interfaces are built specifically for agents, they still depend on human judgments about what those agents need. This practice creates three problems for computer-use. First, it ties progress to manual labor. Computer use is open-ended, and each new family of tasks or model release exposes new failure modes. A human researcher must read trajectories, diagnose failures, and use them to write new primitives, observation formats, or memory mechanisms, and then release the result as a new agent framework with a new preset interface. This loop does not scale with task diversity. Second, a static interface often mismatches the task, and current methods compensate with test-time compute instead of a better interface. For example, an agent may complete a shell task by clicking to open a terminal window, typing commands one character at a time, and reading screenshots of a partly occluded terminal for feedback, when a direct shell interface would be faster and more reliable ( Yuan et al., 2026 ; Jia et al., 2026 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) . Additional sampling can raise benchmark scores under such mismatches, but through wasteful and brittle strategies. Third, methods that compose test-time experience into reusable skills or routines inherit the same limit ( Agashe et al., 2025a ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . Each skill is a composition of the preset observations and actions. Distillation can reorder what the interface allows, but it cannot extend it. These problems arise because the interface is treated as a design decision that humans make before deployment, and not as an object that can be studied and improved from the agent’s own experience. Figure 2 : With Evolving Agent Interfaces built by Agent S4, Qwen3.8-27B exceeds GPT-5.5 and Opus 4.8 in binary success on the challenging OSWorld V2 benchmark at a small fraction of their cost. Instead, computer-use interfaces should evolve from the agent’s own experience. Therefore, we introduce Agent S4 1 1 1 The name reads as Agent S cientist for (4) Evolving Agent Interfaces an autonomous CUA scientist that studies computer-use agents and builds Evolving Agent Interfaces through population-based evolution. Its output is a repository of mixed interfaces and knowledge about when and how to use them. The task agent’s model and harness remain fixed, with the harness governing model invocation, execution, permissions, and task budgets. The task agent uses candidate repositories of Evolving Agent Interfaces to attempt synthetic tasks, producing trajectories without ground-truth success labels. A meta-agent studies these trajectories and forms hypotheses about how changes to actions, observations, or usage knowledge could help the task agent. It constructs descendants through mutation of one repository or crossover between two. Descendants can add, revise, or remove interfaces and knowledge, and the population retains alternative designs for further development and recombination. To limit specialization to the tasks that motivated these changes, Agent S4 separates the evidence used for construction from that used for selection. The meta-agent receives training trajectories, while validation instructions, trajectories, diagnostics, and scores remain hidden from it. Validation performance guides parent selection. We evaluate the final selected repository on the full benchmark. The meta-agent never observes any benchmark task while constructing interfaces, and the validation tasks influence only which repositories are selected during evolution. We evaluate Agent S4 on OSWorld V2 ( Yuan et al., 2026 ) and ScienceBoard ( Sun et al., 2025 ) .
