items.content: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether they respond like a specific student, and whether they update after tutor guidance Across chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics, StudentSim outperforms leading baselines and provides a useful feedback signal for training an AI tutor In research settings, teams are exploring how AI-powered tutoring systems can help explain a math problem, suggest an edit to a writing assignment, or guide a learner through a chess position. Yet the quality of teaching cannot be measured only from the tutor’s answer. A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student. Did the student correct the original mistake? Did the hint help them reason toward the answer, or did it give away too much? Would a different student need a different kind of support? In today’s AI tutor research, answering these questions often requires real learner studies. Those studies are valuable, but they are slow and costly to run, which makes it hard to use student feedback during fast model iteration. StudentSim is an AI system that creates personalized simulators of individual students, modeling how they answer questions and how their answers change after receiving a tutor’s guidance. The goal is to make student feedback more available during AI tutor development. This research also introduces StudentSimEval, a benchmark and evaluation protocol spanning chess, second-language English writing, and mathematics. Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. Figure 1: AI tutors need feedback from students to improve. Student simulators can approximate part of that feedback during research-stage training and evaluation. They provide an early-stage research signal, not a replacement for testing with real learners. Measuring what a student simulator needs to do A simple way to build a student simulator is to ask a large language model to role-play a learner. For example, a prompt might say, “You are an elementary-school student who struggles with math.” The model can change its tone and express uncertainty. The harder part is preserving the learner’s actual ability boundary. A model may speak in a young student’s voice while still relying on knowledge and reasoning far beyond that student’s level. For training an AI tutor, this can produce misleading feedback: the tutor may appear effective because the simulated student is too capable. Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation. Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits. Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input. They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question. StudentSim defines the target through two dimensions inspired by education research. Educators often distinguish what a learner can do independently from what they can do with support. Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development captures this gap between current independent performance and performance with guidance. StudentSim turns this idea into two evaluation goals. Behavioral fidelity measures whether a simulator matches a specific student’s recorded responses on held-out problems. Guidance responsiveness measures whether the simulator updates its response after reading tutor guidance. Figure 2: StudentSimEval evaluates whether a simulator matches a student’s independent behavior and whether it responds to guidance. These two goals are complementary. A simulator that only matches past student behavior may be useful for prediction, but it does not show whether a teaching intervention helped. A simulator that always follows the tutor may respond fluently, but it may fail to represent a particular student’s strengths, weaknesses, and likely mistakes. AI tutor training needs both signals: the learner’s starting point and how guidance affects the learner’s performance. Training personalized simulators from sparse student records StudentSimEval is built entirely from publicly available learner datasets that are released for research use with de-identified records. The records carry no personally identifying information, and each personalized simulator is trained only on the de-identified records of the student it represents. Real student data is often sparse at the individual level. A learner may contribute only a small number of essays, answers, or interactions. Training a separate simulator from scratch for each student would risk overfitting and would require each model to relearn common patterns in the domain. StudentSim uses a two-stage training pipeline. In the first stage, the model trains on records pooled across many students in the same domain. This stage learns common response formats, common errors, and common ways students revise after guidance. In the second stage, the model is specialized on one student’s own records, producing a personalized simulator for that student. Figure 3: StudentSim first learns shared student behavior from pooled records, then adapts to each student’s own data. The evaluation covers three domains with different response types. In chess, the simulator predicts a player’s next move and how that player may revise after coaching. In second-language English writing, it generates essays with error patterns matching a learner and predicts corrections after teacher feedback. In mathematics, it predicts a student’s multiple-choice answer and whether the student updates after an explanation. Across these domains, StudentSimEval uses the same principle: compare all methods on the same per-student training records and the same held-out evaluation records. StudentSim outperforms leading baselines across the three domains. In chess, for example, StudentSim reaches behavioral fidelity of 0.5150 and guidance responsiveness of 0.9067. GPT-5.4 reaches 0.2316 and 0.7186, respectively. Maia2, a chess-specific human move prediction model, reaches 0.4535 and 0.2721. The comparison illustrates the difference between the baseline families: GPT-5.4 can respond to guidance but does not reliably match a specific student’s behavior, while Maia2 predicts human chess moves more closely but lacks a natural-language guidance pathway. Figure 4: In chess, StudentSim improves both behavioral fidelity and guidance responsiveness compared with leading baselines. Using simulated feedback to improve AI tutors The research also tests whether a trained student simulator can provide feedback for tutor optimization. In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance. The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move. The reward is based on the improvement in move quality from the student’s previous move to the simulator’s revised move, using Stockfish as an independent chess engine signal. Figure 5: StudentSim can provide feedback during AI tutor reinforcement learning by estimating how a student response changes after guidance. The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source. All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup. Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition. The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions. The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition. It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization. The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors. Looking ahead StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research. Human studies remain essential for measuring learning outcomes, safety, usability, and classroom fit. The role of student simulators is earlier in the development process: they can help researchers test tutor strategies, compare models, and refine training signals before moving to more expensive studies with real students. The broader direction is to build AI tutor systems that learn from student reactions, not only from expert-written explanations or static correctness labels. StudentSim shows one path: use real learning records to train personalized simulators, evaluate those simulators on both independent behavior and response to guidance, and use them as scalable feedback sources for tutor training. Future work can extend this approach to longer learning trajectories, additional subjects, richer student profiles, and studies that connect simulated feedback with real learning outcomes. The paper and the StudentSim training and evaluation code, including the StudentSimEval protocol, are publicly available. items.content: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. PODCAST SERIES The AI Revolution in Medicine, Revisited Join Microsoft’s Peter Lee on a journey to discover how AI is impacting healthcare and what it means for the future of medicine. Listen now Opens in a new tab More than a decade of work For more than a decade, Microsoft Research has worked on making zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing practical. Early research followed two approaches, both practical only for small programs. The first (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) lets a verifier check a long computation through a short conversation with the prover using a technique called the sum-check protocol (opens in new tab) , but this applied only to computations with a particular layered structure. The second (opens in new tab) (opens in new tab) used elliptic-curve cryptography to create very small proofs for almost any computation. But this requires a one-time trusted setup involving secret information which, if leaked, could allow anyone to forge proofs. This approach is also vulnerable to quantum computers. In 2019, a new zero-knowledge proof system called Spartan returned to the sum-check approach and made it work for general-purpose programs without a trusted setup. Spartan can also be instantiated with different cryptographic building blocks. That flexibility is what later allowed the proof system to be built on hash functions alone. A sequence of results then filled in the remaining pieces: Phalanx (opens in new tab) , in 2021, showed how to exploit repetition, such as a processor running the same instruction cycle on every step, to prove computations an order of magnitude faster than Spartan. Magnetar’s processor description is built on this idea. Nova (opens in new tab) , HyperNova (opens in new tab) , NeutronNova (opens in new tab) , Neo and SuperNeo (opens in new tab) showed that stopping Spartan’s proving early, and folding the partial results together, makes it practical to prove computations of any size at far lower cost. Brakedown (opens in new tab) , in 2021, introduced a fast hash-based commitment scheme and combined it with Spartan, giving the first Spartan variant whose security rests on standard hash functions. Spice (opens in new tab) , Lasso (opens in new tab) , Nebula (opens in new tab) , and then Twist and Shout (opens in new tab) made the memory operations at the heart of a general-purpose processor inexpensive to prove, and Jolt (opens in new tab) showed that combining them with Spartan can efficiently prove the execution of a complete processor. Earlier this year, Vega (opens in new tab) applied this line of work to digital identity, proving facts from a government credential in under a tenth of a second . More recently, BinarySpartan (opens in new tab) brought Spartan to binary fields, where a processor’s logic and standard hash functions can be efficiently expressed. BinarySpartan also relies on Ligerito (opens in new tab) , a Brakedown-style commitment scheme with much shorter proofs, and on ring switching (opens in new tab) , which makes it efficient to commit to vectors of bits. Each of these solved a piece of the problem. Magnetar is where the pieces come together. Magnetar Magnetar is a zero-knowledge virtual machine, or zkVM, and it makes major progress on all three challenges at once. Figure 1. Magnetar proves a program’s execution and returns a small proof that anyone can check, with security resting only on standard hash functions. It is general-purpose. Magnetar proves the execution of RISC-V, an open processor architecture with mature compilers for every mainstream language. A developer writes a program in Rust, Go, or C, compiles it as usual, and Magnetar proves it as written. Consider what this means in practice. A business policy, a data pipeline, or an interpreter for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) is just a program, and the engineers who already maintain it can prove their executions exactly as written. As a result, proving stops being a specialist activity. It is faster than prior systems in the same class. Magnetar proves 7.2 to 8.7 million processor instructions per second on a laptop. Across 15 benchmark programs, from cryptographic hashing to token transfers inside a small EVM interpreter, it is 10 to 39 times faster on average than the fastest existing zkVMs on the same machine, and more than 300 times faster than two others on a token-transfer benchmark. An optimized Magnetar proves 9.5–12.8 million cycles per second, which increases each speedup reported here by about 1.3×. Its proofs verify in about 12 milliseconds. Its security rests on standard cryptography. Magnetar depends on a standard hash function such as SHA-256 or SHA-3, the same primitives that already protect every organization’s systems. It requires no elliptic curves, no lattices, no special-purpose hash functions, no trusted setup, and no unproven conjecture about error-correcting codes. Hash functions are the most thoroughly studied primitives in the cryptographic toolkit, and they are the basis of the stateless hash-based signatures that NIST standardized as its own conservative post-quantum option. For a system that must still be trustworthy in many decades to come, relying only on standard hash functions removes a cryptographic migration from the roadmap. The same design decision pays a second dividend. Checking a Magnetar proof consists mostly of evaluating standard hash functions and binary-field arithmetic, which are exactly the operations Magnetar proves efficiently. Verifying a proof is therefore an ordinary workload for it. This is what allows Magnetar to prove computations of any size, by proving them in pieces and then combining the pieces. This also allows Magnetar to prove a long-running system such as a ledger or a blockchain. The technical paper gives the full design, security analysis, and measurements. Looking ahead Magnetar advances zero-knowledge proofs and verifiable computing to a stage where they can be built on the cryptography that organizations already trust, at speeds that make it usable, by engineers who write normal code. Magnetar enables a future where cryptographic proofs are a routine output of computation. We expect that technology leaders will stop asking whether proofs of execution are practical and focus instead on which results would they prefer to verify rather than taking on trust . If you’re interested in exploring how zero-knowledge proofs can support your use case, we’d love to hear from you (opens in new tab) . items.raw_text: At a glance A new form of computing . Zero-knowledge proofs let you run a workload and receive, alongside the result, a short proof that the program ran correctly. Anyone can check the proof in milliseconds, without rerunning the program, without trusting whoever ran it, and without needing data on which the program was run. Three grand challenges have stood in the way of broad adoption : making proofs fast enough to produce, making them available to normal programs without cryptographic expertise, and resting them on cryptography that will still be trusted many decades from now. Magnetar makes major progress on all three challenges. It proves programs written in Rust, Go, or C, runs 10 to 39 times faster on average than the prior fastest comparable systems, and rests its security only on standard hash functions. It is the latest result of more than a decade of research at Microsoft Research on making zero-knowledge proofs practical. A new form of computing Every result a computer produces comes with an implicit question: did the program run as claimed and produce correct outputs? Today, answering that question often requires a degree of trust alongside verification. We trust the operator, the vendor, the counterparty, or the agent, and we rely on contracts, audits, and logs to establish that trust. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a fundamentally different approach to establishing trust. A program runs, and along with its output it produces a short proof, a cryptographic certificate that this program, on these inputs, produced this output. The proof is small and fast to check. Whoever receives it can confirm the result in milliseconds without rerunning the program, and can pass the proof on to anyone else who needs the same assurance. With the zero-knowledge property, the proof also reveals nothing about inputs that should stay private. This changes what correctness means in the real world. A result no longer has to be trusted because of who produced it. It can be checked because of what accompanies it. An AI agent acting on someone’s behalf could attach a proof that each action complied with the policy it was given. Regulated financial institutions could prove that transactions were processed correctly without making their transactions public. These become possible once producing a proof is as routine as running the program. Three grand challenges Zero-knowledge proofs were invented in the 1980s, and the ideas behind proving program execution have been around nearly as long. What has kept them from becoming a general tool is three challenges that have resisted being solved at the same time. Efficiency . Producing a proof has historically taken millions of times more computation than running the program itself. Years of research have brought that overhead down, but the fastest systems have achieved their speed by making compromises elsewhere. Generality and usability. Many proof systems require developers to manually rewrite their program as a cryptographic circuit, which is a fixed arithmetic description of that exact computation. This takes months. Every change to the application means a new circuit, and the translation is itself a frequent source of security bugs. A general-purpose alternative is to prove the execution of an ordinary processor, so that any compiled program can be proven as written. Until recently, that generality came at a steep cost in speed or security. Security. A proof is only as strong as the cryptography beneath it. Many proof systems rest on elliptic curves, which can be broken by a sufficiently powerful quantum computer. Microsoft is addressing this problem with its Quantum Safe Program, which will move its products and services to post-quantum cryptography, a goal it recently accelerated to 2029 . Post-quantum proof systems already exist, but some rest on lattice assumptions, and most rest on new cryptographic functions invented to reduce the cost of proving. These new cryptographic functions have not faced the decades of scrutiny given to the cryptography protecting today’s internet, and some rest on mathematical conjectures about error-correcting codes that have not been proven. They have bought their speed with strong assumptions. items.title: Called to serve: Tech, research, and positive impact
items.summary: Video playback requires cookie consent In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. Subscribe to the Micros
items.content: Video playback requires cookie consent In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast : Apple Podcasts Email Android Spotify RSS Feed Transcript [MUSIC] CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity. You know, I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so I think that that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts. [THEME MUSIC] STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast , where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI. [MUSIC ENDS] WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. I’m Weishung Liu, a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research, and today I’m talking to Dr. Christopher White, who leads Microsoft Research’s Catalyst Lab . Chris has one of those careers that sounds almost made up: a Harvard postdoc, on-the-ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan, a DARPA program manager, a dark web search pioneer, and a public-good technologist. And his work has been featured in Popular Science (opens in new tab) as well as recognized with honors, including the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons (opens in new tab) . But what I’m most interested in today is the person behind that résumé. How someone who has seen some of the worst as part of his work still comes to the office with a smile and a commitment to building tools that make the world better. Chris, thanks for joining me. WHITE: Thanks for having me, Wei. Nice to see you. LIU: Yeah, good to see you, too. And so let’s get started. So I’ve known you for, I think, maybe around five or maybe six years, and now I work with you in Catalyst Lab. I love your story, and when I tell people about you, I say that you lead the newly formed Cat Lab, or Catalyst Lab, in Microsoft Research, you were a senior executive at DARPA, and you are married to an incredibly accomplished woman and scholar. And I personally think that your life story would make a very watchable Hollywood film. So when you tell your own story, though, where do you start? WHITE: Well, you start from where you are. And where I am today is leading research at Microsoft during a period of great fear and hope about changing technology and society. LIU: But, like, that’s now. There’s clearly lots of time from now into before, you know, the before times. So, like, tell me a little bit about the before times. Like, where were you at—I think you grew up in Oklahoma maybe. Tell me about that. Tell me about Chris White, the child. WHITE: Well, I was nerdy. I was a nerdy Eagle Scout. [LAUGHTER] I liked to build my own computers and have local area network [LAN] parties with my friends. But I also really liked being outside. I liked being in nature and camping and rock climbing. Those were all important to me. LIU: OK, you mentioned LAN parties. Tell me about … what did we play with our friends? WHITE: Well, you know, we played everything. I preferred playing sports games, but I lost a lot of the other ones. LIU: [LAUGHS] Wait, so you played like LAN party sports games, like, in basements? Like, with your … were we all in the same … ? WHITE: Yeah. Attics. It was attics. Yeah, not basements. [LAUGHTER] Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everybody had to bring their own computer or bring their own Ethernet cable. And the more that you had your own machine that was higher powered, the better you were going to play. LIU: So did you have the best machine? WHITE: I had the best machine. I built the best machine. Until someone built a better machine. But it was the best for a while. And I had a budget for it. And my family didn’t understand that the budget also included two giant speakers, like the size of a computer tower, like subwoofer speakers. They didn’t know that was part of the computer building process. But it turns out that excellent audio-visual is a critical part of a well-functioning machine. LIU: I love it. But, OK, we’re going to focus a little bit … continue focusing on childhood. So you mentioned nerdy kid, which means—I’m going to generalize here—debate team or math competition team or chess team? WHITE: Oh, it was the debate team. Yeah. Debate was a really wonderful activity. It taught me how to understand many sides of an issue and taught me how to think about evidence and research in that way. LIU: So, Chris, take me back again. Like, we’re talking a little bit about Oklahoma, and, you know, at some point, you chose researcher. Like, I—for example—when I was a kid, I was convinced I would be an architect. I am not an architect as you can see. But did you always think you were going to be a researcher? Was there an epiphany there? Like … or was it always kind of like a slow hunch that you were going to pursue research as a career? WHITE: Yeah, I kind of always felt like it. You know, as I was applying for school, those were the kinds of jobs I was interested in. You know, the kinds of things that you do, you know, once you finish degrees that have research in them. Those were the people, when I visited their work, I was inspired by. The people that were discovering, you know, that were inventing, that were innovating, that were … they’re pushing the boundaries that were kind of in that unknown, you know, space and making sense of it. And so I’ve always had that curiosity, you know, and that approach to discovery. And so as I increased my education, it just changed the nature of what research meant and the ways in which I imagined that process evolving. LIU: Was a doctorate always on the cards then? Or did that come, like, as you were in college and then gradually learned and thought, you know, I could keep going? WHITE: Yeah, you know, I didn’t know about doctorates really when I went to college. I wasn’t as familiar with higher education. And so I knew that I wanted, you know, advanced degrees. And I knew that I wanted more than was being taught in the undergraduate level. But I didn’t know, you know, for example, that when you apply to PhD programs, that often you get paid to go. You know, you get admitted and you get a stipend. You know, I was familiar with law and medicine and that you take out loans and you have to do it this way. And so for me, it was a surprise to know that I could apply to PhD programs directly from college. And from then, I just really was excited, you know, that I could explore different universities and different areas of focus and build on, you know, strong technical foundations of math and science and physics. And it was really amazing mentors that helped me and opened doors and inspired me. You know, mentors at Oklahoma State University, Johns Hopkins, and Harvard, really people that took their time and helped me. I’m really grateful for my teachers. LIU: So let’s talk about your first mentor of your life, and I’m going to assume … Dad ? WHITE: Yeah, Dad’s a big influence. LIU: OK, Dad’s a big influence. And so we’re going to, I’m going to go down this path. So Catalyst Lab landed a huge commitment from our executive, kind of, leadership team on a project that has been, I think, like a decade in the making. And then … so we all, I know we all came together on a call. We’re like, “Wow, let’s debrief. Let’s talk about it.” Like, oh, energy’s up. And then at the very end of the meeting, you said, “OK, now I’m going to go clean some toilets.” WHITE: [LAUGHS] Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. LIU: And I think all of us kind of thought, like, wha-what does that mean? So before we get kind of more into the specifics of mentorship and the, like, follow-on in your career, what— please tell me —does cleaning toilets have to do with success? WHITE: Well, you know, like I said, Dad’s a big influence, and he taught me so many things, and he taught me about respecting people. And most importantly, he taught me about humility and service. And so his way of making sure I understood that was every time something really good happened to me, he’d remind me to go clean some toilets and, sort of, embody that. And so I did. I did it last weekend actually. I went to a community event and volunteered to do bathroom clean. LIU: Is this like … are you … so in, like, the household chores, are you, like, the bathroom cleaner? Like, is this just always your job when we’re dividing up chores in the house? WHITE: No, no, no. We trade off, and also we have a complicated household, and so we have a lot of help that also helps with cleaning. And so this is something that I choose to do, especially if I can do it in a community context, because it again reminds me, you know, about humility and about service and of respect for other people and other jobs. LIU: So I think this … there’s some Eagle Scout vibes that I’m getting from here, as well, based on sort of humility and service. What is the Boy Scout badge you are most proud of? WHITE: Oh, that’s really hard. Each badge is something that you earn, including the Eagle Scout badge. And the Eagle Scout badge for me was maybe the most difficult to earn because it requires an Eagle project. And I was really close to my Eagle project. I was, I was … had it set up and it was ready to go. And it was in this church in downtown Oklahoma City in 1995. And right as I was about to do this project, the Murrah Building blew up in a terrorist incident (opens in new tab) , … LIU: Whoa. WHITE: … and it blew up part of the church. And, therefore, my Eagle project was not realistic, and it was not a priority, and it got shelved. And it took me several years after that to then come back to plan and execute an ambitious Eagle project right before I turned 18. And so that badge, … LIU: Wow. WHITE: … you know, completing the project, overcoming significant setbacks, including being a teenager and having other interests, to come through and finish it, I’m really proud of finishing it. LIU: That’s awesome. So you … so that was, so there were a few years then in between when you ideated, had the idea for the project, and then … I appreciate the story around resilience because of when you completed the project. Like, what is the biggest takeaway that you took from there? Like what is that big lesson? You turned 18, you finished it, you celebrate. Actually, you know, maybe I’ll ask you, how did you celebrate? WHITE: Oh, with my family. You know, the Boy Scouts is a long process. It’s many years, many kinds of roles, many kinds of learning, and to finish it—I finished it with another of my fellow scouts that had been together for a long time. And so our families, we had a ceremony, and it was something we could celebrate. And every time I think about it, I think about the things that you keep repeating when you attend the scout things, like the motto, “being prepared,” and the, kind of, laws about being respectful and courteous. And those are things that continue to be, you know, principles that influence my priorities and also inspire me and help me in my job. LIU: Before we get to your job then, we’re going to talk about this interim period where I’ll just say you chose to go to war and a few other things in between. Let’s jump to 2010, when you joined DARPA, which is the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, within the Department of War. And then, I think, very quickly afterwards you were sent to Afghanistan to help implement a new approach to wartime analysis. And then … but before that, I think you were a Harvard postdoc, and you had actually mentioned it was a mentor who encouraged you to attend a meeting with DARPA that resulted in this course change. And so now I’m super curious, how did this conversation happen where you were, you know, promising Harvard postdoc, which became a mentor going, “Hey, there’s something happening. You should go attend.” Like, what happened there? WHITE: Yeah. DARPA invests taxpayer money, and they have a record of really creating innovations, massive innovations (opens in new tab) . You know, the internet, GPS, stealth, UAVs. And at the time, there was different ways of building programs, and one of the kind of tested ways was to bring together different fields of expertise. And so we were in wartime in Afghanistan. DARPA was not involved very much. And there was a question: you know, could we bring together social scientists with math people, computer science and defense experts, and together could they help us make sense of what’s happening in the data? Could that be useful to prevent violence and to protect our soldiers? And it was an experiment because it required all these different areas of expertise coming together—from sensors through analysis through social behavior—and a culture change. And so the summer was a Skunk Works to understand, was there something to contribute? And at the end of it, they asked me, they said, “Well, you know, do you believe in your work?” And I was like, “Yeah.” You know, like, “Well, do you … can you prove it? You know, can you go see if it can help protect our soldiers and help prevent violence?” And so they asked me to be of service, and I said yeah. And it was something that I was really unprepared for. I was supposed to go for nine days the first time, and on the third day, I got a battlefield promotion and was put in charge and then ended up staying for 90 days and then went back a few times after that even. And so, you know, our work was towards … oriented towards protecting, you know, soldiers and toward preventing violence and using AI and advanced technology to do that. And it was a, really, a big opportunity. LIU: So you attended a meeting, you contributed some work, and then, you know, “Do you believe in your work? Prove it.” What was the time frame between, you know, like, showing up at meeting, participating in some of the research before, like, “prove it”? Was it years, or was it months? WHITE: The … no, no, the … so the Skunk Works was a summer. It was like, you know, 40 days of, kind of, like focused effort. But at the end of it, I was expecting to go back to Harvard and continue my postdoc. But instead, you know, they sat us down; they said, “Look, you know, we think this can make a difference. You know, do you think so?” And when I said yeah, from then to getting over there was like a week. It was an extremely fast … LIU: What? WHITE: … turnaround. You know, sending researchers—even having a presence from DARPA—in the war zone, (opens in new tab) it was new. And the idea was there could be a difference made because technology was advancing quickly. And that meant that many of the mechanisms in place for other ways of getting prepared were not available. And there was a bunch of training, like crash courses in training on what to do in certain situations, how things work, you know, how to handle yourself in different ways. But it was … it was very brief. And so there wasn’t a lot of preparation because also we were planning to be there for nine days. But because there was an opportunity to do something good, that extended, and there was a lot of learning on the job and a lot of support in theater, a lot of people really willing to help us because we were helping them. I’m not going to focus too much on your time in Afghanistan because that was covered really well in a Popular Science article. But I do have to ask, can you tell me the origin story of the nickname Dr. Spaghetti Man? WHITE: [LAUGHS] Sure. Sure. You know, I’m a long-time yoga practitioner. You know, 20-plus years. It’s how I keep myself calibrated. And in Kabul, I was practicing yoga in the gym, and all these people were staring at me. You know, they were staring at me before their … they had a class; they had, like, a combatives class, a kind of different judo-mixed-martial-arts class. And, you know, I had a little bit of training, and so after a couple of times, I decided I’d just join in. And I joined in, and I won a lot. I won a lot of the matches. He told everyone, you know, that this, like, lanky spaghetti guy, you know, like, got out of things and beat him, and he did it in such a way that everyone in the building knew. WHITE: I mean, everyone that came to that class was game, you know. And I didn’t, you know, I couldn’t beat everybody, but I held my own, and that was really surprising to a lot of people. WHITE: You know, the whole thing, it taught me about, you know, service and what it means to serve, and it taught me about the reality of both peace and violence in the world. And that continued to motivate me to make a difference. LIU: After your time in Afghanistan, you continued on with DARPA as a program manager, and in that role, you developed Memex (opens in new tab) , which I believe is a set of tools that could be mixed and matched to help uncover some really shady and dark parts of the web, which from what I understand was really hard to do up until that point. And coming back to the US, I saw more and more opportunities where collecting evidence at large scale was a really useful mechanism. WHITE: You know, I think what it’s done is it’s really increased my motivation. You know, my motivation to make a contribution. You know, my motivation to stay aware and be realistic. And by being realistic and motivated to address some of these very challenging issues, you know, around violence, around harm, and instead to focus on empowerment and to focus on justice, it gave me something to do. items.raw_text: Video playback requires cookie consent In the summer of 2010, postdoc Chris White worked with a multidisciplinary team at the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, or DARPA, to determine if a new approach to data analysis could prevent violence and protect troops during the war in Afghanistan. At the conclusion of the program, the agency asked White to prove the value of his work—on the ground. In this episode, Principal Technical Program Manager Weishung Liu talks with White, director of Catalyst Lab at Microsoft Research, about his unexpected break from academic research to help lead advanced tech operations in Afghanistan and his later decision to again work on tech with immediate, real-world implications: dark-web search tools used to help combat human trafficking. Liu and White explore the influences that led to these experiences plus the important role of problem selection in innovation and remaining hopeful after seeing the darkest parts of humanity. Subscribe to the Microsoft Research Podcast : Apple Podcasts Email Android Spotify RSS Feed Transcript [MUSIC] CHRIS WHITE: I have seen a lot of really bad humanity. You know, I’ve seen terrorism and trafficking and sophisticated organized crime, you know, designed to take things from people. Designed to hurt people. And I just know that I can do something about it, you know, and that I have and that we can. And so I think that that light, you know, the light of making a difference, you know, allows me to hold and handle, you know, the dark parts. [THEME MUSIC] STANDARD INTRODUCTION: This is the Microsoft Research Podcast , where Microsoft researchers—driving advancement through fundamental science and technology research—explore the who, how, and what’s next in computing and AI. [MUSIC ENDS] WEISHUNG LIU: Hi, and welcome. I’m Weishung Liu, a principal technical program manager here at Microsoft Research, and today I’m talking to Dr. Christopher White, who leads Microsoft Research’s Catalyst Lab . Chris has one of those careers that sounds almost made up: a Harvard postdoc, on-the-ground advanced tech lead during the war in Afghanistan, a DARPA program manager, a dark web search pioneer, and a public-good technologist. And his work has been featured in Popular Science (opens in new tab) as well as recognized with honors, including the 2016 Presidential Award for Extraordinary Efforts to Combat Trafficking in Persons (opens in new tab) . But what I’m most interested in today is the person behind that résumé. How someone who has seen some of the worst as part of his work still comes to the office with a smile and a commitment to building tools that make the world better. Chris, thanks for joining me. WHITE: Thanks for having me, Wei. Nice to see you. LIU: Yeah, good to see you, too. And so let’s get started. So I’ve known you for, I think, maybe around five or maybe six years, and now I work with you in Catalyst Lab. I love your story, and when I tell people about you, I say that you lead the newly formed Cat Lab, or Catalyst Lab, in Microsoft Research, you were a senior executive at DARPA, and you are married to an incredibly accomplished woman and scholar. And I personally think that your life story would make a very watchable Hollywood film. So when you tell your own story, though, where do you start? WHITE: Well, you start from where you are. And where I am today is leading research at Microsoft during a period of great fear and hope about changing technology and society. LIU: But, like, that’s now. There’s clearly lots of time from now into before, you know, the before times. So, like, tell me a little bit about the before times. Like, where were you at—I think you grew up in Oklahoma maybe. Tell me about that. Tell me about Chris White, the child. WHITE: Well, I was nerdy. I was a nerdy Eagle Scout. [LAUGHTER] I liked to build my own computers and have local area network [LAN] parties with my friends. But I also really liked being outside. I liked being in nature and camping and rock climbing. Those were all important to me. LIU: OK, you mentioned LAN parties. Tell me about … what did we play with our friends? WHITE: Well, you know, we played everything. I preferred playing sports games, but I lost a lot of the other ones. LIU: [LAUGHS] Wait, so you played like LAN party sports games, like, in basements? Like, with your … were we all in the same … ? WHITE: Yeah. Attics. It was attics. Yeah, not basements. [LAUGHTER] Mm-hmm. Yeah. Everybody had to bring their own computer or bring their own Ethernet cable. And the more that you had your own machine that was higher powered, the better you were going to play. LIU: So did you have the best machine? WHITE: I had the best machine. I built the best machine. Until someone built a better machine. But it was the best for a while. And I had a budget for it. And my family didn’t understand that the budget also included two giant speakers, like the size of a computer tower, like subwoofer speakers. They didn’t know that was part of the computer building process. But it turns out that excellent audio-visual is a critical part of a well-functioning machine. LIU: I love it. But, OK, we’re going to focus a little bit … continue focusing on childhood. So you mentioned nerdy kid, which means—I’m going to generalize here—debate team or math competition team or chess team? WHITE: Oh, it was the debate team. Yeah. Debate was a really wonderful activity. It taught me how to understand many sides of an issue and taught me how to think about evidence and research in that way. LIU: So, Chris, take me back again. Like, we’re talking a little bit about Oklahoma, and, you know, at some point, you chose researcher. Like, I—for example—when I was a kid, I was convinced I would be an architect. I am not an architect as you can see. But did you always think you were going to be a researcher? Was there an epiphany there? Like … or was it always kind of like a slow hunch that you were going to pursue research as a career? WHITE: Yeah, I kind of always felt like it. You know, as I was applying for school, those were the kinds of jobs I was interested in. You know, the kinds of things that you do, you know, once you finish degrees that have research in them. Those were the people, when I visited their work, I was inspired by. The people that were discovering, you know, that were inventing, that were innovating, that were … they’re pushing the boundaries that were kind of in that unknown, you know, space and making sense of it. And so I’ve always had that curiosity, you know, and that approach to discovery. And so as I increased my education, it just changed the nature of what research meant and the ways in which I imagined that process evolving. LIU: Was a doctorate always on the cards then? Or did that come, like, as you were in college and then gradually learned and thought, you know, I could keep going? WHITE: Yeah, you know, I didn’t know about doctorates really when I went to college. I wasn’t as familiar with higher education. And so I knew that I wanted, you know, advanced degrees. And I knew that I wanted more than was being taught in the undergraduate level. But I didn’t know, you know, for example, that when you apply to PhD programs, that often you get paid to go. You know, you get admitted and you get a stipend. You know, I was familiar with law and medicine and that you take out loans and you have to do it this way. And so for me, it was a surprise to know that I could apply to PhD programs directly from college. And from then, I just really was excited, you know, that I could explore different universities and different areas of focus and build on, you know, strong technical foundations of math and science and physics. And it was really amazing mentors that helped me and opened doors and inspired me. You know, mentors at Oklahoma State University, Johns Hopkins, and Harvard, really people that took their time and helped me. I’m really grateful for my teachers. So Catalyst Lab landed a huge commitment from our executive, kind of, leadership team on a project that has been, I think, like a decade in the making. WHITE: Well, you know, like I said, Dad’s a big influence, and he taught me so many things, and he taught me about respecting people. And most importantly, he taught me about humility and service. And so his way of making sure I understood that was every time something really good happened to me, he’d remind me to go clean some toilets and, sort of, embody that. And so I did. I did it last weekend actually. I went to a community event and volunteered to do bathroom clean. LIU: Is this like … are you … so in, like, the household chores, are you, like, the bathroom cleaner? Oct 13, 2026 By Ekin Karabulut and Sam Heywood Like Discuss (0) L T F R E AI-Generated Summary NVIDIA is releasing the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform as open source software, expanding the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform with a foundation for AI workload and GPU orchestration. The release includes four modular components that can be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler for GPU-aware Kubernetes scheduling, GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA-native GPU sharing, KAI Resource Management for organizational quota and hierarchy, and Workload Map for a consistent workload-management contract. Eight NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners including Crusoe, Mirantis, Nebius, OpenNebula Systems, Rafay, Saturn Cloud, Spectro Cloud, and vCluster are integrating the open source platform into their offerings. Related open source projects Model Streamer and Grove complement the platform by accelerating model loading and orchestrating multicomponent inference workloads. Next Steps Explore the NVIDIA Run:ai full platform repository to inspect code and begin adoption. Review the KAI Scheduler project for GPU-aware Kubernetes scheduling capabilities. Try the GPU Fractioning Operator to enable CUDA-native GPU fractions on Kubernetes clusters. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more NVIDIA is making the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform available as open source software, giving customers, developers, and ecosystem partners access to production-grade AI workload and GPU orchestration capabilities. This release expands the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform by establishing NVIDIA Run:ai as an open foundation that enables the broader ecosystem to bring differentiated solutions to market faster in response to evolving customer needs. Over the past several years, NVIDIA Run:ai has helped organizations run AI workloads on Kubernetes at scale by dynamically allocating GPU resources and managing workloads across the full lifecycle, from data processing and training to inference. By open sourcing NVIDIA Run:ai platform capabilities as part of NVIDIA DSX AI Factory, it is now possible for every NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner and AI cloud to increase workload throughput, improve GPU utilization, and operate shared AI infrastructure more efficiently and effectively. This post details the open source release, which includes the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform and four components that can also be adopted independently: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator , KAI Resource Management , Workload Map . Together with additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Platform teams and ecosystem partners can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole, build on it for their own products and services, or integrate individual components based on their requirements. How to adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai NVIDIA Run:ai can be adopted directly as open source software or through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partner offerings. Deploy the open source platform directly The complete source code for NVIDIA Run:ai is available in the NVIDIA Run:ai repository within the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization . Teams can inspect the code, contribute to its development, build on top of the platform or adopt its modular components independently. The complete open source NVIDIA Run:ai platform is also available on NVIDIA NGC as a Community Product, with a Helm chart for installing the integrated stack. Note: The NVIDIA Run:ai source code is governed by its applicable open source licenses. Downloading the Community Product from NGC requires acceptance of the applicable NVIDIA Software License Agreement and Product-Specific Terms for NVIDIA AI Products. No paid NVIDIA Run:ai subscription or NVIDIA support entitlement is required for the Community Product, and NVIDIA enterprise support is not included. Adopt open source NVIDIA Run:ai through NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners Open source NVIDIA Run:ai gives NVIDIA DSX ecosystem partners direct access to AI workload and GPU orchestration innovations they can use in their own NVIDIA DSX AI factory solutions. By adopting the complete platform or integrating individual components, partners can bring those innovations to market faster and respond more quickly to evolving customer and operational requirements. Crusoe integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with Crusoe Managed Kubernetes, combining GPU workload orchestration with managed Kubernetes and GPU infrastructure. Mirantis extends k0rdent AI with NVIDIA Run:ai to deliver a lifecycle-managed, Metal-to-Model AI factory stack that automates infrastructure provisioning and maximizes GPU utilization. Nebius offers NVIDIA Run:ai as a one-click application deployment in Nebius AI Cloud, giving customers a streamlined way to deploy and operate the complete platform on Nebius Managed Service for Kubernetes. OpenNebula Systems integrates NVIDIA Run:ai with the OpenNebula AI Cloud Platform through OneKS, combining GPU workload orchestration with infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle management for open and sovereign AI clouds. Rafay is expanding its NVIDIA Run:ai integration to deliver it as a fully managed service. Rafay automates the entire stack, from GPU infrastructure and clusters to the NVIDIA Run:ai control plane and tenants, so AI cloud providers and enterprises can offer it through their own self-service catalogs. Saturn Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai to help AI cloud operators launch white-label AI inference services through its Token Factory platform, combining GPU orchestration with dedicated and multi-tenant model serving, per-token metering, and automated billing. Spectro Cloud integrates NVIDIA Run:ai into PaletteAI, enabling customers to deploy it through PaletteAI Studio and manage it with the same lifecycle automation used across their AI infrastructure. vCluster provides NVIDIA Run:ai through pre-validated deployment templates that stand up a complete environment per tenant, allowing operators to strengthen tenant boundaries while NVIDIA Run:ai continues to schedule across one GPU fleet. For NVIDIA Enterprise AI Factory deployments, NVIDIA Run:ai continues to be available through NVIDIA-supported commercial offerings including as a standalone product, through NVIDIA Mission Control and NVIDIA AI Enterprise, and select cloud marketplaces. Availability, licensing, and support terms vary by offering. For teams that already have a platform and need to fill a specific capability gap, the following sections describe when and how to use each modular component independently. Modular open source components of the NVIDIA Run:ai platform This section details the four components included in the open source release: KAI Scheduler, GPU Fractioning Operator, KAI Resource Management, and Workload Map. With additional platform code, these components form the integrated NVIDIA Run:ai platform. You can adopt NVIDIA Run:ai as an integrated whole or integrate individual components based on your unique requirements. KAI Scheduler: The scheduling engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai KAI Scheduler is the Kubernetes-native scheduler that powers the NVIDIA Run:ai platform. NVIDIA released KAI Scheduler as open source software under the Apache 2.0 license and contributed it to CNCF as a Sandbox project. KAI remains the upstream engine behind NVIDIA Run:ai, and all scheduler development happens in the community repository, so every improvement flows through the same codebase. NVIDIA continues to support the project’s maintainers and work with the broader ecosystem to advance AI workload scheduling at scale. KAI Scheduler is purpose-built for GPU workloads at scale, coordinating: Gang scheduling with prescheduling in-memory simulation, so multipod jobs are placed all-or-nothing and aren’t evicted needlessly Fair-share (including time-based fair-share) and quota allocation that keeps resource shares balanced across teams Topology awareness and bin-packing at the scheduling-decision level GPU sharing, which allows multiple workloads to share single or multiple GPUs (MIG, MPS, time sharing, HAMi, CUDA 13.4 MPS fractioning) Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) support To learn more about key features, visit the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo. Use KAI Scheduler for diverse AI workloads that require fair access to cluster resources and topology-aware placement. It can be deployed in an existing cluster alongside the current software stack without requiring the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform. Follow the project, ask questions in the #kai-scheduler channel on CNCF Slack, and contribute on the kai-scheduler/KAI-Scheduler GitHub repo. GPU Fractioning: An operator for GPU fractions on Kubernetes The NVIDIA Run:ai platform has long supported fractional GPU allocation, enabling multiple workloads to share a GPU with hard memory isolation. Fractions can be requested on demand and set up on the fly, with no per-node setup from an administrator in advance. It is one of the most widely used capabilities among ML teams running workloads that do not require the full memory of a GPU, including interactive notebooks and inference for smaller models. NVIDIA Run:ai pioneered that experience with a proprietary implementation. GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and the proprietary implementation has been retired in favor of the native capability available in CUDA 13.4 . The CUDA driver enforces a hard limit on GPU memory for each workload, and each workload sees only the GPU memory allocated to its fraction. What is still needed is a clean way to consume it on Kubernetes. This is what GPU Fractioning Operator provides: an operator that enables CUDA GPU fractions on a cluster, along with a metrics exporter for per-pod visibility into fractions in use. It is a Kubernetes integration layer that allows workloads to use CUDA-native fractioning, and it is scheduler-agnostic. Use the GPU Fractioning Operator for workloads that can share underutilized GPU capacity, including notebooks, development sessions, and smaller models. GPU Fractioning Operator integrates with KAI Scheduler to translate available GPU capacity into an actual placement decision, while remaining compatible with other schedulers. GPU Fractioning Operator brings CUDA 13.4-native GPU fractioning to Kubernetes and integrates with KAI Scheduler. To get started, refer to the GPU Fractioning Operator documentation . KAI Resource Management: The organizational layer While the scheduler decides how work is placed, KAI Resource Management governs who gets what: Projects and departments: The organizational structure, or “org layer,” that maps resources to the teams and initiatives that consume them. Resource management with an organizational hierarchy: The ability to allocate, guarantee, and share GPU capacity across that org structure, with fair-share and quota semantics. Node pools: Grouping and targeting of heterogeneous hardware so workloads land on the right resources. Together, these let platform teams move beyond raw Kubernetes scheduling and manage GPUs the way organizations actually operate: by team, by department, by initiative, and by resource guarantee. Use KAI Resource Management for heterogeneous clusters shared by multiple teams that require defined shares of capacity. For example, a platform team could guarantee 50% of the cluster to research while preventing any one team from monopolizing the remaining capacity. If you are already tracking quota entitlements in a spreadsheet or hand-maintaining namespaces per team, this is the layer that replaces it. It can be combined with KAI Scheduler in your clusters. Read more about how these concepts map to real deployments in the KAI Resource Management documentation . Workload Map: A workload-management contract for Kubernetes Workload Map is the contract NVIDIA Run:ai uses to support any workload type. KAI Scheduler uses it for scheduling and gang semantics; the rest of the platform uses it for workload discovery, monitoring and lifecycle management. In Kubernetes, an AI workload is almost never a bare Deployment or Job. It is a PyTorchJob, a RayCluster, a JobSet, a KServe InferenceService, a Dynamo graph deployment, or a company’s own custom resource. Each type has its own internal structure, components with different roles (driver and workers, head and workers, prefill and decode), its own scaling and gang semantics, and its own way of reporting status. Workload Map provides a consistent way to treat these workloads as first-class objects throughout their lifecycle: Describing pods, components, and roles Submitting and configuring Scheduling with gang and topology awareness Observing status and health consistently Applying policy at admission or runtime This workload-management layer sits between Kubernetes primitives and the schedulers, dashboards, SRE and troubleshooting tools, cost tools, backup tools, and ML platforms that serve users. Instead of each tool building a private, partial integration for every CRD, Workload Map defines each workload type once so any platform or tool can schedule, observe, act on, and govern it consistently without hardcoding each CRD. Use Workload Map for platforms and tools that must understand and manage multiple Kubernetes workload types without hardcoding each CRD. It ships as a Go library that works offline on unstructured objects, so you can adopt it without adding anything to your cluster. It is deliberately narrow: Workload Map describes workload structure and does not schedule, queue, autoscale, or propagate across clusters. Learn more in the dsx-ai-factory/workload-map GitHub repo and check out the adopter projects . Related open source platform software The following open source projects address complementary AI infrastructure challenges. They can be adopted independently or incorporated into broader solutions that include the complete NVIDIA Run:ai platform or selected components. Model Streamer: Reducing cold-start latency Cold-starting an inference workload on Kubernetes can take several minutes, during which time GPUs are allocated but idle for a single step: loading model weights from storage onto the GPU. Model Streamer reads weights concurrently and streams them directly into GPU memory, cutting load time for large models. Since its release, Model Streamer has been adopted across the inference stack, including by inference engines, cloud providers and storage platform vendors. Inference engines Model Streamer is integrated upstream in vLLM and SGLang , where it can be enabled with the --load-format runai_streamer flag, as well as in ModelExpress . Support covers local filesystems, S3-compatible stores, and network file shares alongside several cloud backends detailed below. Clouds Major cloud providers now document Model Streamer in their own guidance. AWS : Model Streamer ships in the vLLM Deep Learning Container and is the recommended fast path in the official EKS documentation for running AI/ML inference , with tuned concurrency and chunk sizing for S3 . Google Cloud : Native Cloud Storage support built in collaboration with NVIDIA , including GKE documentation for streaming straight from a bucket into accelerator memory. Microsoft Azure : Azure Blob Storage integration, jointly developed by Microsoft and NVIDIA Run:ai to provide first-class model streaming for Azure customers. Published benchmarks on eight NVIDIA H100 VMs shows 3x-6x faster loading than the default loader and a steady 80 Gbps, compared with approximately 40 Gbps for the default path. Storage platforms Several AI data infrastructure partners have independently benchmarked Model Streamer and published their results: WEKA loaded into GPU memory in just 3.5 seconds, roughly 40% faster than loading from local NVMe—enabling organizations to build petabyte-scale shared model repositories that accelerate model readiness without the time, effort, and capacity required to maintain duplicate model copies across the inference environment. VAST Data measured 1.7 seconds, a 60% improvement over loading from local NVMe DDN streamed the 65.5 GB Qwen3-32B across 8 GPUs in under four seconds, and translated it into cost: saving up to 10% of daily GPU runtime compared to using local storage. Use Model Streamer when starting new replicas and loading model weights is the primary bottleneck. Grove: One API, any inference architecture Emerging workload patterns—including agentic pipelines, disaggregated serving and mixture-of-experts training—consist of multiple connected components that must scale together. Grove provides a Kubernetes API for orchestrating these workloads, from a single pod to deployments spanning tens of thousands of GPUs. Grove provides topology-aware autoscaling and hierarchical gang scheduling, allowing components such as prefill and decode to start as all-or-nothing units. On NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 , it also manages ComputeDomain resources automatically, enabling multinode NVLink performance through a single annotation instead of hand-authored YAML. Grove is a modular part of NVIDIA Dynamo that can be used independently, and it already powers training and inference pipelines at scale across a range of companies. Recent work includes support for llm-d and Volcano as a scheduler backend, with Kueue support in progress. Use Grove for graph-based workloads with distinct roles and coupled scaling requirements. Get started with open source NVIDIA Run:ai NVIDIA Run:ai is available now as open source software in the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory GitHub organization. To learn more and get started, check out these resources: NVIDIA Run:ai full platform KAI Scheduler scheduling engine KAI Resource Management for projects, departments, quotas, and node pools GPU Fractioning Operator for CUDA GPU fractions on Kubernetes, with per-pod metrics Workload Map workload-management contract Related open source projects include: Model Streamer for fast model weight loading Grove for multicomponent inference orchestration We’re excited to bring this work to the community and to build the next generation of AI workload and GPU orchestration in the open. We welcome your contributions, issues, and feedback. Previously she worked on privacy implications of federated learning, focused on distributed training techniques and got fascinated by inefficiencies in GPU usage in research and industry settings. She established the AI Infrastructure Club and is based in Munich, Germany. View all posts by Ekin Karabulut About Sam Heywood Sam Heywood is director of Product Marketing at NVIDIA, focused on AI infrastructure, GPU orchestration, and Kubernetes technologies that help organizations build and operate AI at scale. His technology interests include accelerated computing, cloud-native infrastructure, distributed AI workloads, and the systems that enable efficient training and inference. Sam brings extensive experience in enterprise technology and product marketing, translating complex technical capabilities into clear strategies for customers and the market. He holds a bachelor’s degree in Computer Science from The University of Texas at Austin and an MBA. View all posts by Sam Heywood Comments
