The model combines reasoning, instruction following, tool use, and text, image, document, and video understanding in a single model, eliminating the need for separate vision-language models. On a single GPU, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category. Organizations including Scale AI, Ramp, and AI21 have post-trained the model for specialized workflows, achieving improvements such as 40x lower inference cost, 10x lower latency, and 40% higher accuracy. Developers can customize the model using NVIDIA NeMo with supervised fine-tuning, low-rank adaptation, and reinforcement learning on open datasets released on Hugging Face. The model uses LiLiCorr speculative decoding, NVFP4 quantization with quantization-aware distillation, multi-token prediction, and context reuse to optimize inference efficiency on platforms including NVIDIA DGX Spark . Next Steps Read the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details. Explore the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub for customization resources. Get started with NVIDIA NIM for optimized deployment. Powered by NVIDIA Nemotron. AI-generated content may summarize information incompletely. Verify important information. Learn more Always-on agents are taking on longer, more complex enterprise workflows. A single request can involve reading a document, checking information across sources, following company policy, and calling several tools. NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open, customizable multimodal model for these specialized workflows. Its 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture activates 12B parameters per token, balancing model capacity with inference efficiency. On a single GPU, this model delivers up to 5x higher throughput for agentic tasks compared to other open models in its size category. Figure 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers over 600 TPS on Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index agentic tasks on the Baseten endpoint The model combines reasoning, instruction following, and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding. By combining these capabilities into one model, teams can handle text and visual tasks without deploying separate text and vision-language models or passing task context between them. Developers can post-train Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with NVIDIA NeMo using their own data, tools, policies, and workflows. This post explains how to use that foundation to build specialized enterprise agents and describes the training and inference techniques that power it. Why Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for specialized agents? Agents need to understand both their tasks and operating environments. A customer-service agent must follow company return policies. Research agents connect evidence across sources, while document agents interpret tables, charts, and page layouts. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines reasoning and visual understanding across a range of agent workflows, including: Coding: Test and validate code, analyze errors, and recommend fixes. Web research: Search across websites, connect information, and verify answers. Document intelligence: Extract information from tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries and reports. Cybersecurity: Identify security vulnerabilities and triage threats to prioritize remediation. Video understanding: Extract information for search, content review, and incident analysis. Within a system of models, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL handles specialized, multistep work that needs reasoning, tool use, and text and visual understanding together. Smaller models, such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning , handle high-volume text tasks, while frontier models such as NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra tackle complex planning and orchestration. Customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain data, tools, and policies Specialized agents must learn how an organization works. Domain terminology, tool interfaces, operating procedures, and policy requirements shape how agents complete tasks successfully. Organizations in industries ranging from cybersecurity and finance to healthcare are post-training Nemotron 3.5 Super VL to outperform frontier models in accuracy and efficiency across their production workflows. For example: Scale AI, an AI data and technology provider, post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for automated vendor credit processing at Skydance Corporation, a media and entertainment company. Inference cost for this workload will decrease by 40x and latency by 5x. Ramp, a financial operations platform provider, is converting receipt images into structured JSON containing merchant information, dates, and payment data. Ramp expects up to 50% higher throughput and 10x lower latency. AI21 and Alice post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for threat intelligence and vulnerability analysis, improving accuracy by 41%. Figure 2. Post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL achieves leading performance for specialized tasks across industries Teams can use NVIDIA NeMo open libraries to post-train models to meet these requirements. Developers can use NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel for supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) to teach domain-specific behavior. Reinforcement learning (RL) improves performance in agentic environments that reflect organizational workflows. Alongside Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, NVIDIA is releasing open datasets on Hugging Face. These include agentic tool-use and conversational data, finance reasoning and tool-calling datasets, instruction-following and chat data, long-context transduction and translation data, fairness data, and 40 vision-language datasets. These datasets can supplement proprietary data for SFT and RL. For multimodal data, start with NeMo Data Designer resources for chart question answering and long-document understanding . Explore NVIDIA NeMo RL and NVIDIA NeMo Gym for RL and environment-based evaluation. Organizations can adapt and deploy the model’s open weights in supported local, data center, or cloud environments to meet their infrastructure and data requirements. For customization resources, see the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL usage cookbook on GitHub. Combine text and visual understanding in one workflow Nemotron 3.5 Super VL combines text, image, document, and video understanding with reasoning and instruction following to answer questions across these inputs. Its visual training covers charts, tables, optical character recognition (OCR), multipage documents, and video understanding. A two-stage SFT pipeline trains the language and vision components, combining visual evidence with reasoning, chat, safety, long-context data, and agent trajectories. For document intelligence, the same model can interpret a chart, connect it with a table elsewhere in a document, and summarize both. Developers can tailor the workflow to their own documents and evaluation criteria. Diverse training data generated with NeMo Data Designer helped the model better understand complex charts. On CharXiv, a chart-reasoning benchmark, the model scored 80.8%, compared with 63% for Nemotron 3 Nano Omni . With Python code interpretation, it reached 84%. For the approach and lessons learned, read the chart-understanding deep dive and the open-source chart question-answering pipeline . This model was built with support and expertise from Nemotron Coalition organizations. For instance, high-quality datasets from Perplexity helped improve and streamline the model’s mid-training. Environments from Prime Intellect enabled building better teacher models. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is also one of the top open models on the OCRBench v2 leaderboard . Accuracy and efficiency across agent tasks Evaluations of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL span Hermes, LangChain, OpenClaw, OpenCode, Pi, Codex, and Claude. In addition to coding tasks, agent harness providers use their own evaluations to test a wide range of agent tasks. On Hermes Bench and LangChain behavioral evaluations, Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra. Model Hermes Bench LangChain Evals Nemotron 3 Ultra 56.33% 84.3% Nemotron 3.5 Super VL 63.44% 87.05% Table 1. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher than Nemotron 3 Ultra on Hermes Bench and LangChain evaluations For always-on agents, efficiency determines how much work a deployment can complete. Throughput, token usage, tool calls, and the steps needed to reach a correct result all affect task completion time. Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses higher throughput and token efficiency to deliver 4x faster task completion This model was also optimized to run locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark . An independent evaluation by EXO Labs placed Nemotron 3.5 Super VL on the Pareto frontier for accuracy and task completion time. Figure 4. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL balances accuracy and speed for agent tasks on DGX Spark Nemotron 3.5 Super VL under the hood The model builds on a strong foundation and uses a hybrid architecture, speculative decoding, context reuse, and mixed precision to reduce inference work across repeated agent calls. Building a strong base model Nemotron 3.5 Super VL was distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. Ultra’s coding capabilities, combined with the SkewReverse loss used during distillation, helped improve coding accuracy. During post-training, multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) combines guidance from specialized teachers across text and vision. The model generates responses, and the teachers score them for video reasoning and tracking, vision tool use, and alignment. Additional training on examples of agent actions, code repositories, and software engineering tasks improved the model’s performance on agent tasks. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL outperforms Nemotron 3 Super on SWE-bench and Terminal-Bench across multiple evaluation setups. Continued pretraining with high-quality natural and synthetic data improved Indic-language capabilities and contributed to higher overall scores after post-training. This stage added 10B Indic tokens, drawn from a 12-language subset of Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 and natural Indic text. NVIDIA is releasing the full dataset, which contains about 2.8T tokens across 22 Indian languages and was developed with IIT Madras and its AI4Bharat lab. The following results are based on the post-trained Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. Figure 5. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL delivers leading accuracy on Indic benchmarks, thanks to specialized Indic data Developers can use NeMo to build on this foundation and customize Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for their applications, adapting its reasoning and agentic capabilities to their data, tools, and workflows. LiLiCorr: An open speculative decoding technique LiLiCorr improves parallel speculative decoding by jointly evaluating token candidates across an entire draft, capturing dependencies that independent token predictions miss. A lightweight network computes compatibility scores in a single pass to produce more coherent drafts, leaving only a low-cost, sequential final selection step. On DGX Spark, LiLiCorr is the recommended drafter for low-latency inference with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL. It delivers up to 2.3x faster token generation than decoding without speculation. NVFP4 and mixed precision The model uses NVIDIA Model Optimizer for post-training quantization and quantization-aware distillation (QAD). The NVFP4 recipe uses 4-bit weights and activations on the NVIDIA Blackwell architecture . The same checkpoint runs on non-Blackwell platforms with 4-bit weights and 16-bit activations. Precision is selected separately for sensitive components. NVFP4 makes the model smaller, and QAD helps it retain its accuracy at lower precision. During QAD, the quantized model learns to match the outputs of the original BF16 model, which closes the accuracy gap that quantization introduces. QAD also supports storing the key-value (KV) cache in NVFP4 instead of FP8 while still meeting accuracy targets. Because QAD happens during training, it adds no inference overhead. Multi-token prediction Multi-token prediction (MTP) gives Nemotron 3.5 Super VL an internal drafter that proposes several tokens for the main model to verify in one forward pass. Accepting multiple tokens at once reduces the number of compute-intensive verification steps needed to generate a response. A dedicated MTP-boosting training phase further aligned the drafter with the final model. Context reuse across agent turns Agents repeatedly pass system instructions, tool definitions, and conversation history back to the model. Prefix caching reuses computation from those shared inputs. The model’s serving optimizations preserve both attention caches and Mamba recurrent states. Additional Mamba checkpoints reduce the replay needed to recover inputs for speculative decoding, while internal checkpointing avoids extra model passes during prompt processing. Simplify production deployment with NVIDIA NIM and NVIDIA Dynamo NVIDIA NIM packages models with optimized inference engines, validated configurations, and standard APIs for cloud and data center deployment. NIM receives ongoing security, feature, and performance updates. Enterprise support is available through NVIDIA AI Enterprise. Get started with NIM . NVIDIA Dynamo supports distributed inference optimizations to increase throughput and reduce latency, including KV-cache-aware routing, KV cache management, and disaggregated serving. On 16 NVIDIA B200 GPUs at 50 tokens per second per user, KV-aware routing with session affinity and KV cache offload serves up to 8x as many users while reducing first-token latency by 85%. Get started with the Dynamo deployment recipes . Figure 6. NVIDIA Dynamo serves 8x as many users and reduces first-token latency by 85% at the same per-user token rate Get started with Nemotron 3.5 Super VL Build specialized agents with multimodal reasoning and tool use. Customize the model for specialized workflows, then deploy it in a supported environment. The release includes base, post-trained, and NVFP4-quantized checkpoints with training recipes, data, and reinforcement-learning environments. See the Nemotron 3.5 technical report for model details and Hugging Face or ModelScope for deployment instructions. For hosted model access, see OpenRouter . Partner ecosystem Partners support customization and deployment of Nemotron 3.5 Super VL for domain-specific workflows. Chris comes from a machine learning and data science background, and he is obsessed with everything and anything about large language models. View all posts by Chris Alexiuk About Chintan Patel Chintan Patel is a senior product manager at NVIDIA focused on bringing GPU-accelerated solutions to the HPC community. He leads the management and offering of the HPC application containers on the NVIDIA GPU Cloud registry. Prior to NVIDIA, he held product management, marketing and engineering positions at Micrel, Inc. He holds an MBA from Santa Clara University and a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering and computer science from UC Berkeley. View all posts by Chintan Patel Comments

Learn more Meta launches Muse Spark Open, a coding-optimized 816B mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 42B active parameters and a 1M token context window. Trained on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 Blackwell Ultra specifically for agentic coding workflows, it delivers higher first attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. The 1M token context window holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking a task into pieces. As a reasoning model, Muse Spark Open adds audio and video perception alongside image and document understanding, working natively and reliably across what it sees, hears, and reads. NVFP4 checkpoints generated by Meta and optimized for NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra shrink the memory footprint of all 816B parameters with native FP4 Tensor Core acceleration. Fewer bytes moved per token to increase tokens per second per user, and the freed-up memory supports larger KV cache for concurrent long context sessions, delivering higher throughput, a lower cost per token. Custom-built for agentic coding multimodal understanding across text, image, video, and audio General coding models are optimized for single-shot completions such as generating a function, writing a unit test, or suggesting an inline fix. They excel at discrete, well-scoped tasks where the context is small, and the answer is immediate. Agentic coding demands something fundamentally different. Planning a multifile refactor, navigating thousands of files, recovering from failing tests, and coordinating subagents over long horizons requires a model built for sustained, multistep work. Muse Spark Open is built for exactly these workloads, delivering higher first-attempt accuracy, reliable tool calling, and deep codebase understanding across repositories. It plans, acts, observes, and self corrects. It supports multistep task execution with tool use, output evaluation, and iterative refinement. The model uses goal conditioning to hold direction and context compaction to retain the knowledge needed to sustain progress across long-running sessions. With a 1M token context window, it holds an entire project, including complex dependencies, legacy code, and thousands of files without breaking tasks into pieces. Beyond coding, it searches the web (including multimodal browsing), spawns and coordinates subagents for decomposable tasks, and leverages computer use capabilities unified across desktop, mobile, and browser. It generates separate commentary before each action, so developers know what the agent is doing and why. The model’s 1.8B perception encoder natively processes interleaved text, images, video frames, and audio without separate pipelines per modality. This means that the model reasons over what it sees, hears, and reads in a single unified pass. This suits developer workflows spanning screenshots, diagrams, error logs, and video walkthroughs within the same agent session. Sparse MoE routing activates only 42B of 816B total parameters per token, delivering frontier agentic capability at a fraction of the serving cost of dense models at equivalent scale. Figure 1 . Muse Spark Open sparse MoE architecture activates 42B of 816B parameters per token through top 8 routing across 256 experts Video 1. Muse Spark Open diagnoses a bug from a screen recording with narrated audio, reading the codebase to identify the root cause Muse Spark Open optimized performance on GB300 NVL72 The NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 features a rack scale architecture that integrates 72 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs into a single platform. Its large, 72-GPU NVIDIA NVLink domain enables efficient communication at 130 TB/s, eliminating bottlenecks that appear when expert traffic must cross traditional off-the-shelf networks. For a sparse MoE model like Muse Spark Open, which routes each token to eight of 256 experts, that bandwidth directly determines how much of the theoretical throughput a deployment realizes. Agentic workloads turn static single-turn interactions into multistep workflows that reason, invoke tools, coordinate subagents, and carry growing context from one turn to the next. Out of the box, Muse Spark Open running agentic workloads on NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 delivers up to 50K per second per GPU and up to 600 tokens per second per user, enabling AI factories to run large parameter models in production at high throughput and low latency. F igure 2. Running agentic workloads, Muse Spark Open on four NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with speculative decode achieved over 50K tokens per second per GPU and over 600 tokens per user Flexible deployment options for Muse Spark Open NVIDIA supports multiple inference stacks to meet a variety of developer needs. SGLang, vLLM , and TensorRT LLM give developers direct control over serving configuration, parallelism, and batching on the NVIDIA accelerated computing platform. TensorRT LLM adds compiled engines tuned for NVIDIA GPUs. NVIDIA Dynamo publishes deployment recipes for all three, and separates prefill from decode across dedicated GPU pools, so compute bound prompt processing doesn’t slow token generation. Its KV cache-aware routing sends each request to the worker already holding the relevant prefix, avoiding precomputation as context accumulates across long agentic sessions. Post-train Muse Spark Open with NeMo AutoModel and Megatron Bridge Developers can post-train Muse Spark Open on domain specific datasets using NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel , a PyTorch native training library with native Hugging Face checkpoint support and no model conversion required. It enables full SFT and LoRA fine tuning out of the box, optimized for rapid experimentation over a wide variety of industry specific cases. Developers can also leverage NVIDIA Megatron Bridge to convert Hugging Face checkpoints to Megatron format when they are ready for large production-scale training to take advantage of the optimizations. Get started with GPU-accelerated Muse Spark Open To get started, download Muse Spark Open NVFP4 weights from Hugging Face. For production deployments, try the downloadable NVIDIA NIM . The NIM reduces setup to a single command, replacing benchmarking and tuning cycles with a container that automatically selects the best serving backend and precision for the detected hardware. items.content: Back to Articles The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. Enterprise Article Published October 3, 2026 Upvote 88 +82 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face. Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper . This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Tommy Guy (founder at Enderis AI, previously Microsoft), Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former interns Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh), Ali Keramati (UC Irvine), Youngmin Ko (Northwestern) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date. The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation. Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ” Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold , pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked. An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees . That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv . You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006 , and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper . Contents A tool call is not an outcome One success is not reliability Can you depend on the model behind your agent? What consistency costs Failure signatures How it works Run it yourself Where this goes next Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself . A tool call is not an outcome Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question. The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap. A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test. One success is not reliability An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times , each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things: Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers. Metric What it measures What it answers pass@1 Share of all attempts that succeeded How does it usually do? pass@20 Share of tasks solved at least once in 20 tries Can it ever do this? Breadth. Observed 20/20 Tasks that actually passed all 20 recorded attempts Can it always be correct? We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing. Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking. Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper . Model Retail (98) Auto insurance (100) Travel (104) Neobank (104) Consulting (101) Overall, task-weighted (507) Proprietary models Claude Opus 5.5 80.97 68.40 54.28 71.25 61.58 67.16 Claude Opus 5 80.71 65.80 49.95 70.62 66.19 66.50 GPT-5.4 76.33 62.65 68.12 65.34 54.60 65.36 GPT-5.6 Sol 67.65 65.30 60.34 59.09 57.52 61.91 Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.35 54.40 58.94 56.39 54.31 59.19 GPT-6 Astra 71.73 46.55 55.87 60.87 56.83 58.31 GPT-5.2 70.20 22.40 53.70 51.15 34.06 46.28 Claude Opus 4.6 68.62 8.30 21.11 35.67 27.82 32.09 o3-pro 37.70 2.95 17.31 24.28 14.60 19.31 Grok-4.3 43.93 2.60 15.14 1.78 9.55 14.38 Open-weight models Kimi-K3 82.24 50.80 61.83 41.35 51.63 57.37 Qwen3.8-27B 64.03 47.85 53.41 47.88 45.69 51.70 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 68.21 29.65 43.13 44.86 31.04 43.26 Kimi-K2.6 53.72 24.50 39.52 33.65 37.33 37.66 GLM-5.1 58.67 25.70 35.43 13.27 34.06 33.19 Qwen3.6-27B 43.11 29.00 46.39 27.84 18.37 32.94 Qwen3.5-9B 19.90 0.70 4.71 1.15 2.33 5.65 Mistral-Large-3 11.28 1.30 8.99 1.15 0.74 4.66 Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model , within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much : Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance. One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives. Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats. Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%. The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story. Can you depend on the model behind your agent? Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility. Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model. Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt. A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all. Kimi-K3 solves 75 more tasks at least once than Opus 5. Opus 5 solves 173 more tasks consistently than Kimi-K3. If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at. What consistency costs Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator. We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter + , reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model. Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded : Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1) This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next. Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt. Pareto cost frontier A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate . Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis. Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models. The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1. Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%. Now price consistency Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts. Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20 Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task. Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills. Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%. What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it. Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges. Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked. Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful. At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics. The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side. Run it yourself ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset . ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. OpenEnv + the ThinkingBox environment git clone https://github.com/huggingface/OpenEnv cd OpenEnv uv sync --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen # 2. The executable benchmark, at the pinned release git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 # 3. The ThinkingBox CLI, which provides `tb` uv tool install "thinkingbox @ git+https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox" Start Typesense In a second terminal , start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check: mkdir -p .typesense-data docker run -- rm -d --name thinkingbox-typesense \ -p 8108:8108 \ -v " $PWD /.typesense-data:/data" \ typesense/typesense:30.1 \ --data-dir /data --api-key=Fake --enable-cors until curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8108/health; do sleep 1; done Start the MCP servers In a third terminal , start the Session Proxy and MCP servers. cd OpenEnv tb mcp-start --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7111 \ --servers " $PWD /thinkingbox-data/servers/servers.yaml" curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:7111/health Start the OpenEnv server Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models ( config guide ): OPENENV_TB_CONFIG= " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen server Check readiness Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. Whatever k your use case justifies; say whether you are reporting best-of-k or every-of-k, and how you computed it. Enterprise Article Published October 3, 2026 Upvote 88 +82 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face. Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper . This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Tommy Guy (founder at Enderis AI, previously Microsoft), Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former interns Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh), Ali Keramati (UC Irvine), Youngmin Ko (Northwestern) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date. The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation. Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ” Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold , pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked. An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees . That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv . You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006 , and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper . Contents A tool call is not an outcome One success is not reliability Can you depend on the model behind your agent? What consistency costs Failure signatures How it works Run it yourself Where this goes next Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself . A tool call is not an outcome Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question. The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap. A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test. One success is not reliability An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times , each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things: Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers. Metric What it measures What it answers pass@1 Share of all attempts that succeeded How does it usually do? pass@20 Share of tasks solved at least once in 20 tries Can it ever do this? Breadth. Observed 20/20 Tasks that actually passed all 20 recorded attempts Can it always be correct? We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing. Starting with the familiar view. items.content: Back to Articles The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself Published October 8, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 57 +51 yuvraj sharma ysharma Follow Abubakar Abid abidlabs Follow Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern , and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16. Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware. How I prompt ML Intern The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts , exactly as I wrote them. A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky. Two lines in the prompt are critical . The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run. At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer. You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days. 1. A model that knows your field A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand. On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90. Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App 2. A model that draws your character Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B , trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset. The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model . From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60. Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App 3. A model that does a new trick Camera-angle LoRAs are among the most-liked community add-ons for earlier Qwen-Image models. You can give the model a picture of an object and ask to see it 45 degrees from the left. When I checked a few days after the Qwen-Image 2.1 model release, nobody had made one, so I tasked ML-intern to build it. ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions. Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App Doodle-in LoRA is another cool idea. Upload a photo with a magenta scribble on it and add a short prompt naming an object. The LoRA replaces the scribble with that object while keeping the original lighting and composition consistent. No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely. Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500. Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24. Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App 4. A model that fits your device The Pocket Rewriter from the top of this post is the first one. ML-intern started by generating 8,797 short image requests with a small instruct model through Inference Providers, following a mix set in my prompt: photos, posters, logos, infographics and more, about a third of them asking for exact text in quotes, and many in languages other than English. The 9B teacher then rewrote all of them on one A100 in 2 hours 37 minutes (~USD 6.50). After filtering for quality, 1,840 examples were selected for training dataset. Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16. Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena Agate-Preview-002-4step is the second. Logolabs' Agate Preview 002 is a 260M-parameter text-to-image model, small enough for a browser, but it needs 50 steps with guidance, which is 100 network passes per image. I asked ML-intern to distill it down to just 4 passes! It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22. I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37. Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE What it cost Model Base model Compute Citrus Doctor Qwen3.5-2B USD 1.90 Huggy LoRA FLUX.2 klein base 4B USD 7.60 Pocket rewriter (0.8B and 2B) Qwen3.5-0.8B and 2B USD 16.05 Viewpoint Orbit LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 16 Doodle-in LoRA Qwen-Image 2.1 USD 24.30 Agate 4-step (two runs) Agate Preview 002 USD 37 Total about USD 103 These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session. Make yours ML-intern is in HuggingChat . Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap. If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace . We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you. items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 65 +59 Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow merve merve Follow ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow Guarin Flück guarin Follow Quentin Gallouédec qgallouedec Follow Alvaro Bartolome alvarobartt Follow Serveurperso Serveurperso Follow Jun Kim Jundot Follow Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. Inference Support Transformers The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template. Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed. You can initialize the model and processor as follows. import os from transformers import AutoModelForMultimodalLM, AutoTokenizer, DistributedConfig distributed_config = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B " ) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" , distributed_config=distributed_config, ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Explain in one sentence why the sky is usually blue." }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, reasoning_effort= "medium" , # default: xhigh, options: low/medium/high/xhigh add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) Text-only Inference Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template , enabling add_generation_prompt=True , tokenize=True , return_dict=True , and return_tensors="pt" . Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt. messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "high" , # options:low/medium/high/xhigh ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) output = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) generated_tokens = output[ 0 ][inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] :] print (processor.decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens= False )) Images and Text The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt. image_url = ( "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/" "resolve/main/pills.jpg" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : image_url, }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?" , }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tokenize= True , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_effort= "medium" , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) response = processor.decode(outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], skip_special_tokens= False ) processor.parse_response(response) Video Inference Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. You can make the model call tools as follows. from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" # Load model processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) tools = [ { "type" : "function" , "function" : { "name" : "weather.get" , "description" : "Get the current weather for a city." , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "city" : { "type" : "string" }, }, "required" : [ "city" ], }, }, } ] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning <|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response. Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template : <|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|> <atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="weather.get"> <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls> <|eot|> Llama.cpp Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP

The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input. Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date. Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here . Overall Capabilities and Architecture Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images. Feature Muse Spark Open Model size ~816B total parameters; ~42B active per token Expert routing 256 experts per MoE layer; 8 selected per token Inputs Text, images, audio, and video Output Text Context window Up to 1M tokens Checkpoint formats BF16 and NVFP4 The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4. Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each. Mixture of Experts The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum. Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp , vLLM, and SGLang recipes below. Perception Encoder A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention. Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images. Audio Encoder Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm. Long Context The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text. Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.
