Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference. If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood: import torch from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM model_id = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained(model_id). eval () messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "audio" , "url" : "https://huggingface.co/buckets/huggingface/audio-samples/resolve/bbaudio_question_39.mp3" , }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "Answer the question." , }, ], } ] # Downloads the audio, decodes it as mono, resamples it to 24 kHz, pads it, creates input_values_mask, and expands the audio placeholders. inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , load_audio_backend= "auto" , ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) with torch.inference_mode(): output_ids = model.generate( **inputs, max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , ) # Decode only newly generated tokens prompt_length = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] generated_text = processor.batch_decode( output_ids[:, prompt_length:], skip_special_tokens= True , ) print (generated_text[ 0 ]) The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings. Tool Calling Muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows. from transformers import AutoProcessor, AutoModelForMultimodalLM MODEL_ID = "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B" # Load model processor = AutoProcessor.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) model = AutoModelForMultimodalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) tools = [ { "type" : "function" , "function" : { "name" : "weather.get" , "description" : "Get the current weather for a city." , "parameters" : { "type" : "object" , "properties" : { "city" : { "type" : "string" }, }, "required" : [ "city" ], }, }, } ] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : [ { "type" : "image" , "image" : "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/SF.png" }, { "type" : "text" , "text" : "I'm going to the city in this picture. What clothes should I wear?" }, ], }, ] inputs = processor.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , add_generation_prompt= True , reasoning_strength= "high" ).to(model.device).to(model.dtype) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs) response = processor.parse_response( completion, prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools, ) print (response) Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below: <|begin_of_text|> <|start|>system<|message|> You are a helpful AI assistant. Knowledge cutoff: 2026-01-04. Current date: ... ... <|eot|> <|start|>user<|message|>... <|eot|> <|start|>assistant <|start|>assistant is intentionally left open, it’s the model that chooses recipient with to= . The model has different recipients, e.g. self asks the model to reason, to=self<|message|>the model reasons here<|eom|> # reasoning <|start|>assistant to=user<|message|>final answer<|eot|> # final answer self is for reasoning, commentary are comments before and between tool calls visible to the end user, user is the final response. Tool-call routing is parsed as follows (assuming you have passed tools to apply_chat_template : <|start|>assistant to=weather.get<|message|> <atem:function_calls> <atem:invoke name="weather.get"> <atem:parameter name="city">San Francisco</atem:parameter> </atem:invoke> </atem:function_calls> <|eot|> Llama.cpp Muse Spark 2-bit running on Llama Server Muse Spark Open is integrated in llama.cpp and comes in the prebuilt binaries. You can install this with following command: curl -LsSf https://llama.app/install.sh | sh You can start the server as follows with quant suffix attached to model ID: llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-GGUF:Q2_K The repository containing quants is here . Once the server has started, you can head to localhost:9931 to chat with the built-in WebUI. From the web UI you can add audio and images for inference and adjust the reasoning lever. Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. We tested quants on Mac M3 Ultra (512GB). An imatrix-calibrated 2-bit quant runs at 18 tokens/s, with plenty of room free for the KV cache (304 GB used by the model). You can also query the server as follows. Feel free to check out the API reference for multimodality, tool calls and more. ## Text-only inference curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "messages": [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a helpful assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about python exceptions"} ] }' ## Image-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"What is in this image?"}, {"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"data:image/png;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' ## Audio-text inference curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" -H "Authorization: Bearer <your-key>" \ -d '{"model":"muse-spark-open","messages":[{"role":"user","content":[ {"type":"text","text":"Transcribe this audio."}, {"type":"input_audio","input_audio":{"data":"data:audio/wav;base64,..."}} ]}],"temperature":0}' llama.cpp team ships different quantized versions. We have tested Q2_K, Q4_K_S and Q_8 on Apple Silicon chips. You can run each quant by adding the quant id as suffix, llama serve -hf ggml-org/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B:Q2_K . SGLang The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs. From the SGLang integration environment, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and start the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" SGLANG_FLASHINFER_NVFP4_PER_TOKEN_ACTIVATION=1 \ uv run sglang_meta serve \ --model-path "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --quantization modelopt_fp4 \ --moe-runner-backend flashinfer_trtllm \ --tp-size 4 \ --ep-size 4 \ --port 30000 The checkpoint includes the chat template, which we pass explicitly. The launcher configures the Muse reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request through the OpenAI-compatible API: curl http://localhost:30000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' The response separates the reasoning trace in reasoning_content from the final answer in content . vLLM The Muse Spark Open reference integration for vLLM supports text and image inputs with the NVFP4 checkpoint that require blackwell series GPUs. After installing the reference plugin and its dependencies, download the checkpoint from the Hugging Face Hub and launch the server: export MODEL_ID=meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 export CKPT="$(hf download "$MODEL_ID")" VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1 \ VLLM_PLUGINS=musespark1x_models,ptq_nvfp4 \ vllm serve "$CKPT" \ --served-model-name "$MODEL_ID" \ --tokenizer-mode musespark1x \ --config-format auto \ --load-format internal_safetensor \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 \ --enable-expert-parallel \ --max-model-len 131072 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92 \ --reasoning-parser musespark1x \ --tool-call-parser musespark1x \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --port 8000 This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers. Send a request using the same Hub model ID: curl http://localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": "Explain how a mixture-of-experts model works." }], "max_tokens": 2048 }' MLX Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit , ready to use right away. We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens. Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer. Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks. The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this: mlx_lm.generate --model mlx-community/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-oQ3e \ --prompt "Explain convolutional networks like I am 5" \ --max-tokens 5000 This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details. Deploying Muse Spark Open with Inference Endpoints You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead. To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --name muse-spark Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint. The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses . curl "https://<your-endpoint>.endpoints.huggingface.cloud/v1/chat/completions" \ -H "Authorization: Bearer $HF_TOKEN " \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "model": "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4", "messages": [{ "role": "user", "content": [ {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "https://huggingface.co/datasets/merve/vl-test-suite/resolve/main/pills.jpg"}}, {"type": "text", "text": "Do any of the components in this supplement interact?"} ] }], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} }' Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key. Fine-tuning with TRL You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer . This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples . First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP

items.content: Back to Articles Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 48 +42 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn. Train with LoRA You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading. python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 Build with Beam: Demos If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . To inspire you, here are a few things we built. Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application! At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out. We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text. Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account. Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery. We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements. You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions . Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. items.content: Back to Articles TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 23 +17 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! Acknowledgments Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible. More Articles from our Blog torch profile CUDA Profiling in PyTorch (Part 2): From nn.Linear to a Fused MLP +1 65 June 11, 2026 torch profile CUDA Profiling in PyTorch (Part 1): A Beginner's Guide to torch.profiler +1 184 May 29, 2026 Community Gerald001 about 9 hours ago hi, which models are supported with this? is mobernbert and t5gemma2 on the list? See translation Reply Edit Preview Upload images, audio, and videos by dragging in the text input, pasting, or clicking here . Tap or paste here to upload images Comment · Sign up or log in to comment Upvote 23 +11

The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! items.content: Back to Articles ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model Enterprise Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 20 +14 Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan ashwath-vaithina Follow ibm-research Vatche Isahagian Vatche Follow ibm-research Vinod Muthusamy vinodmut Follow ibm-research Jayaram Radhakrishnan jayaramkr Follow ibm-research Evelyn Duesterwald evduester Follow ibm-research Gaodan Fang gaodan-fang Follow ibm-research Punleuk Oum illeatmyhat Follow ibm-research G Thomas gsthomasx Follow ibm-research Michał Ulewicz Michal Follow ibm-research Merve Unuvar mrvnvr Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights. Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt. ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed. Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions. τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline . We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list: You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below. Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed. <policy> # Retail agent policy As a retail agent, you can help users: - cancel or modify pending orders - return or exchange delivered orders - modify their default user address … </policy> ## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully): - Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. If email is unavailable, verify identity via full name and zip code using the find_user_id_by_name_zip API. - Always confirm all intended changes (modify, cancel, return, exchange) with a clear, structured summary, and require explicit user approval before executing any database-updating action. - When processing a return or exchange, communicate the refund with an itemized breakdown and clarify refund timing — don't wait for the user to ask. - Take one action per step: never combine a tool call with a user-facing message in the same turn, and wait for the tool's result before replying. - Before looking a user up, parse and clean their name — e.g. split a combined handle like `daiki_johnson_9523` into first/last name — and after a couple of failed lookups, state the exact format you need. … We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using gpt-4.1 , the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set. Guidelines improve capability and reliability In a prior post , we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model. Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1). Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain. Variant Guidelines included in context Retail Airline baseline no guidelines 0 0 sup3 support n ≥ 3 (high-support core) 31 14 lossless all guidelines 292 101 The metrics we track. Every task is attempted 4 times , and we read those trials two ways: Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right? Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average. Figure 1. Mean Accuracy and Pass^4 on held-out retail and airline tasks for agents using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Agent model: gpt-4.1 (user simulator: gpt-5.5 ). Table 2. Held-out agent performance using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task. Parentheses show percentage-point changes from baseline. Domain (test tasks) Config Mean Accuracy Pass^4 Retail (40) baseline 78.1% 57.5% sup3 78.8% (+0.7) 60.0% (+2.5) lossless 82.5% (+4.4) 67.5% (+10.0) Airline (20) baseline 57.5% 35.0% sup3 60.0% (+2.5) 45.0% (+10.0) lossless 65.0% (+7.5) 40.0% (+5.0) Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below. The best amount of guidance depends on the domain The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail , more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant , support count is a knob worth tuning per domain , not a value to hard-code. Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns Guidelines aren't free, but the cost lands where you'd expect — in prompt input tokens , not in a longer, more meandering conversation: Figure 2. Total LLM cost per conversation by domain and guideline configuration on the full base split. Table 3. Total LLM cost per conversation (agent and user simulator) on the full base split across four trials. Lower is better. Domain Config Cost / conversation vs. baseline Retail baseline $0.084 — sup3 $0.095 +12% lossless $0.139 +65% Airline baseline $0.081 — sup3 $0.097 +19% lossless $0.107 +32% Does the agent get there by talking longer ? To answer that cleanly we compare like for like : the task runs solved under both baseline and the guideline variant — identical scenario and seed, a true "same task, done right" set — and count assistant turns on each side. Table 4. Assistant turns per conversation for matched runs solved under both settings on the test split, pooling four trials. Domain Shared set Solved under both (n) Baseline turns +Guidelines Δ Retail baseline ∩ sup3 108 10.40 10.35 −0.05 baseline ∩ lossless 111 10.59 10.16 −0.43 Airline baseline ∩ sup3 38 8.97 8.53 −0.45 baseline ∩ lossless 40 9.15 8.82 −0.33 The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter : lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching , since the guideline block is identical across every call. So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together. Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — gpt-4.1 . A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using gpt-5.5 for both the agent and guideline extraction , on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3. Table 5. Held-out airline performance for the gpt-5.5 agent across four trials per task. Airline · gpt-5.5 (20 held-out test tasks) Accuracy Pass^4 baseline (0 guidelines) 72.5% 55.0% sup2 (103 guidelines) 80.0% (+7.5) 70.0% (+15.0) lossless (146 guidelines) 82.5% (+10.0) 70.0% (+15.0) The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with gpt-4.1 on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw. ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4 . Because that covers the full task set rather than the held-out test split, these figures differ from the test-task numbers reported above. This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into , or past , current frontier company: Retail: #1 . On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5% , ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data . Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points . Airline: #1 using gpt-5.5 , #8 using gpt-4.1 Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using gpt-4.1 Pass^4 = 44% — 8th , beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using gpt-5.5 reaches 82.0% , clearing every frontier entry (66–72%). Figure 3. Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026. Same message in both domains: learning guidelines around the model works across different base models — bringing an agent using an older, non-reasoning model into frontier company on retail, and taking an agent using a frontier model to the top on airline. Agents can improve without weight updates Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs , automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs , automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage. items.content: Back to Articles AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms Published October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 4 Mattt mattt Follow Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback. Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task. A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0 . Here's what changed, and what's next: A drop-in compatible API The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement: - import FoundationModels + import AnyLanguageModel The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below. Over the past year, we've added several major features: Tool calling works with every provider. Guided generation works with every provider, too, including nested @Generable types and arrays of them. Image support lets you attach images to prompts using Foundation Models 27's syntax, including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27. On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models. Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps. Hosted models, too Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports: OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs Open Responses , for any provider with a compatible endpoint Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options Google's Gemini API Ollama Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27 Hugging Face Inference Providers , and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter, through a custom base URL With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code: let model = OpenAILanguageModel ( baseURL: URL (string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/" ) ! , apiKey: ProcessInfo .processInfo.environment[ "HF_TOKEN" ] ! , model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b" , apiVariant: .chatCompletions ) Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses. Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them. API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy. AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server. Open-weight models got better While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now: Gemma 4 E2B from Google, in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training. LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI, in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M . Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba, about 16 GB at 4 bits. The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line: let model = MLXLanguageModel (modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit" ) And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers. Upgrading to 1.0 dependencies: [ .package( url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel" , from: "1.0.0" , traits: [ "MLX" ] ) ] If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel , swift-huggingface , and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code. Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers. What's next Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28623 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators Authors: Michael Chen , Hong Chul Nam , Xi Deng , Anima Anandkumar View a PDF of the paper titled Planning under Noise with Neural Operators, by Michael Chen and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster.
