items.raw_text: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28623 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators Authors: Michael Chen , Hong Chul Nam , Xi Deng , Anima Anandkumar View a PDF of the paper titled Planning under Noise with Neural Operators, by Michael Chen and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN), a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt), to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95-100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D, PUN achieves 10.7-60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29-32.15 times faster. items.content: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators Michael Chen Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Hong Chul Nam Affiliation: Center for Data Science, New York University * Equal contribution Xi Deng Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Anima Anandkumar Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Abstract Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN) , a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt) , to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95–100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D ( λ = 4 \lambda=4 ), PUN achieves 10.7–60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29–32.15 × \times faster. 1 Introduction Planning ( Latombe, 1991 ) is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics. Given a robot’s configuration space ( LaValle, 2006 ) , planning computes a path from the current configuration to a goal that is optimal under a given cost function. Real robots do not execute a commanded motion exactly ( Thrun, 2002 ) . These errors accumulate along a motion, so a route planned with a few centimetres of clearance can be executed into a wall. Sampling-based planners such as PRM ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ) and RRT ( LaValle and Kuffner, 2001 ) , and graph search such as A ⋆ ( Hart et al., 1968 ) , plan for a nominal system that executes commands exactly and leave the noise to a tracking controller. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI ( Williams et al., 2017a ) and PI 2 -CMA ( Stulp and Sigaud, 2012 ) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Optimal feedback under execution noise can be derived from a value function, which gives the minimum expected cost of reaching the goal from each configuration and satisfies the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation ( Fleming and Soner, 2006 ) . Solving this equation on a grid scales exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space ( Bellman, 1957 ; Han et al., 2018 ) . While the problem can be converted into a linear screened Poisson equation ( Theodorou et al., 2010 ) under control–noise matching (Assumption 1 ), a central difficulty in Poisson-based planning is specifying boundary conditions that produce a reliable value field across varying geometries. Fig. 1: (a) Fast replanning. PUN has the lowest mean runtime on unseen 4D maps: 10.8 ms/start, compared with 32.8–387.1 ms/start for the baselines. Runtimes are averaged equally over the four execution-noise levels in Table 5 and plotted on a logarithmic axis. (b) Resolution transfer. FNO maintains over 90% local-search success across all five resolutions without retraining, reaching 92.50% at 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 after training at 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Missing points indicate out-of-memory failures. (c, d) Continued goal seeking. In the illustrated geometry, the solution induced by the Dirichlet boundary cannot propagate goal information further since most trajectories are absorbed by obstacles. Consequently, it is more difficult for planners to find the target than with the mixed boundary condition. Conventional mesh-based numerical methods can solve the screened Poisson equation efficiently in two and three dimensions. However, a robot with d d degrees of freedom (DoF) induces a d d -dimensional configuration space, making volumetric discretizations and numerical PDE solution increasingly expensive. Planning must also accommodate complex and previously unseen obstacle geometries, for which constructing a new mesh and solving the PDE from scratch can be costly. Mesh-free Monte Carlo methods ( Muller, 1956 ; Sawhney and Crane, 2020 ; Sawhney et al., 2023 ; Jambon et al., 2026 ) support PDE solution on complex geometries, motivating their use for planning in higher-dimensional configuration spaces. Among these, Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) ( Muller, 1956 ) estimates the solution at a point by jumping repeatedly to a uniformly sampled point on the largest ball fitting in free space, until it reaches a boundary of known value, which requires every reachable boundary to be Dirichlet. Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) accommodates reflecting obstacles by replacing that ball with a star-shaped region that may contain part of the obstacle boundary, keeping every boundary point visible from the center so that one ray continues the walk instead of branching at each contact. The screened kernels for Walk-on-Stars have been derived only in two and three dimensions ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) . Moreover, directly planning with Monte Carlo estimates is unreliable: trajectories depend on local value gradients, and even modest estimator noise can corrupt or reverse the estimated direction, leading to planning failure. Neural operators ( Kovachki et al., 2023 ) can amortize expensive PDE solves by learning mappings from input geometries directly to solution fields. Moreover, prior work has shown that fully converged labels are unnecessary when training from Monte Carlo simulations: neural operators can recover accurate predictions from noisy, partially converged estimates ( Viswanath et al., 2026 ) . This enables training of neural operators with inexpensive Monte Carlo supervision while providing fast, smooth value-field predictions at inference time. We propose P lanning U nder N oise (PUN), shown in Fig. 2 , an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to value fields that account for control noise. Boundary conditions can be understood through a heat analogy. With unit desirability at the goal and zero desirability on obstacle boundaries, the goal acts like a hot source, while the obstacle walls act like cold sinks. The zero-Dirichlet condition fixes the field to zero along each obstacle surface, making the entire obstacle boundary a heat sink. In a long or narrow passage, heat spreading from the goal therefore leaks into the walls along the route. The farther the goal’s influence must travel, the more it is attenuated, leaving a weak signal in distant parts of free space that discretization, sampling, or learning errors can obscure. Narrow passages make this particularly pronounced because the absorbing walls remain close on both sides. This attenuation is visible in Fig. 1 (c), where the weak goal signal provides insufficient directional guidance for starting points far from the goal, making it difficult to navigate toward the target. Moreover, the screened Poisson equation already includes decay throughout free space through its screening term; absorbing obstacle boundaries introduce an additional source of attenuation. We therefore keep a Dirichlet condition at the goal but impose homogeneous Neumann (zero-flux) conditions on obstacle boundaries. The walls now act like insulation: they prevent heat from escaping through the boundary without forcing the desirability itself to vanish there. Heat can spread along a corridor without continually draining into its walls, allowing the goal’s influence to reach farther into free space. Screening still causes decay, but the additional loss through obstacles is removed. This is precisely the effect illustrated in Fig. 1 (d): compared with the absorbing Dirichlet field in Fig. 1 (c), the mixed-boundary field extends the goal’s influence much farther through the environment, preserving a stronger signal for planning along long routes. The Neumann condition also makes the value gradient parallel to smooth obstacle boundaries; therefore, gradient-based planning directs motion along walls rather than into them. This permits guidance along walls in narrow passages without the strong repulsion induced by zero-Dirichlet conditions. Under our regularity assumptions, the value field and control remain bounded at obstacles, whereas zero-Dirichlet desirability makes both diverge there (Appendix C.4 ). We first derive dimension-general Poisson kernels and Monte Carlo weights, extending mesh-free supervision beyond three dimensions for scalability. This enables supervision generation without a volumetric configuration-space mesh. We then train PUN using noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo estimates in the weak supervision paradigm. By amortizing the PDE solution across geometries, PUN produces spatially coherent value fields that guide gradient following and local search without requiring a fully converged Monte Carlo solve for every environment. We evaluate PUN across 2D–4D environments and compare its planning success and runtime with nominal planners and stochastic controllers under execution noise. In the experiments varying the execution noise level λ \lambda , we plan a path from the current state at each control step, follow it briefly, and repeat from the updated state; we refer to this as replanning. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries. • We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves. • We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation. • We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11 ). (B) Training: Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) estimates provide pointwise supervision; neural caching supplies learned continuation at the walk horizon. On 2D application benchmarks, zero-shot WoSt-supervised FNO reaches 93.62% local-search success, up from 83.87% with gradient following on the same fields (Table 1 ). With the same local-search, FNO-based PUN achieves approximately 941 × 941\times and 58 × 58\times speedups over direct WoSt on the 2D zero-shot application benchmarks and 4D manipulator test set, respectively (Table 12 ). In 4D replanning, PUN achieves 95.00–100% success at 10.51–11.66 ms/start across the tested noise levels (Table 5 ; Fig. 1 (a)). At λ = 4 \lambda=4 , PUN is 3.29 × 3.29\times faster than RRT and 5.09 5.09 – 32.15 × 32.15\times faster than A ⋆ , Dijkstra, MPPI, and PI 2 -CMA. Columns show successive execution states; PUN’s trajectory is orange. PUN reaches the goal in both illustrated rollouts. Aggregate success and runtime are reported in Table 5 . Path Planning. Classical planners divide into two families. Sampling-based methods such as PRM ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ) , RRT ( LaValle and Kuffner, 2001 ) , and RRT ⋆ ( Karaman and Frazzoli, 2011 ) build a graph of collision-free motions, while search-based methods such as A ⋆ ( Hart et al., 1968 ) , Dijkstra ( Dijkstra, 1959 ) , and fast marching ( Sethian, 1996 ) compute a cost-to-go over a discretization; both plan for a deterministic system and defer execution noise to tracking and replanning. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI ( Williams et al., 2017a ; Williams et al., 2017b ) and PI 2 -CMA ( Stulp and Sigaud, 2012 ) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Our implementations and their treatment of execution noise are described in Appendix D.1 . We compare against these planners in Table 5 . Planning Neural Operator (PNO) ( Matada et al., 2025 ) learns the solution operator of the Eikonal equation from labels produced by a deterministic solver, but it is limited to deterministic systems. NTFields ( Ni and Qureshi, 2023 ) and EikoNet ( Smith et al., 2021 ) train a physics-informed network on the Eikonal residual, which fits a single geometry per model and must be retrained for each new environment. In contrast, PUN is trained over a family of geometry classes with approximate Monte Carlo supervision across diverse noise ranges to support planning with different noise spectra while achieving reliable stability. Monte Carlo Methods. Monte Carlo estimators for PDEs can be categorized depending on the type of PDE, include Walk-on-Spheres ( Sawhney and Crane, 2020 ) , Walk-on-Boundaries ( Sugimoto et al., 2023 ) , and Backward Stochastic Differential Equations (BSDE) ( Zhang, 2017 ) . items.raw_text: Planning under Noise with Neural Operators Michael Chen Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Hong Chul Nam Affiliation: Center for Data Science, New York University * Equal contribution Xi Deng Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Anima Anandkumar Affiliation: Computing and Mathematical Sciences, California Institute of Technology Abstract Planning under uncertain control execution noise requires reliable feedback policies across diverse environments. We introduce Planning Under Noise (PUN) , a neural operator that learns noise-aware value fields for planning in unseen geometries. Building on an established screened-Poisson formulation of stochastic optimal control, we address two challenges: specifying boundary conditions that support navigation across varying geometries and efficiently computing fields with reliable gradients. Zero-Dirichlet obstacle boundaries terminate sampled paths at walls, weakening the goal signal along long routes and making it harder to estimate reliably. We instead impose reflecting Neumann conditions on obstacles and a Dirichlet condition at the goal, allowing sampled paths to continue exploring free space until they reach the target. To solve the resulting PDE without a configuration-space mesh, we extend a Monte Carlo (MC) solver, Walk on Stars (WoSt) , to higher dimensions. However, local MC fluctuations can reverse estimated gradient directions and cause planning failures, making direct planning require costly sampling. PUN amortizes this computation by learning geometry-to-field mappings from noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo labels, avoiding expensive convergence for every training example. At inference, test-time scaling uses bounded local search guided by the predicted global field. We evaluate PUN on planning tasks across dimensions. Across four noise levels, PUN matches or outperforms all compared planners, achieving 95–100% success on the 4D replanning benchmark while maintaining the lowest runtime. At the highest tested noise level in 4D ( λ = 4 \lambda=4 ), PUN achieves 10.7–60.6% relative gains in success rate over other methods while running 3.29–32.15 × \times faster. 1 Introduction Planning ( Latombe, 1991 ) is one of the most fundamental problems in robotics. Given a robot’s configuration space ( LaValle, 2006 ) , planning computes a path from the current configuration to a goal that is optimal under a given cost function. Real robots do not execute a commanded motion exactly ( Thrun, 2002 ) . These errors accumulate along a motion, so a route planned with a few centimetres of clearance can be executed into a wall. Sampling-based planners such as PRM ( Kavraki et al., 1996 ) and RRT ( LaValle and Kuffner, 2001 ) , and graph search such as A ⋆ ( Hart et al., 1968 ) , plan for a nominal system that executes commands exactly and leave the noise to a tracking controller. Sampling-based methods such as MPPI ( Williams et al., 2017a ) and PI 2 -CMA ( Stulp and Sigaud, 2012 ) optimize control sequences or policy parameters using sampled trajectory costs. Optimal feedback under execution noise can be derived from a value function, which gives the minimum expected cost of reaching the goal from each configuration and satisfies the nonlinear Hamilton–Jacobi–Bellman (HJB) equation ( Fleming and Soner, 2006 ) . Solving this equation on a grid scales exponentially with the dimension of the configuration space ( Bellman, 1957 ; Han et al., 2018 ) . While the problem can be converted into a linear screened Poisson equation ( Theodorou et al., 2010 ) under control–noise matching (Assumption 1 ), a central difficulty in Poisson-based planning is specifying boundary conditions that produce a reliable value field across varying geometries. Fig. 1: (a) Fast replanning. PUN has the lowest mean runtime on unseen 4D maps: 10.8 ms/start, compared with 32.8–387.1 ms/start for the baselines. Runtimes are averaged equally over the four execution-noise levels in Table 5 and plotted on a logarithmic axis. (b) Resolution transfer. FNO maintains over 90% local-search success across all five resolutions without retraining, reaching 92.50% at 4096 × 4096 4096\times 4096 after training at 256 × 256 256\times 256 . Missing points indicate out-of-memory failures. (c, d) Continued goal seeking. In the illustrated geometry, the solution induced by the Dirichlet boundary cannot propagate goal information further since most trajectories are absorbed by obstacles. Consequently, it is more difficult for planners to find the target than with the mixed boundary condition. Conventional mesh-based numerical methods can solve the screened Poisson equation efficiently in two and three dimensions. However, a robot with d d degrees of freedom (DoF) induces a d d -dimensional configuration space, making volumetric discretizations and numerical PDE solution increasingly expensive. Planning must also accommodate complex and previously unseen obstacle geometries, for which constructing a new mesh and solving the PDE from scratch can be costly. Mesh-free Monte Carlo methods ( Muller, 1956 ; Sawhney and Crane, 2020 ; Sawhney et al., 2023 ; Jambon et al., 2026 ) support PDE solution on complex geometries, motivating their use for planning in higher-dimensional configuration spaces. Among these, Walk-on-Spheres (WoS) ( Muller, 1956 ) estimates the solution at a point by jumping repeatedly to a uniformly sampled point on the largest ball fitting in free space, until it reaches a boundary of known value, which requires every reachable boundary to be Dirichlet. Walk-on-Stars (WoSt) ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) accommodates reflecting obstacles by replacing that ball with a star-shaped region that may contain part of the obstacle boundary, keeping every boundary point visible from the center so that one ray continues the walk instead of branching at each contact. The screened kernels for Walk-on-Stars have been derived only in two and three dimensions ( Sawhney et al., 2023 ) . Moreover, directly planning with Monte Carlo estimates is unreliable: trajectories depend on local value gradients, and even modest estimator noise can corrupt or reverse the estimated direction, leading to planning failure. Neural operators ( Kovachki et al., 2023 ) can amortize expensive PDE solves by learning mappings from input geometries directly to solution fields. Moreover, prior work has shown that fully converged labels are unnecessary when training from Monte Carlo simulations: neural operators can recover accurate predictions from noisy, partially converged estimates ( Viswanath et al., 2026 ) . This enables training of neural operators with inexpensive Monte Carlo supervision while providing fast, smooth value-field predictions at inference time. We propose P lanning U nder N oise (PUN), shown in Fig. 2 , an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to value fields that account for control noise. Boundary conditions can be understood through a heat analogy. With unit desirability at the goal and zero desirability on obstacle boundaries, the goal acts like a hot source, while the obstacle walls act like cold sinks. The zero-Dirichlet condition fixes the field to zero along each obstacle surface, making the entire obstacle boundary a heat sink. In a long or narrow passage, heat spreading from the goal therefore leaks into the walls along the route. The farther the goal’s influence must travel, the more it is attenuated, leaving a weak signal in distant parts of free space that discretization, sampling, or learning errors can obscure. Narrow passages make this particularly pronounced because the absorbing walls remain close on both sides. This attenuation is visible in Fig. 1 (c), where the weak goal signal provides insufficient directional guidance for starting points far from the goal, making it difficult to navigate toward the target. Moreover, the screened Poisson equation already includes decay throughout free space through its screening term; absorbing obstacle boundaries introduce an additional source of attenuation. We therefore keep a Dirichlet condition at the goal but impose homogeneous Neumann (zero-flux) conditions on obstacle boundaries. The walls now act like insulation: they prevent heat from escaping through the boundary without forcing the desirability itself to vanish there. Heat can spread along a corridor without continually draining into its walls, allowing the goal’s influence to reach farther into free space. Screening still causes decay, but the additional loss through obstacles is removed. This is precisely the effect illustrated in Fig. 1 (d): compared with the absorbing Dirichlet field in Fig. 1 (c), the mixed-boundary field extends the goal’s influence much farther through the environment, preserving a stronger signal for planning along long routes. The Neumann condition also makes the value gradient parallel to smooth obstacle boundaries; therefore, gradient-based planning directs motion along walls rather than into them. This permits guidance along walls in narrow passages without the strong repulsion induced by zero-Dirichlet conditions. Under our regularity assumptions, the value field and control remain bounded at obstacles, whereas zero-Dirichlet desirability makes both diverge there (Appendix C.4 ). We first derive dimension-general Poisson kernels and Monte Carlo weights, extending mesh-free supervision beyond three dimensions for scalability. This enables supervision generation without a volumetric configuration-space mesh. We then train PUN using noisy, partially converged Monte Carlo estimates in the weak supervision paradigm. By amortizing the PDE solution across geometries, PUN produces spatially coherent value fields that guide gradient following and local search without requiring a fully converged Monte Carlo solve for every environment. We evaluate PUN across 2D–4D environments and compare its planning success and runtime with nominal planners and stochastic controllers under execution noise. In the experiments varying the execution noise level λ \lambda , we plan a path from the current state at each control step, follow it briefly, and repeat from the updated state; we refer to this as replanning. Our contributions can be summarized as follows: • We formulate Poisson-based path planning as a mixed boundary-value problem, imposing a Dirichlet condition at the goal and homogeneous Neumann conditions on obstacle boundaries. • We introduce an operator-learning framework that maps environment geometry to noise-aware value fields, enabling zero-shot planning in unseen complex geometries without per-instance retraining or numerical PDE solves. • We generalize the mesh-free Monte Carlo solver WoSt beyond three dimensions by deriving the dimension-dependent Green’s function and step weights for the screened Poisson equation. • We introduce a test-time scaling strategy that evaluates reachable candidate states on a local lattice using a fixed global learned field, without retraining, improving planning success over direct gradient following in the reported 2D–4D evaluations (Tables 1 and 11 ). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28618 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation Authors: Vincent Jung , Alba Carballo-Castro , Yiming Qin , Lonneke van der Plas , Pascal Frossard View a PDF of the paper titled Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation, by Vincent Jung and 4 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch's FlexAttention. We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models. items.content: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation Vincent Jung Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano, Switzerland Alba Carballo-Castro Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Yiming Qin Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Lonneke van der Plas Affiliation: Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano, Switzerland Pascal Frossard Correspondence to: first_name.last_name@epfl.ch Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Abstract Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch’s FlexAttention . We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution Code 1 Introduction Graph generation ( Simonovsky & Komodakis, 2018 ; Martinkus et al., 2022 ; Jo et al., 2024 ) has advanced substantially with discrete diffusion and flow-based models. A particularly influential line of work, initiated by the diffusion model DiGress ( Vignac et al., 2023 ) , and then flow-based models such as CatFlow ( Eijkelboom et al., 2024 ) , DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) , BWFlow ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and VBFN ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion models such as Cometh ( Siraudin et al., 2025 ) , relies on a specific transformer backbone to denoise categorical node and edge features. This architecture is inspired by the original Graph Transformer ( Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021 ) , which already updates edge states from attention scores and uses edge states to modulate self-attention. The main differences are that it computes attention between all nodes as opposed to restricting it to neighbors, maintains a graph-level feature vector and uses FiLM ( Perez et al., 2018 ) modules to couple node, edge, and graph-level features. This dense, layered interaction is central to its success in graph generation, where the model must capture both local connectivity and global graph structure. However, this expressivity comes with a computational cost. Since the model must maintain dense pairwise edge states, both attention computation and dynamic edge representations scale quadratically with the number of nodes, making training expensive and difficult under limited GPU resources. A large body of work addresses this bottleneck through sparse attention patterns ( Shirzad et al., 2023 ) ; hybrid local-global designs ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) ; linear and operator-based alternatives ( Deng et al., 2024 ; Sancak et al., 2025 ) ; or tokenization-based formulations that cast graphs as sequences of node and edge tokens and apply standard Transformers with minimal graph-specific modifications ( Kim et al., 2022 ) . These methods are effective, but typically modify or replace dense self-attention altogether. In graph generation specifically, SparseDiff ( Qin et al., 2025b ) exploits sparsity to enable training on larger graphs, although this increases sampling time. In this work, we take a complementary route and ask whether the original dense edge-aware architecture can be implemented more efficiently while fully preserving its inductive bias. We focus on the computationally-expensive and memory-hungry attention layer in the original implementation, and design a kernel-friendly version which still modulates attention scores using edge and global features, respects graph masks, and enables edge features update from its attention map. This version can be implemented entirely using FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , which supports custom attention score modifications and masking. This enables us to use fused attention kernels, bringing throughput and memory gains. Empirically, our proposed model (FlexAttentionGT) matches the generation quality of DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) ’s original backbone while reducing peak memory by 65% and improving training and inference throughput by 45% and 94% on average. Ablations show that the edge update is critical: simplifying it causes generation collapse, whereas reducing model size leads to slower convergence and worse final performance. Together, these results demonstrate that edge-aware graph Transformers can be made more efficient with tailored design while preserving their expressivity, supporting their scalability to the larger graphs encountered in foundation model settings. 2 Background and related work Generative Graph Transformer Recent works in graph generation such as DiGress ( Vignac et al., 2023 ) or BWFlow ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) employ a Graph Transformer (GT) backbone that jointly updates node features 𝑿 ∈ ℝ N × d x \bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{x}} , edge features 𝑬 ∈ ℝ N × N × d e \bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}} , and graph-level features 𝒚 ∈ ℝ d y \bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} , with N N the number of nodes of the largest graph in a batch. In contrast to the original Graph Transformer ( Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021 ) , this backbone keeps dense edge features and graph-level features, and injects them into node attention through FiLM-style score modulation ( Perez et al., 2018 ) (Further details in Appendix C.1 ). The attention map is then reused to update edge features, while graph-level features are updated from pooled node and edge representations. This design is effective for graph generation because it tightly couples node-, edge-, and graph-level information. However, it bottlenecks efficiency: the model maintains dense pairwise edge states 𝑬 \bm{E} , which need to be included in the node attention, and themselves updated using these attention scores, resulting in quadratic computational and memory costs per layer. Structural attention biases and edge-aware architectures. A central approach to injecting graph structure into Transformers is modulating attention logits with structural features. Graphormer ( Ying et al., 2021 ) introduced spatial and edge encodings as additive biases on pre-softmax logits. EGT ( Hussain et al., 2022 ) proposed bidirectional coupling between explicit edge channels and node attention, architecturally close to the generative GT backbone we build upon. Relational Attention ( Diao & Loynd, 2023 ) similarly updates edge vectors at each layer. Our work preserves this dense edge coupling while making it compatible with fused attention kernels. Adjacency masking and hybrid designs. Exphormer ( Shirzad et al., 2023 ) builds sparse attention from local neighborhoods, expander graphs and virtual global nodes, yielding a scalable graph transformer; GraphGPS ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) runs a local MPNN and a global Transformer in parallel, avoiding committing entirely to dense or sparse attention. In graph generation, SparseDiff ( Qin et al., 2025b ) exploits graph sparsity to scale to larger graphs, but relies on message-passing layers that are less amenable to efficient parallel computation. Scalable alternatives. Polynormer ( Deng et al., 2024 ) combines linear-time attention with a polynomial-expressive formulation to balance scalability and expressivity, GECO ( Sancak et al., 2025 ) proposes a scalable operator-based alternative, and tokenization-based methods ( Kim et al., 2022 ) apply standard Transformers to node and edge token sequences with minimal graph-specific modifications. These approaches are effective, but typically modify or replace dense attention altogether. Graph foundation models. As graph learning scales toward foundation model settings, the cost of dense edge-aware attention becomes increasingly prohibitive. GraphBFF ( Bechler-Speicher et al., 2026 ) addresses this for large heterogeneous graphs by replacing dense attention with type-aware sparse attention. Our work takes a complementary route: rather than replacing the dense backbone, we make it hardware-efficient through fused kernels, preserving the inductive bias that drives generation quality and enabling its application at larger scales. We refer the reader to Appendix A for a more detailed overview of the relevant literature. 3 Efficient Attention Layers for Graph Generation We identify three challenges in making the generative GT backbone compatible with fused attention kernels. (i) The original architecture uses element-wise outer-product attention, producing a d f d_{f} -dimensional tensor per node pair that standard fused kernels cannot process. (ii) Edge and global features must still modulate pairwise attention scores in a way that is both expressive and kernel-compatible. (iii) Edge representations depend on the softmax attention probabilities α \alpha , which fused kernels do not materialize in global memory. We address each challenge in turn, with further implementation details in Appendices C.2 and C.3 . FlexAttention . We leverage FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , a PyTorch interface that lowers customized attention variants to fused Triton kernels. It exposes two hooks: score_mod modifies each pre-softmax attention logit, enabling structural biases and edge-dependent score modulation; mask_mod specifies which query-key pairs are valid, compiled into a block-sparse BlockMask that allows the kernel to skip fully-masked blocks. This interface is well-suited for injecting graph masks and structural biases into attention; however, it does not natively support the edge update used in generative graph Transformers, since it only returns the attended node values. We address this below. From element-wise to scalar dot-product attention. The original backbone computes an unnormalized attention tensor 𝒀 ∈ ℝ N × N × H × d f \bm{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H\times d_{f}} via the element-wise outer product 𝒀 i ​ j , h = 𝒒 i , h ⊙ 𝒌 j , h \bm{Y}_{ij,h}=\bm{q}_{i,h}\odot\bm{k}_{j,h} , retaining a d f d_{f} -dimensional feature vector per node pair and head. Softmax is then applied independently per channel , yielding d f d_{f} separate attention distributions per query-head pair. While expressive, this formulation cannot be lowered to a standard fused kernel. We replace it with standard scaled dot-product attention. The unnormalized scalar logit for each head h h is s i ​ j , h = 𝒒 i , h ⋅ 𝒌 j , h d f ∈ ℝ , s_{ij,h}=\frac{\bm{q}_{i,h}\cdot\bm{k}_{j,h}}{\sqrt{d_{f}}}\in\mathbb{R}, (1) giving a single attention distribution per query-head pair and making the node-update compatible with standard FlexAttention. Head-wise structural FiLM layer To inject edge features 𝑬 ∈ ℝ N × N × d e \bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}} and global features 𝒚 ∈ ℝ d y \bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} into attention, we learn one scalar per edge and attention head: s i ​ j , h ′ = s i ​ j , h ⋅ ( E i ​ j , h mul + 1 ) + E i ​ j , h add , s^{\prime}_{ij,h}=s_{ij,h}\cdot\bigl(E^{\mathrm{mul}}_{ij,h}+1\bigr)+E^{\mathrm{add}}_{ij,h}, (2) where 𝑬 mul , 𝑬 add ∈ ℝ N × N × H \bm{E}^{\mathrm{mul}},\bm{E}^{\mathrm{add}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H} are obtained by linearly projecting E E and y y to H H -dimensional vectors. This head-wise FiLM-style modulation is applied inside the fused kernel via the score_mod hook, so no quadratic tensor is written to global memory during the attention pass. Padding and graph masks are handled via a BlockMask , allowing the kernel to skip fully-masked blocks. Single-pass node and edge update via 𝑰 𝑵 \bm{I_{N}} concatenation. A key challenge is that edge representations in the original backbone are updated from pre-softmax attention scores, which FlexAttention does not return. Instead, we use the normalized attention coefficients 𝜶 ∈ ℝ N × N × H \bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H} and recover them in a single FlexAttention call by concatenating an identity matrix 𝑰 𝑵 ∈ ℝ N × N \bm{I_{N}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} to the value matrix: FlexAttn ( 𝑸 , 𝑲 , [ 𝑽 ∥ 𝑰 𝑵 ] ) = 𝜶 [ 𝑽 ∥ 𝑰 𝑵 ] = [ 𝜶 𝑽 ∥ 𝜶 ] . \mathrm{FlexAttn}(\bm{Q},\,\bm{K},\,[\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{I_{N}}])\;=\;\bm{\alpha}[\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{I_{N}}]\;=\;[\bm{\alpha}\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{\alpha}]. (3) The kernel simultaneously produces the aggregated node values 𝑽 ′ = 𝜶 ​ 𝑽 ∈ ℝ N × H × d f \bm{V^{\prime}}=\bm{\alpha}\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times d_{f}} and the attention maps 𝜶 ∈ ℝ N × H × N \bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times N} as the trailing output channels. Edge representations are updated using: E i ​ j ′ = Linear ⁡ ( α i ​ j ⊙ ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒚 ) ) + E i ​ j , E^{\prime}_{ij}=\mathrm{Linear}\!\left(\alpha_{ij}\odot\phi(\bm{y})\right)+E_{ij}, (4) where ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒚 ) \phi(\bm{y}) provides a FiLM scale and bias learned from the global features 𝒚 \bm{y} . Node and edge updates thus share a single function call. This works well for the benchmark datasets we consider here, which contain graphs with fewer than 256 nodes. For larger graphs, the concatenation of N N channels to the value vectors increases the SRAM requirements, which necessitates a smaller block size and leads to worse throughput. In these cases, we calculate the attention output and the attention map in two separate passes, which allows us to keep an appropriate block size. We address this in more details in Appendix B.2 . The edge update remains quadratic in N N , but the dominant constant is reduced because the heavy attention computation itself is handled by FlexAttention. 4 Experiments We train our FlexAttentionGT architecture and the original GT backbone using the DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) framework, and evaluate on the Planar, SBM, and Tree datasets originally used in DeFoG, while keeping all training hyperparameters fixed across configurations. Performance is assessed using validity, uniqueness, and novelty (V.U.N. ↑ \uparrow ), as well as the Ratio ↓ \downarrow metric comparing graph-statistic distances between generated and test graphs relative to the train–test baseline. Percentages denote the relative change compared to the original implementation. 4.1 Graph generation performance Table 1 reports generation quality across all datasets. Our updated architecture matches or slightly improves upon the original GT on V.U.N. metrics, including a small gain on SBM. Although the Ratio metric is marginally higher on the SBM dataset, the differences remain within one standard deviation, which indicates comparable structural fidelity overall. We evaluate 1000 and 50 generation steps, respectively. 4.2 Speedup and memory usage improvement Figure 1 compares inference throughput, training speed, and peak GPU memory across datasets. Our model is substantially faster than the original one on both training and inference, with speedups ranging from 23% to 116% depending on the dataset and regime. Peak memory is reduced by approximately 65% across all datasets, roughly one third of the original. These gains are consistent across datasets, indicating that the efficiency improvements are not dataset-specific. 4.3 Additional experiments To isolate the contribution of our key design choices, we explore the effect of the number of generation steps (1000 vs. 50), model size via a scaled-down version of the original implementation ( Scaled Down ), and the edge update strategy via a variant without per-edge modulation of attention scores ( Light Edge ), both matched to our architecture in peak memory. Generation quality across training with 1000 steps. Figures 2(a) and 2(b) show V.U.N. curves on Planar and SBM with 1000 generation steps. Our model matches or improves on all baselines on convergence and final performance. GT (Scaled Down) learns more slowly and underperforms, showing that matching memory by reducing capacity is a poor trade-off. GT (Light Edge) fails to learn entirely, confirming that per-edge modulation of attention scores is a critical component. The effect is most pronounced on Planar, but our model also converges fastest on SBM. Generation quality across training with 50 steps. Figures 2(c) and 2(d) repeat the same comparison under a reduced budget of 50 generation steps. Under this constrained setting, GT (Light Edge) again fails to learn, and GT (Scaled Down) also fails in the Planar dataset. The original GT shows moderate but inconsistent performance, while our model achieves the best and most stable results across training, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and robustness in the low-step regime. Training dynamics. Figure 3 shows training loss curves on Planar for the original and updated models. The two curves overlap closely throughout training, indicating that the architectural changes do not alter the optimization landscape. This suggests that the observed quality differences are unlikely to originate from a change in how the model optimizes, but rather a benefit of the inductive biases of our attention layer. Figure 3 : Training loss comparison between FlexAttentionGT (Ours) and GT (Original), smoothed with a window size of 20. Similar optimization dynamics suggest that gains stem from the attention layer’s inductive bias. Edge update using normalized attention coefficients. Our edge updates use the normalized attention coefficients α i ​ j , h \alpha_{ij,h} recovered using (Eq. 3 ), whereas the baseline implementation uses unnormalized attention scores. To isolate the effect of this change, we implement a version of FlexAttentionGT which separately calculates the unnormalized attention coefficients and uses those for edge updates. We train this version on the planar dataset and report the V.U.N. curves with 1000 generation steps for both implementations in Figure 4 . The unnormalized variant converges more slowly, showing that the normalization provided by softmax is beneficial for stable edge feature learning. 0 10k 20k 30k 0 0 0.5 0.5 1 1 Training steps V.U.N. 4 Figure 4 : V.U.N. curves comparing normalized and unnormalized networks over training steps on the Planar dataset, evaluated with 1000 generation steps. 5 Conclusion In this work, we presented an efficient and expressive edge-aware graph Transformer that leverages recent fused attention kernels for graph generation. By shifting from element- to head-wise FiLM transformations, we eliminated major memory bottlenecks while preserving nuanced structural bias injection. Furthermore, our approach allows us to seamlessly extract the attention map and concurrently update edge features within a single kernel pass. Our empirical benchmarks across Planar, Tree, and SBM datasets demonstrate that this architectural refinement yields an average of 44.8 % \bm{44.8\%} speedup in training, an average of 94.4 % \bm{94.4\%} speedup in inference, and consumes 𝟔𝟓 % \bm{65\%} less peak GPU memory compared to the original dense implementation, with no loss in generation fidelity. These gains can be particularly relevant in the context of graph foundation models, where scaling edge-aware architectures to larger and more diverse graphs is a key challenge. Beyond graph generation, the design principles introduced here (head-wise structural conditioning inside a fused kernel and single-pass node-edge updates) could be applicable to any edge-aware transformer setting, including those used in graph classification, regression, and link prediction, offering a practical path toward more scalable graph learning. items.raw_text: Efficient Edge-aware Attention Network for Graph Generation Vincent Jung Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Affiliation: Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano, Switzerland Alba Carballo-Castro Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Yiming Qin Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Lonneke van der Plas Affiliation: Università della Svizzera italiana, Lugano, Switzerland Pascal Frossard Correspondence to: first_name.last_name@epfl.ch Affiliation: LTS4, EPFL, Lausanne, Switzerland Abstract Graph generative models commonly use graph-specific Transformer architectures to jointly update node and edge features. However, these architectures do not directly benefit from recent hardware-aware attention implementations, limiting their scalability. The adaptation is, however, non-trivial: edge and graph-level features must be injected into pairwise attention scores, graph masks must be respected, and dynamic edge updates remain a major source of quadratic memory usage. We propose an edge-aware attention layer for graph generation that incorporates structural information through head-wise score modulation, while updating edge representations with a lightweight residual mechanism that retains attention-score dependent edge updates. This layer can be effectively implemented using PyTorch’s FlexAttention . We achieve similar generation quality to our baseline while reducing peak GPU memory by around 65% and substantially improving training and sampling throughput. These results suggest that the proposed architecture is a practical step toward scalable graph foundation models. Keywords: Machine Learning, ICML † † affiliationnotice: Equal contribution Code 1 Introduction Graph generation ( Simonovsky & Komodakis, 2018 ; Martinkus et al., 2022 ; Jo et al., 2024 ) has advanced substantially with discrete diffusion and flow-based models. A particularly influential line of work, initiated by the diffusion model DiGress ( Vignac et al., 2023 ) , and then flow-based models such as CatFlow ( Eijkelboom et al., 2024 ) , DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) , BWFlow ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) , and VBFN ( Xiong et al., 2026 ) , and diffusion models such as Cometh ( Siraudin et al., 2025 ) , relies on a specific transformer backbone to denoise categorical node and edge features. This architecture is inspired by the original Graph Transformer ( Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021 ) , which already updates edge states from attention scores and uses edge states to modulate self-attention. The main differences are that it computes attention between all nodes as opposed to restricting it to neighbors, maintains a graph-level feature vector and uses FiLM ( Perez et al., 2018 ) modules to couple node, edge, and graph-level features. This dense, layered interaction is central to its success in graph generation, where the model must capture both local connectivity and global graph structure. However, this expressivity comes with a computational cost. Since the model must maintain dense pairwise edge states, both attention computation and dynamic edge representations scale quadratically with the number of nodes, making training expensive and difficult under limited GPU resources. A large body of work addresses this bottleneck through sparse attention patterns ( Shirzad et al., 2023 ) ; hybrid local-global designs ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) ; linear and operator-based alternatives ( Deng et al., 2024 ; Sancak et al., 2025 ) ; or tokenization-based formulations that cast graphs as sequences of node and edge tokens and apply standard Transformers with minimal graph-specific modifications ( Kim et al., 2022 ) . These methods are effective, but typically modify or replace dense self-attention altogether. In graph generation specifically, SparseDiff ( Qin et al., 2025b ) exploits sparsity to enable training on larger graphs, although this increases sampling time. In this work, we take a complementary route and ask whether the original dense edge-aware architecture can be implemented more efficiently while fully preserving its inductive bias. We focus on the computationally-expensive and memory-hungry attention layer in the original implementation, and design a kernel-friendly version which still modulates attention scores using edge and global features, respects graph masks, and enables edge features update from its attention map. This version can be implemented entirely using FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , which supports custom attention score modifications and masking. This enables us to use fused attention kernels, bringing throughput and memory gains. Empirically, our proposed model (FlexAttentionGT) matches the generation quality of DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) ’s original backbone while reducing peak memory by 65% and improving training and inference throughput by 45% and 94% on average. Ablations show that the edge update is critical: simplifying it causes generation collapse, whereas reducing model size leads to slower convergence and worse final performance. Together, these results demonstrate that edge-aware graph Transformers can be made more efficient with tailored design while preserving their expressivity, supporting their scalability to the larger graphs encountered in foundation model settings. 2 Background and related work Generative Graph Transformer Recent works in graph generation such as DiGress ( Vignac et al., 2023 ) or BWFlow ( Jiang et al., 2026 ) employ a Graph Transformer (GT) backbone that jointly updates node features 𝑿 ∈ ℝ N × d x \bm{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{x}} , edge features 𝑬 ∈ ℝ N × N × d e \bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}} , and graph-level features 𝒚 ∈ ℝ d y \bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} , with N N the number of nodes of the largest graph in a batch. In contrast to the original Graph Transformer ( Dwivedi & Bresson, 2021 ) , this backbone keeps dense edge features and graph-level features, and injects them into node attention through FiLM-style score modulation ( Perez et al., 2018 ) (Further details in Appendix C.1 ). The attention map is then reused to update edge features, while graph-level features are updated from pooled node and edge representations. This design is effective for graph generation because it tightly couples node-, edge-, and graph-level information. However, it bottlenecks efficiency: the model maintains dense pairwise edge states 𝑬 \bm{E} , which need to be included in the node attention, and themselves updated using these attention scores, resulting in quadratic computational and memory costs per layer. Structural attention biases and edge-aware architectures. A central approach to injecting graph structure into Transformers is modulating attention logits with structural features. Graphormer ( Ying et al., 2021 ) introduced spatial and edge encodings as additive biases on pre-softmax logits. EGT ( Hussain et al., 2022 ) proposed bidirectional coupling between explicit edge channels and node attention, architecturally close to the generative GT backbone we build upon. Relational Attention ( Diao & Loynd, 2023 ) similarly updates edge vectors at each layer. Our work preserves this dense edge coupling while making it compatible with fused attention kernels. Adjacency masking and hybrid designs. Exphormer ( Shirzad et al., 2023 ) builds sparse attention from local neighborhoods, expander graphs and virtual global nodes, yielding a scalable graph transformer; GraphGPS ( Rampášek et al., 2022 ) runs a local MPNN and a global Transformer in parallel, avoiding committing entirely to dense or sparse attention. In graph generation, SparseDiff ( Qin et al., 2025b ) exploits graph sparsity to scale to larger graphs, but relies on message-passing layers that are less amenable to efficient parallel computation. Scalable alternatives. Polynormer ( Deng et al., 2024 ) combines linear-time attention with a polynomial-expressive formulation to balance scalability and expressivity, GECO ( Sancak et al., 2025 ) proposes a scalable operator-based alternative, and tokenization-based methods ( Kim et al., 2022 ) apply standard Transformers to node and edge token sequences with minimal graph-specific modifications. These approaches are effective, but typically modify or replace dense attention altogether. Graph foundation models. As graph learning scales toward foundation model settings, the cost of dense edge-aware attention becomes increasingly prohibitive. GraphBFF ( Bechler-Speicher et al., 2026 ) addresses this for large heterogeneous graphs by replacing dense attention with type-aware sparse attention. Our work takes a complementary route: rather than replacing the dense backbone, we make it hardware-efficient through fused kernels, preserving the inductive bias that drives generation quality and enabling its application at larger scales. We refer the reader to Appendix A for a more detailed overview of the relevant literature. 3 Efficient Attention Layers for Graph Generation We identify three challenges in making the generative GT backbone compatible with fused attention kernels. (i) The original architecture uses element-wise outer-product attention, producing a d f d_{f} -dimensional tensor per node pair that standard fused kernels cannot process. (ii) Edge and global features must still modulate pairwise attention scores in a way that is both expressive and kernel-compatible. (iii) Edge representations depend on the softmax attention probabilities α \alpha , which fused kernels do not materialize in global memory. We address each challenge in turn, with further implementation details in Appendices C.2 and C.3 . FlexAttention . We leverage FlexAttention ( Dong et al., 2025 ) , a PyTorch interface that lowers customized attention variants to fused Triton kernels. It exposes two hooks: score_mod modifies each pre-softmax attention logit, enabling structural biases and edge-dependent score modulation; mask_mod specifies which query-key pairs are valid, compiled into a block-sparse BlockMask that allows the kernel to skip fully-masked blocks. This interface is well-suited for injecting graph masks and structural biases into attention; however, it does not natively support the edge update used in generative graph Transformers, since it only returns the attended node values. We address this below. From element-wise to scalar dot-product attention. The original backbone computes an unnormalized attention tensor 𝒀 ∈ ℝ N × N × H × d f \bm{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H\times d_{f}} via the element-wise outer product 𝒀 i ​ j , h = 𝒒 i , h ⊙ 𝒌 j , h \bm{Y}_{ij,h}=\bm{q}_{i,h}\odot\bm{k}_{j,h} , retaining a d f d_{f} -dimensional feature vector per node pair and head. Softmax is then applied independently per channel , yielding d f d_{f} separate attention distributions per query-head pair. While expressive, this formulation cannot be lowered to a standard fused kernel. We replace it with standard scaled dot-product attention. The unnormalized scalar logit for each head h h is s i ​ j , h = 𝒒 i , h ⋅ 𝒌 j , h d f ∈ ℝ , s_{ij,h}=\frac{\bm{q}_{i,h}\cdot\bm{k}_{j,h}}{\sqrt{d_{f}}}\in\mathbb{R}, (1) giving a single attention distribution per query-head pair and making the node-update compatible with standard FlexAttention. Head-wise structural FiLM layer To inject edge features 𝑬 ∈ ℝ N × N × d e \bm{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times d_{e}} and global features 𝒚 ∈ ℝ d y \bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{y}} into attention, we learn one scalar per edge and attention head: s i ​ j , h ′ = s i ​ j , h ⋅ ( E i ​ j , h mul + 1 ) + E i ​ j , h add , s^{\prime}_{ij,h}=s_{ij,h}\cdot\bigl(E^{\mathrm{mul}}_{ij,h}+1\bigr)+E^{\mathrm{add}}_{ij,h}, (2) where 𝑬 mul , 𝑬 add ∈ ℝ N × N × H \bm{E}^{\mathrm{mul}},\bm{E}^{\mathrm{add}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H} are obtained by linearly projecting E E and y y to H H -dimensional vectors. This head-wise FiLM-style modulation is applied inside the fused kernel via the score_mod hook, so no quadratic tensor is written to global memory during the attention pass. Padding and graph masks are handled via a BlockMask , allowing the kernel to skip fully-masked blocks. Single-pass node and edge update via 𝑰 𝑵 \bm{I_{N}} concatenation. A key challenge is that edge representations in the original backbone are updated from pre-softmax attention scores, which FlexAttention does not return. Instead, we use the normalized attention coefficients 𝜶 ∈ ℝ N × N × H \bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N\times H} and recover them in a single FlexAttention call by concatenating an identity matrix 𝑰 𝑵 ∈ ℝ N × N \bm{I_{N}}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N} to the value matrix: FlexAttn ( 𝑸 , 𝑲 , [ 𝑽 ∥ 𝑰 𝑵 ] ) = 𝜶 [ 𝑽 ∥ 𝑰 𝑵 ] = [ 𝜶 𝑽 ∥ 𝜶 ] . \mathrm{FlexAttn}(\bm{Q},\,\bm{K},\,[\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{I_{N}}])\;=\;\bm{\alpha}[\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{I_{N}}]\;=\;[\bm{\alpha}\bm{V}\,\|\,\bm{\alpha}]. (3) The kernel simultaneously produces the aggregated node values 𝑽 ′ = 𝜶 ​ 𝑽 ∈ ℝ N × H × d f \bm{V^{\prime}}=\bm{\alpha}\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times d_{f}} and the attention maps 𝜶 ∈ ℝ N × H × N \bm{\alpha}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times H\times N} as the trailing output channels. Edge representations are updated using: E i ​ j ′ = Linear ⁡ ( α i ​ j ⊙ ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒚 ) ) + E i ​ j , E^{\prime}_{ij}=\mathrm{Linear}\!\left(\alpha_{ij}\odot\phi(\bm{y})\right)+E_{ij}, (4) where ϕ ⁡ ( 𝒚 ) \phi(\bm{y}) provides a FiLM scale and bias learned from the global features 𝒚 \bm{y} . Node and edge updates thus share a single function call. This works well for the benchmark datasets we consider here, which contain graphs with fewer than 256 nodes. For larger graphs, the concatenation of N N channels to the value vectors increases the SRAM requirements, which necessitates a smaller block size and leads to worse throughput. In these cases, we calculate the attention output and the attention map in two separate passes, which allows us to keep an appropriate block size. We address this in more details in Appendix B.2 . The edge update remains quadratic in N N , but the dominant constant is reduced because the heavy attention computation itself is handled by FlexAttention. 4 Experiments We train our FlexAttentionGT architecture and the original GT backbone using the DeFoG ( Qin et al., 2025a ) framework, and evaluate on the Planar, SBM, and Tree datasets originally used in DeFoG, while keeping all training hyperparameters fixed across configurations. Performance is assessed using validity, uniqueness, and novelty (V.U.N. ↑ \uparrow ), as well as the Ratio ↓ \downarrow metric comparing graph-statistic distances between generated and test graphs relative to the train–test baseline. Our model is substantially faster than the original one on both training and inference, with speedups ranging from 23% to 116% depending on the dataset and regime. Peak memory is reduced by approximately 65% across all datasets, roughly one third of the original. These gains are consistent across datasets, indicating that the efficiency improvements are not dataset-specific. 4.3 Additional experiments To isolate the contribution of our key design choices, we explore the effect of the number of generation steps (1000 vs. 50), model size via a scaled-down version of the original implementation ( Scaled Down ), and the edge update strategy via a variant without per-edge modulation of attention scores ( Light Edge ), both matched to our architecture in peak memory. Generation quality across training with 1000 steps. Figures 2(a) and 2(b) show V.U.N. curves on Planar and SBM with 1000 generation steps. Our model matches or improves on all baselines on convergence and final performance. GT (Scaled Down) learns more slowly and underperforms, showing that matching memory by reducing capacity is a poor trade-off. GT (Light Edge) fails to learn entirely, confirming that per-edge modulation of attention scores is a critical component. The effect is most pronounced on Planar, but our model also converges fastest on SBM. Generation quality across training with 50 steps. Figures 2(c) and 2(d) repeat the same comparison under a reduced budget of 50 generation steps. Under this constrained setting, GT (Light Edge) again fails to learn, and GT (Scaled Down) also fails in the Planar dataset. The original GT shows moderate but inconsistent performance, while our model achieves the best and most stable results across training, demonstrating improved sample efficiency and robustness in the low-step regime. Training dynamics. Figure 3 shows training loss curves on Planar for the original and updated models. The two curves overlap closely throughout training, indicating that the architectural changes do not alter the optimization landscape. This suggests that the observed quality differences are unlikely to originate from a change in how the model optimizes, but rather a benefit of the inductive biases of our attention layer. Similar optimization dynamics suggest that gains stem from the attention layer’s inductive bias. Edge update using normalized attention coefficients. Our edge updates use the normalized attention coefficients α i ​ j , h \alpha_{ij,h} recovered using (Eq. 3 ), whereas the baseline implementation uses unnormalized attention scores. To isolate the effect of this change, we implement a version of FlexAttentionGT which separately calculates the unnormalized attention coefficients and uses those for edge updates. We train this version on the planar dataset and report the V.U.N. curves with 1000 generation steps for both implementations in Figure 4 . The unnormalized variant converges more slowly, showing that the normalization provided by softmax is beneficial for stable edge feature learning. 0 10k 20k 30k 0 0 0.5 0.5 1 1 Training steps V.U.N. 4 Figure 4 : V.U.N. curves comparing normalized and unnormalized networks over training steps on the Planar dataset, evaluated with 1000 generation steps. 5 Conclusion In this work, we presented an efficient and expressive edge-aware graph Transformer that leverages recent fused attention kernels for graph generation. By shifting from element- to head-wise FiLM transformations, we eliminated major memory bottlenecks while preserving nuanced structural bias injection. Furthermore, our approach allows us to seamlessly extract the attention map and concurrently update edge features within a single kernel pass. Our empirical benchmarks across Planar, Tree, and SBM datasets demonstrate that this architectural refinement yields an average of 44.8 % \bm{44.8\%} speedup in training, an average of 94.4 % \bm{94.4\%} speedup in inference, and consumes 𝟔𝟓 % \bm{65\%} less peak GPU memory compared to the original dense implementation, with no loss in generation fidelity. These gains can be particularly relevant in the context of graph foundation models, where scaling edge-aware architectures to larger and more diverse graphs is a key challenge. Beyond graph generation, the design principles introduced here (head-wise structural conditioning inside a fused kernel and single-pass node-edge updates) could be applicable to any edge-aware transformer setting, including those used in graph classification, regression, and link prediction, offering a practical path toward more scalable graph learning. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28602 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification Authors: Vasilii Feofanov , Zhenghan Tai , Andrei Ermakov , Irina Rish View a PDF of the paper titled Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification, by Vasilii Feofanov and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an "old-school" convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an "old-school" convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem.
