items.content: \workshoptitle WORKSHOP TITLE Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification Vasilii Feofanov Affiliation: 42 NL Email: vfeofanov@42.com Zhenghan Tai Affiliation: University of Toronto Andrei Ermakov Affiliation: 42 NL Irina Rish Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: Mila - Quebec AI Institute Abstract TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an “old-school” convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem. 1 Introduction Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to provide a single frozen encoder whose features are useful across downstream datasets, removing the need to train a specialized model per task ( Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Goswami et al., 2024 ) . Most of TSFMs use transformer architecture pre-trained on a large corpus of time series, real and / or synthetic ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . Prior to foundation models, the same problem was attacked from another angle: self-supervised methods such as TS2Vec ( Yue et al., 2022 ) , T-Loss ( Franceschi et al., 2019 ) and TNC ( Tonekaboni et al., 2021 ) train a small encoder separately on each target dataset . TS2Vec in particular remains a standard and strong baseline, but its design is viewed as somewhat outdated, and it has never been evaluated as a universal encoder itself. This paper asks whether it can become one. The answer is yes, with three changes (Figure 1 ): pretrain once on synthetic data; give the encoder raw and instance-normalized input views through separate stems; and distill ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) two resulting specialists into a single encoder. The specialists retain the original TS2Vec architecture and contrastive objective, while the student uses the same residual-block design with modified input and output layers and is trained by distillation. The result is notable for two reasons. First, the resulting 1.6M-parameter encoder is competitive: frozen, it outperforms per-dataset TS2Vec and the evaluated forecasting-based extractors, and comes within a few tenths of a percentage point of MantisV2 while using about 25% fewer parameters. Second, it reaches this performance with a markedly different design — convolutions instead of attention, a two-layer MLP stem instead of a hand-designed multi-view tokenizer, and the final representation rather than a selected intermediate layer. This near-parity suggests that the information exposed to the encoder may matter more than the specific tokenizer design; our ablations point in particular to the complementarity of amplitude and shape. Figure 1: TS2Vec-FM architecture and training. (a) Raw and instance-normalized inputs pass through an MLP and a linear stem, respectively. Their concatenation feeds a shared convolutional trunk and temporal max pooling. (b) Two specialists are pretrained on synthetic data with the TS2Vec objective and then frozen. On the same data, each teacher supervises one 320-dimensional half of the student through timestamp-level and pooled cosine losses. Downstream, only a classifier on frozen student features is fitted. 2 From per-dataset TS2Vec to a foundation model Original TS2Vec. The reference encoder first maps each timestamp to 64 channels, then applies ten hidden residual blocks and one output block with exponentially increasing dilation, producing a 320-dimensional representation at every timestamp. It is trained on aligned regions of two overlapping contextual crops with a hierarchical objective that contrasts both timestamps within a series and instances within a batch. A global series embedding is the temporal maximum of these representations. Appendix A specifies the architecture, crops, and losses exactly. Step 1: the pre-training regime. We pretrain once on univariate synthetic series generated by CauKer ( Xie et al., 2026 ) algorithm, so all encoder weight updates use synthetic data. The advantage of the TS2Vec architercture is that a convolutional encoder needs no fixed input size, so series keep their native lengths. However, similar to most time series foundation models, our encoder is univariate, so for multivariate datasets, we encode channels independently with the embeddings concatenated. Step 2: normalization. Original TS2Vec does not apply instance-wise normalization. For classification, however, absolute signal values may contain discriminative information. We therefore pretrain separate TS2Vec encoders on raw and instance-normalized inputs. The results (Table 2 ) have been quite unexpected. The encoder without normalization performs significantly better on the multivariate (UEA) datasets, while the encoder with normalization greatly outperforms its counterpart on the univariate (UCR) datasets: instance normalization gains 2.9 pp on UCR but costs 1.5 pp on UEA, and the raw-input encoder is the mirror image. We suggest that this phenomenon is explained by the nature of contrastive pre-training which looks for shortcuts to discriminate different samples in the embedding space. In the un-normalized case, the shortcut is the amplitude of the signal, so embeddings encode mostly this kind of information. In the normalized case, the shortcut is rather the shape of the signal. More arguments to this hypothesis gives the fact that in many multivariate datasets a deviation of one channel compared to the others gives a discriminative signal, so encoding signal amplitude is important. Step 3: architecture. Given the aforementioned results, we slightly modify the encoder to include both normalized and raw views: the instance-normalized view is linearly mapped into 32 channels, while the raw view is embedded through a two-layer MLP with a GELU nonlinearity. Their concatenation forms the 64-channel input of the shared convolutional part. So, we retain the TS2Vec residual-block design and increase the output dimension from 320 to 640, yielding a 1.64M-parameter encoder. We note that the asymmetry between the two views matters as the raw view needs the extra nonlinearity to align its encodings with the normalized one. Step 4: distillation. The performance discrepancy between the normalized and un-normalized encoders has motivated us to use them as teachers (further also called specialists) to distill their knowledge into our dual-input single encoder. We use a factorized objective, matching each half of the 640-dimensional student representation to its corresponding teacher by cosine loss, per timestamp and after pooling. What is interesting is that directly pre-training the dual-input encoder with the usual TS2Vec contrastive objective yields inferior results (Table 2 ). 3 Experimental Results Setup. Further, we refer our approach (synthetic pre-training, dual-input architecture, distillation) as TS2Vec-FM . We compare it with other methods by evaluating frozen representations on UCR-128 ( Dau et al., 2019 ) and UEA-27 ( Bagnall et al., 2018 ) , following Feofanov et al. (2026a) . Dataset-specific classifiers are a 200-tree random forest (RF), averaged over three predictor seeds, and logistic regression (LogReg) preceded by StandardScaler. Pre-training checkpoints are selected by UCR RF accuracy at seed 42; UEA is not used for checkpoint selection. We compare against Catch22+ ( Lubba et al., 2019 ) , MOMENT ( Goswami et al., 2024 ) , TiRex ( Auer et al., 2025b ) , Chronos-2 ( Ansari et al., 2025 ) , TiViT-H / TiConvNext ( Roschmann et al., 2025 ) , NuTime ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , and Mantis (V2 checkpoint, Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Feofanov et al., 2026b ). Table 1: Zero-shot feature extraction accuracy (%), with parameters counted after layer pruning where applicable. The dashed rule separates the original per-dataset TS2Vec, which is not a foundation model: it trains one encoder on each dataset’s own training split (128 UCR and 27 UEA encoders of 0.6M parameters). ‡ With its original RBF-SVM probe it reaches 82.10 on UCR. Random forest LogReg Model Type Params UCR UEA UCR UEA Catch22+ statistics — 79.69 69.63 77.04 67.56 MOMENT forecasting 161.4M 77.89 69.91 79.84 71.74 NuTime classification 2.0M 77.32 71.99 79.05 74.91 TiRex forecasting 16.5M 80.13 69.52 82.02 72.48 Chronos-2 forecasting 44.0M 80.02 69.67 82.44 72.43 TiViT-H vision 276.6M 79.43 70.91 82.88 73.30 TiConvNext vision 180.3M 80.29 71.05 83.47 73.50 MantisV2 classification 2.2M 81.95 74.20 83.60 75.52 TS2Vec-FM, one encoder classification 1.64M 81.76 73.60 83.32 75.30 Reference (not zero-shot: one encoder trained per target dataset) TS2Vec, per dataset ‡ self-supervised 0.6M each 79.83 69.50 81.36 70.79 The recipe produces a competitive TSFM (Table 1 ). The proposed TS2Vec-FM shows the second-best result, trailing MantisV2 by 0.19 / 0.60 pp with RF and 0.28 / 0.22 pp with LogReg, respectively, while using about 25% fewer parameters. At the same time, it outperforms the forecasting- and vision-based extractors (10–170 × \times as many parameters), except TiConvNext on UCR LogReg. We would like to note that unlike MantisV2, our encoder uses native lengths and does not need interpolate each series to a fixed length. In Appendix D , we show that interpolating series worsen the performance of TS2Vec-FM. It also beats TS2Vec trained per dataset. Under both the random forest and logistic regression probe, the margin between the foundation model and per-dataset encoder is more that 1.9 % on UCR. The gap widens even more on multivariate UEA-27, even though TS2Vec-FM was pre-trained on univariate data. Note that in the original TS2Vec paper, they use an RBF-SVM with hyperparameters tuned, which increases the probing performance, though still below TS2Vec-FM with logistic regression. We have also tried to reproduce the results published by Yue et al. (2022) in two different setups: first, our reimplementation of the original protocol that reproduces the published UCR-128 performance to within 0.8 pp with a per-dataset correlation of 0.984, and second, we have run the authors’ unmodified code that reproduces fifteen of the sixteen evaluable headline metrics of the original paper (across all classification, forecasting and anomaly detection) within 5% relative (see Appendix C ). Table 2: What each ingredient contributes (random forest, %) at 100K, 1M and 2M synthetic series. Instance normalization trades UEA for UCR at every scale, the specialists and the direct contrastive baseline do not improve with more data, and distillation consolidates the two specialists into the stronger single encoder at every scale. † mean over three pre-training seeds; ‡ with gradient clipping. 100K series 1M series 2M series Encoder input Training UCR UEA UCR UEA UCR UEA raw only contrastive 77.43 † 72.02 † 76.99 71.56 77.68 72.22 normalized only contrastive 80.35 † 70.56 † 80.26 69.78 79.89 70.19 dual-input contrastive 80.52 † 73.41 † 80.52 ‡ 73.41 ‡ 80.52 ‡ 73.07 ‡ dual-input distillation (ours) 81.08 † 73.90 † 81.62 † 73.48 † 81.76 73.60 Ablation of the recipe (Table 2 ). We first ask whether more synthetic data helps. For the ingredients taken alone the answer is negative: from 100K to 1M and 2M series, the two specialists and the dual-input encoder pre-trained directly with the contrastive TS2Vec loss stay within seed noise or slightly degrade (the instance-normalized specialist loses 0.5 pp on UCR). The distilled encoder is the only one that benefits: on UCR it gains 0.54 pp from 100K to 1M (81.08 to 81.62%, three pre-training seeds each, seed standard deviation 0.12 pp) and a further 0.14 pp at 2M, while on UEA it stays flat (73.9, 73.5 and 73.6%). We detail the scaling experiments further in Appendix D . The comparison with the directly pre-trained dual-input encoder also isolates the contribution of distillation: it is superior at every scale, and its margin widens with data, from 0.56 pp at 100K to 1.10 pp at 1M and 1.24 pp at 2M on UCR. We also note that we had to use gradient clipping for the contrastive baseline due to numerical instability. The pattern suggests that direct training underuses the complementary views, while already-specialized teachers keep both subspaces alive. This is, in effect, a learned substitute for what hand-designed TSFM tokenizers provide by construction when they devote separate branches to the normalized signal and to raw patch statistics ( Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . 4 Discussion In this paper, we introduced TS2Vec-FM, showing that synthetic pretraining and specialist distillation can make a compact convolutional encoder competitive for cross-dataset classification while retaining native-length processing. The results motivate revisiting earlier self-supervised architectures, adapting them to the current setup and thereby enriching the family of available time series foundation models. Limitations. The 2M headline model is trained at a single pre-training seed, although the 100K ablations and the 1M student use three seeds. TS2Vec-FM remains slightly below MantisV2 on all four metrics, so our claim is competitive performance with a smaller encoder rather than superiority. Evaluation is limited to UCR and UEA, and whether specialist distillation generalizes to other backbones and tokenizer designs remains open. References Ansari et al. (2025) A. F. Ansari, O. Cited by: Appendix B . Appendix A TS2Vec: architecture and objective This section gives more details on the TS2Vec model and training objective. Our implementation follows the authors’ released code [ Yue et al., 2022 ] . Figure 2: Reference TS2Vec encoder. Ten width-64 residual blocks with dilation 2 i 2^{i} are followed by a width-320 output block; one block is detailed in Figure 3 . Figure 3: One TS2Vec residual block: two GELU–dilated-convolution pairs plus a skip connection (identity, or a 1 × 1 1\times 1 convolution when the width changes). Encoder. items.raw_text: \workshoptitle WORKSHOP TITLE Turning TS2Vec into a Foundation Model for Time Series Classification Vasilii Feofanov Affiliation: 42 NL Email: vfeofanov@42.com Zhenghan Tai Affiliation: University of Toronto Andrei Ermakov Affiliation: 42 NL Irina Rish Affiliation: Université de Montréal Affiliation: Mila - Quebec AI Institute Abstract TS2Vec is one of the strongest self-supervised methods for time series classification, introduced in 2022. It is designed to be trained anew on every dataset: self-supervised pre-training followed by linear probing. Since then, the field has shifted towards foundation models that reuse one encoder across datasets. Yet TS2Vec offers a compact convolutional architecture that operates directly on temporal samples and accepts variable-length inputs without resampling. We ask whether these properties can be retained when the encoder is pre-trained only once, and show that they can: TS2Vec can essentially be turned into a foundation model. Three changes suffice: pre-train on a synthetic corpus, feed the encoder a raw amplitude view and an instance-normalized shape view of the input through two small stems, and distill one specialist encoder per view into a single encoder. The result, TS2Vec-FM, is a 1.6M-parameter dilated convolutional network that, kept frozen, reaches 83.3% on UCR-128 and 75.3% on UEA-27 under linear probing, within 0.3 pp of MantisV2, the current state of the art, and above TS2Vec trained separately on each target dataset. What we find most interesting is how different TS2Vec-FM is from other foundation models in design: near-parity is reached without attention, without a patch tokenizer, and without intermediate-layer extraction, using an “old-school” convolutional encoder and a two-layer MLP stem. 1 Introduction Time series foundation models (TSFMs) aim to provide a single frozen encoder whose features are useful across downstream datasets, removing the need to train a specialized model per task ( Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2024 ; Goswami et al., 2024 ) . Most of TSFMs use transformer architecture pre-trained on a large corpus of time series, real and / or synthetic ( Xie et al., 2026 ) . Prior to foundation models, the same problem was attacked from another angle: self-supervised methods such as TS2Vec ( Yue et al., 2022 ) , T-Loss ( Franceschi et al., 2019 ) and TNC ( Tonekaboni et al., 2021 ) train a small encoder separately on each target dataset . TS2Vec in particular remains a standard and strong baseline, but its design is viewed as somewhat outdated, and it has never been evaluated as a universal encoder itself. This paper asks whether it can become one. The answer is yes, with three changes (Figure 1 ): pretrain once on synthetic data; give the encoder raw and instance-normalized input views through separate stems; and distill ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) two resulting specialists into a single encoder. The specialists retain the original TS2Vec architecture and contrastive objective, while the student uses the same residual-block design with modified input and output layers and is trained by distillation. The result is notable for two reasons. First, the resulting 1.6M-parameter encoder is competitive: frozen, it outperforms per-dataset TS2Vec and the evaluated forecasting-based extractors, and comes within a few tenths of a percentage point of MantisV2 while using about 25% fewer parameters. Second, it reaches this performance with a markedly different design — convolutions instead of attention, a two-layer MLP stem instead of a hand-designed multi-view tokenizer, and the final representation rather than a selected intermediate layer. This near-parity suggests that the information exposed to the encoder may matter more than the specific tokenizer design; our ablations point in particular to the complementarity of amplitude and shape. Figure 1: TS2Vec-FM architecture and training. (a) Raw and instance-normalized inputs pass through an MLP and a linear stem, respectively. Their concatenation feeds a shared convolutional trunk and temporal max pooling. (b) Two specialists are pretrained on synthetic data with the TS2Vec objective and then frozen. On the same data, each teacher supervises one 320-dimensional half of the student through timestamp-level and pooled cosine losses. Downstream, only a classifier on frozen student features is fitted. 2 From per-dataset TS2Vec to a foundation model Original TS2Vec. The reference encoder first maps each timestamp to 64 channels, then applies ten hidden residual blocks and one output block with exponentially increasing dilation, producing a 320-dimensional representation at every timestamp. It is trained on aligned regions of two overlapping contextual crops with a hierarchical objective that contrasts both timestamps within a series and instances within a batch. A global series embedding is the temporal maximum of these representations. Appendix A specifies the architecture, crops, and losses exactly. Step 1: the pre-training regime. We pretrain once on univariate synthetic series generated by CauKer ( Xie et al., 2026 ) algorithm, so all encoder weight updates use synthetic data. The advantage of the TS2Vec architercture is that a convolutional encoder needs no fixed input size, so series keep their native lengths. However, similar to most time series foundation models, our encoder is univariate, so for multivariate datasets, we encode channels independently with the embeddings concatenated. Step 2: normalization. Original TS2Vec does not apply instance-wise normalization. For classification, however, absolute signal values may contain discriminative information. We therefore pretrain separate TS2Vec encoders on raw and instance-normalized inputs. The results (Table 2 ) have been quite unexpected. The encoder without normalization performs significantly better on the multivariate (UEA) datasets, while the encoder with normalization greatly outperforms its counterpart on the univariate (UCR) datasets: instance normalization gains 2.9 pp on UCR but costs 1.5 pp on UEA, and the raw-input encoder is the mirror image. We suggest that this phenomenon is explained by the nature of contrastive pre-training which looks for shortcuts to discriminate different samples in the embedding space. In the un-normalized case, the shortcut is the amplitude of the signal, so embeddings encode mostly this kind of information. In the normalized case, the shortcut is rather the shape of the signal. More arguments to this hypothesis gives the fact that in many multivariate datasets a deviation of one channel compared to the others gives a discriminative signal, so encoding signal amplitude is important. Step 3: architecture. Given the aforementioned results, we slightly modify the encoder to include both normalized and raw views: the instance-normalized view is linearly mapped into 32 channels, while the raw view is embedded through a two-layer MLP with a GELU nonlinearity. Their concatenation forms the 64-channel input of the shared convolutional part. So, we retain the TS2Vec residual-block design and increase the output dimension from 320 to 640, yielding a 1.64M-parameter encoder. We note that the asymmetry between the two views matters as the raw view needs the extra nonlinearity to align its encodings with the normalized one. Step 4: distillation. The performance discrepancy between the normalized and un-normalized encoders has motivated us to use them as teachers (further also called specialists) to distill their knowledge into our dual-input single encoder. We use a factorized objective, matching each half of the 640-dimensional student representation to its corresponding teacher by cosine loss, per timestamp and after pooling. What is interesting is that directly pre-training the dual-input encoder with the usual TS2Vec contrastive objective yields inferior results (Table 2 ). 3 Experimental Results Setup. Further, we refer our approach (synthetic pre-training, dual-input architecture, distillation) as TS2Vec-FM . We compare it with other methods by evaluating frozen representations on UCR-128 ( Dau et al., 2019 ) and UEA-27 ( Bagnall et al., 2018 ) , following Feofanov et al. (2026a) . Dataset-specific classifiers are a 200-tree random forest (RF), averaged over three predictor seeds, and logistic regression (LogReg) preceded by StandardScaler. Pre-training checkpoints are selected by UCR RF accuracy at seed 42; UEA is not used for checkpoint selection. We compare against Catch22+ ( Lubba et al., 2019 ) , MOMENT ( Goswami et al., 2024 ) , TiRex ( Auer et al., 2025b ) , Chronos-2 ( Ansari et al., 2025 ) , TiViT-H / TiConvNext ( Roschmann et al., 2025 ) , NuTime ( Lin et al., 2024 ) , and Mantis (V2 checkpoint, Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Feofanov et al., 2026b ). Table 1: Zero-shot feature extraction accuracy (%), with parameters counted after layer pruning where applicable. The dashed rule separates the original per-dataset TS2Vec, which is not a foundation model: it trains one encoder on each dataset’s own training split (128 UCR and 27 UEA encoders of 0.6M parameters). ‡ With its original RBF-SVM probe it reaches 82.10 on UCR. Random forest LogReg Model Type Params UCR UEA UCR UEA Catch22+ statistics — 79.69 69.63 77.04 67.56 MOMENT forecasting 161.4M 77.89 69.91 79.84 71.74 NuTime classification 2.0M 77.32 71.99 79.05 74.91 TiRex forecasting 16.5M 80.13 69.52 82.02 72.48 Chronos-2 forecasting 44.0M 80.02 69.67 82.44 72.43 TiViT-H vision 276.6M 79.43 70.91 82.88 73.30 TiConvNext vision 180.3M 80.29 71.05 83.47 73.50 MantisV2 classification 2.2M 81.95 74.20 83.60 75.52 TS2Vec-FM, one encoder classification 1.64M 81.76 73.60 83.32 75.30 Reference (not zero-shot: one encoder trained per target dataset) TS2Vec, per dataset ‡ self-supervised 0.6M each 79.83 69.50 81.36 70.79 The recipe produces a competitive TSFM (Table 1 ). The proposed TS2Vec-FM shows the second-best result, trailing MantisV2 by 0.19 / 0.60 pp with RF and 0.28 / 0.22 pp with LogReg, respectively, while using about 25% fewer parameters. At the same time, it outperforms the forecasting- and vision-based extractors (10–170 × \times as many parameters), except TiConvNext on UCR LogReg. We would like to note that unlike MantisV2, our encoder uses native lengths and does not need interpolate each series to a fixed length. In Appendix D , we show that interpolating series worsen the performance of TS2Vec-FM. It also beats TS2Vec trained per dataset. Under both the random forest and logistic regression probe, the margin between the foundation model and per-dataset encoder is more that 1.9 % on UCR. The gap widens even more on multivariate UEA-27, even though TS2Vec-FM was pre-trained on univariate data. Note that in the original TS2Vec paper, they use an RBF-SVM with hyperparameters tuned, which increases the probing performance, though still below TS2Vec-FM with logistic regression. We have also tried to reproduce the results published by Yue et al. (2022) in two different setups: first, our reimplementation of the original protocol that reproduces the published UCR-128 performance to within 0.8 pp with a per-dataset correlation of 0.984, and second, we have run the authors’ unmodified code that reproduces fifteen of the sixteen evaluable headline metrics of the original paper (across all classification, forecasting and anomaly detection) within 5% relative (see Appendix C ). Table 2: What each ingredient contributes (random forest, %) at 100K, 1M and 2M synthetic series. Instance normalization trades UEA for UCR at every scale, the specialists and the direct contrastive baseline do not improve with more data, and distillation consolidates the two specialists into the stronger single encoder at every scale. † mean over three pre-training seeds; ‡ with gradient clipping. 100K series 1M series 2M series Encoder input Training UCR UEA UCR UEA UCR UEA raw only contrastive 77.43 † 72.02 † 76.99 71.56 77.68 72.22 normalized only contrastive 80.35 † 70.56 † 80.26 69.78 79.89 70.19 dual-input contrastive 80.52 † 73.41 † 80.52 ‡ 73.41 ‡ 80.52 ‡ 73.07 ‡ dual-input distillation (ours) 81.08 † 73.90 † 81.62 † 73.48 † 81.76 73.60 Ablation of the recipe (Table 2 ). We first ask whether more synthetic data helps. For the ingredients taken alone the answer is negative: from 100K to 1M and 2M series, the two specialists and the dual-input encoder pre-trained directly with the contrastive TS2Vec loss stay within seed noise or slightly degrade (the instance-normalized specialist loses 0.5 pp on UCR). The distilled encoder is the only one that benefits: on UCR it gains 0.54 pp from 100K to 1M (81.08 to 81.62%, three pre-training seeds each, seed standard deviation 0.12 pp) and a further 0.14 pp at 2M, while on UEA it stays flat (73.9, 73.5 and 73.6%). We detail the scaling experiments further in Appendix D . The comparison with the directly pre-trained dual-input encoder also isolates the contribution of distillation: it is superior at every scale, and its margin widens with data, from 0.56 pp at 100K to 1.10 pp at 1M and 1.24 pp at 2M on UCR. We also note that we had to use gradient clipping for the contrastive baseline due to numerical instability. The pattern suggests that direct training underuses the complementary views, while already-specialized teachers keep both subspaces alive. This is, in effect, a learned substitute for what hand-designed TSFM tokenizers provide by construction when they devote separate branches to the normalized signal and to raw patch statistics ( Feofanov et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . 4 Discussion In this paper, we introduced TS2Vec-FM, showing that synthetic pretraining and specialist distillation can make a compact convolutional encoder competitive for cross-dataset classification while retaining native-length processing. The results motivate revisiting earlier self-supervised architectures, adapting them to the current setup and thereby enriching the family of available time series foundation models. Limitations. The 2M headline model is trained at a single pre-training seed, although the 100K ablations and the 1M student use three seeds. TS2Vec-FM remains slightly below MantisV2 on all four metrics, so our claim is competitive performance with a smaller encoder rather than superiority. Evaluation is limited to UCR and UEA, and whether specialist distillation generalizes to other backbones and tokenizer designs remains open. References Ansari et al. (2025) A. F. Ansari, O. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.28591 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures Authors: Arthur Bizzi , Márcio Marques , Kleyton Da Costa , Vitor Balestro , Tiago Novello , João M. Pereira , Daniel Yukimura View a PDF of the paper titled PaPi: Parallel Picard-Duhamel Integration for Fast Neuro-Spectral Architectures, by Arthur Bizzi and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Neuro-spectral architectures (NeuSA) are a class of physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) that have proven effective for solving time-dependent PDEs in the frequency domain. However, training and inference often rely on costly numerical integration of the learned vector field, typically using sequential Runge-Kutta time stepping, which limits temporal parallelism. We introduce PaPi, an integration scheme inspired by weakly nonlinear flows that enables time-Parallel inference through exponential integration and a Duhamel-Picard scheme. We show that the Duhamel-Picard iteration converges exponentially for all flows, and provide explicit error bounds that depend on how close the flow is to linear. Experiments show that PaPi accelerates training and inference by up to two orders of magnitude, achieving training times of under one second for low-dimensional PDE learning problems, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy. Authors: Emile Anand , Mohammed Rehan Parwani , Xinyuan Cao View a PDF of the paper titled Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go?, by Emile Anand and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival, the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner's prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft-target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta's MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1x faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%. items.content: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go? Emile Anand Mohammed Rehan Parwani Xinyuan Cao Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: {eanand,mparwani3,xcao78}@gatech.edu Abstract Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival , the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner’s prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft–target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta’s MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1 × \times faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%. 1 Introduction Autoregressive decoding generates each new token through an evaluation of a target language model. Speculative decoding reduces this sequential bottleneck by using a cheaper draft mechanism to propose several tokens and evaluating them in parallel with the target model ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . With an appropriate acceptance-and-correction rule, this procedure preserves the target distribution while committing multiple tokens in a single round ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . Multi-token prediction (MTP) provides a natural proposal mechanism by predicting several future tokens from a shared representation ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) , and have witnessed enormous success in practice: for instance, MTP modules are now shipped in frontier models ( DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) , and pretrained next-token models can be converted into MTP drafters without architectural changes ( Samragh et al., 2025 ; Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These methods create an inference-time decision that is distinct from learning a good draft model: how many tokens should be proposed before the next verification step? We refer to this quantity as the speculation horizon . The speculation horizon directly affects decoding efficiency . A longer horizon amortizes verification over more committed tokens when the draft is reliable, but after an early rejection the discarded suffix adds latency and no output. Horizon selection therefore balances the expected gain from additional accepted tokens against the risk of speculating too far. We evaluate each horizon by its conditional throughput: the ratio of its expected number of committed tokens to its expected round latency. Even for a fixed draft-target pair, the throughput-maximizing horizon varies with context, because acceptance probabilities at each draft position depend on context. For MTP, this choice has a structure that isn’t exploited in current methods ( Anand et al., 2026 ) : an autoregressive drafter can decide token by token whether to keep drafting, but MTP heads produce all draft tokens in a single forward pass, so the horizon must be fixed before drafting, from information available at that point. Existing adaptive methods do not make this decision without additional training. Most stop an autoregressive drafter token by token, using a trained classifier or acceptance head ( Mamou et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , entropy-based bounds ( Agrawal et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , or parallel drafting and verification ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Others shape draft trees from confidence after drafting ( Li et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen, 2026 ) , prune verification prefixes with predicted survival probabilities ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) , or train reinforcement-learning policies for draft depth ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work trains a router that selects the span length before decoding, but requires new prediction heads and verifies against greedy decoding only ( Chintha et al., 2026 ) . In fact, to our knowledge, AMTP is the first training-free method that selects the MTP horizon before drafting at every round. A complementary line of work uses verification feedback online to adapt the draft model ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) or to select among drafters and hyperparameter configurations with regret guarantees against the best fixed choice ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Hou et al., 2025 ) . However, in this work, we compare against the stronger benchmark of the best horizon at each visited context. We study how learning acceptance behavior from verification feedback affects horizon-selection performance, and, for a given target model and draft mechanism, we develop an online controller and bound its conditional throughput regret relative to the best horizon at each visited context in terms of cumulative prediction error. Section 2 discusses related work in detail. To relate prediction error to horizon-selection, we first identify the acceptance statistics that influence the expected number of committed tokens for each horizon. A draft token can be committed as an accepted proposal only if all prior proposals are also accepted. We characterize the joint acceptance event via acceptance survival , the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted, which further determines the expected number of committed tokens exactly. We express them in terms of conditional rejection hazards , where the hazard at a position is its rejection probability given acceptance of all prior proposals. Our analyses holds for general causal proposals, including independent and correlated prediction heads ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) . Estimating the hazards requires distinguishing between proposed and surviving prefixes: verification provides draft-target discrepancies along sampled proposal prefixes, whereas the hazards average these discrepancies under the distribution of prefixes that survive verification. So, we derive a survival-weighted regression objective that targets these conditional hazards, and its excess population loss is the survival-weighted hazard-prediction error that enters our throughput-regret bound, mirroring decision-focused learning, where prediction losses are judged by the induced decisions ( Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022 ) . We use this objective to develop Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP), a training-free horizon controller equipped with an online adaptive learning algorithm. Before drafting, AMTP combines hazard-based forecasts of committed tokens with estimates of round latency to evaluate the throughput of each horizon. Short horizons, however, conceal verification feedback at later positions. To learn under this partial feedback, AMTP combines greedy throughput-based selection with randomized full-horizon exploration ( Langford and Zhang, 2007 ) and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain unbiased estimates of the survival-weighted regression loss. Our contributions are as follows: • Acceptance survival. We characterize horizon selection through accepted-prefix survival and round cost for general causal proposals, showing how survival determines the expected number of committed tokens for each horizon (§ 3 ). • AMTP. We introduce a training-free online controller that chooses the MTP horizon before each round, by maximizing predicted tokens per second, learning from partial feedback of short horizons via randomized exploration and inverse-probability weighting (§ 4 ). • Prediction error to wall-clock time. We show that the prediction error of any online learner translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on expected completion time. With online gradient descent ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) under partial feedback, the regret is O ⁡ ( T 4 / 5 ​ ( 1 + P T ) 1 / 5 ) O(T^{4/5}(1+P_{T})^{1/5}) , which is sublinear (§ 5 ). • Experiments. Across five draft–target pairings and two reasoning benchmarks, AMTP decodes up to 4.1 × \times faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10% (§ 6 ). 2 Related Work Speculative decoding and multi-token proposals. Speculative decoding drafts tokens with a cheap proposal and verifies them in parallel with the target model, using an acceptance-and-correction rule that leaves the target distribution unchanged ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Most work uses a separate next-token draft model, or, as in EAGLE, a lightweight head that drafts autoregressively at the feature level ( Li et al., 2024b ) . Multi-token prediction (MTP) instead trains several future-token heads on a shared representation ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) ; Medusa adds such heads to an existing model and verifies candidate continuations with tree attention ( Cai et al., 2024 ) , and recent work obtains MTP models from pretrained next-token models by self-distillation ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ) . Joint multi-token prediction studies how to learn representations that support predicting several tokens at once ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . We keep the exact verifier and study a different question: given a fixed proposal, how many tokens should we draft in each round? Adaptive draft length for autoregressive drafters. A substantial line of work adapts the draft length of a next-token drafter. DISCO trains a classifier that decides after each drafted token whether to continue ( Mamou et al., 2024 ) ; SpecDec++ adds an acceptance-prediction head to the draft model and stops once the predicted probability of a rejection crosses a threshold ( Huang et al., 2024 ) ; AdaEDL stops when an entropy-based lower bound on the acceptance probability falls below a threshold ( Agrawal et al., 2024 ) ; and SVIP derives a similar entropy-based stopping policy for long-form generation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . EAGLE-2 instead grows a draft tree whose shape follows context-dependent confidence ( Li et al., 2024a ) , and Learning to Draft trains reinforcement-learning policies for draft depth and verification size with throughput rewards ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These methods share a structural assumption: drafting is sequential, so the decision to stop can be made token by token , after each drafted token is observed and before the next one is paid for. However, MTP removes this option. All heads fire in the same forward pass, so the cost of drafting is incurred up front and the horizon must be fixed before any draft token is sampled. Truncating a complete MTP draft afterwards saves verification cost but not drafting cost, and choosing the cut point after inspecting sampled tokens can break exactness (Appendix 3.1 ). AMTP is designed for this setting: it chooses the horizon from pre-draft information only, and our statistical and online-optimization analysis of horizon selection and acceptance survival applies to any causal proposal, including both independent and correlated heads. Online learning for speculative decoding. Verification feedback has also been used to adapt speculative decoding online. OnlineSpec updates an evolving draft model and relates its dynamic regret to accepted length at a fixed candidate length ( Qian et al., 2026 ) . Not-a-Bandit gives no-regret guarantees for selecting among draft models ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . BanditSpec treats speculative-decoding hyperparameters, including the speculation length, as bandit arms and bounds regret against the best fixed configuration ( Hou et al., 2025 ) . Our guarantee uses a stronger comparator, the best horizon for each context along the realized decoding trajectory, and is learner-agnostic: any online regression method’s prediction error transfers to throughput regret, with online gradient descent ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) as one instantiation. The broader strategy of translating prediction or optimization error into decision quality is related to perturbation-based model predictive control ( Lin et al., 2022 ) and online adaptive policy selection ( Lin et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , which rely on assumptions about the controlled dynamics, such as contractive perturbations, that we do not impose on the language-model prefixes. 3 Speculation as a Survival Problem We first describe one round of speculation, and then show that a single sequence of rejection hazards determines the expected gain of every horizon. 3.1 One Round of Speculation: Draft, Verify, Commit At round t t , let H t = x 1 : n t H_{t}=x_{1:n_{t}} be the committed prefix and let ℱ t \mathcal{F}_{t} contain all information available before the next horizon is chosen, including H t H_{t} , system state, and the controller parameters. items.raw_text: Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction: How far should we go? Emile Anand Mohammed Rehan Parwani Xinyuan Cao Affiliation: Georgia Institute of Technology Email: {eanand,mparwani3,xcao78}@gatech.edu Abstract Multi-token prediction (MTP) can accelerate language-model decoding by drafting several tokens and verifying them in a single target-model pass. However, the best speculation horizon changes with context: longer drafts offer greater amortization when reliable, but can waste compute on suffixes discarded after a rejection. Unlike autoregressive drafting, where a stopping rule can decide token by token, MTP must fix the horizon before drafting, as all heads fire in the same forward pass. We therefore formulate horizon selection as an online control problem, using verification feedback to learn how far the draft can be trusted in each context, and introduce Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP): a lightweight controller that requires no retraining and leaves the exact verifier unchanged. To guide horizon selection, we characterize the expected number of tokens committed at each horizon via acceptance survival , the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted. Before each round, AMTP predicts how far the draft is likely to survive and picks the horizon with the highest expected tokens per second, learning freely from every verification pass. Theoretically, we show that any online learner’s prediction error translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on wall-clock completion time. With online gradient descent, this regret is sublinear. Across five draft–target pairings built on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with Medusa heads, Meta’s MTP models, and Qwen3-4B-Inst-2507-MTP, evaluated on AIME 2025 and GSM8K, AMTP decodes up to 4.1 × \times faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10%. 1 Introduction Autoregressive decoding generates each new token through an evaluation of a target language model. Speculative decoding reduces this sequential bottleneck by using a cheaper draft mechanism to propose several tokens and evaluating them in parallel with the target model ( Stern et al., 2018 ; Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . With an appropriate acceptance-and-correction rule, this procedure preserves the target distribution while committing multiple tokens in a single round ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2024 ) . Multi-token prediction (MTP) provides a natural proposal mechanism by predicting several future tokens from a shared representation ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ; Cai et al., 2024 ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) , and have witnessed enormous success in practice: for instance, MTP modules are now shipped in frontier models ( DeepSeek-AI, 2024 ) , and pretrained next-token models can be converted into MTP drafters without architectural changes ( Samragh et al., 2025 ; Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026 ) . These methods create an inference-time decision that is distinct from learning a good draft model: how many tokens should be proposed before the next verification step? We refer to this quantity as the speculation horizon . The speculation horizon directly affects decoding efficiency . A longer horizon amortizes verification over more committed tokens when the draft is reliable, but after an early rejection the discarded suffix adds latency and no output. Horizon selection therefore balances the expected gain from additional accepted tokens against the risk of speculating too far. We evaluate each horizon by its conditional throughput: the ratio of its expected number of committed tokens to its expected round latency. Even for a fixed draft-target pair, the throughput-maximizing horizon varies with context, because acceptance probabilities at each draft position depend on context. For MTP, this choice has a structure that isn’t exploited in current methods ( Anand et al., 2026 ) : an autoregressive drafter can decide token by token whether to keep drafting, but MTP heads produce all draft tokens in a single forward pass, so the horizon must be fixed before drafting, from information available at that point. Existing adaptive methods do not make this decision without additional training. Most stop an autoregressive drafter token by token, using a trained classifier or acceptance head ( Mamou et al., 2024 ; Huang et al., 2024 ) , entropy-based bounds ( Agrawal et al., 2024 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) , or parallel drafting and verification ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Others shape draft trees from confidence after drafting ( Li et al., 2024a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Chen, 2026 ) , prune verification prefixes with predicted survival probabilities ( Cheng et al., 2026 ) , or train reinforcement-learning policies for draft depth ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . Concurrent work trains a router that selects the span length before decoding, but requires new prediction heads and verifies against greedy decoding only ( Chintha et al., 2026 ) . In fact, to our knowledge, AMTP is the first training-free method that selects the MTP horizon before drafting at every round. A complementary line of work uses verification feedback online to adapt the draft model ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Qian et al., 2026 ) or to select among drafters and hyperparameter configurations with regret guarantees against the best fixed choice ( Liu et al., 2026 ; Hou et al., 2025 ) . However, in this work, we compare against the stronger benchmark of the best horizon at each visited context. We study how learning acceptance behavior from verification feedback affects horizon-selection performance, and, for a given target model and draft mechanism, we develop an online controller and bound its conditional throughput regret relative to the best horizon at each visited context in terms of cumulative prediction error. Section 2 discusses related work in detail. To relate prediction error to horizon-selection, we first identify the acceptance statistics that influence the expected number of committed tokens for each horizon. A draft token can be committed as an accepted proposal only if all prior proposals are also accepted. We characterize the joint acceptance event via acceptance survival , the probability that a draft prefix is fully accepted, which further determines the expected number of committed tokens exactly. We express them in terms of conditional rejection hazards , where the hazard at a position is its rejection probability given acceptance of all prior proposals. Our analyses holds for general causal proposals, including independent and correlated prediction heads ( Cai et al., 2024 ; Ankner et al., 2024 ) . Estimating the hazards requires distinguishing between proposed and surviving prefixes: verification provides draft-target discrepancies along sampled proposal prefixes, whereas the hazards average these discrepancies under the distribution of prefixes that survive verification. So, we derive a survival-weighted regression objective that targets these conditional hazards, and its excess population loss is the survival-weighted hazard-prediction error that enters our throughput-regret bound, mirroring decision-focused learning, where prediction losses are judged by the induced decisions ( Elmachtoub and Grigas, 2022 ) . We use this objective to develop Adaptive Multi-Token Prediction (AMTP), a training-free horizon controller equipped with an online adaptive learning algorithm. Before drafting, AMTP combines hazard-based forecasts of committed tokens with estimates of round latency to evaluate the throughput of each horizon. Short horizons, however, conceal verification feedback at later positions. To learn under this partial feedback, AMTP combines greedy throughput-based selection with randomized full-horizon exploration ( Langford and Zhang, 2007 ) and uses inverse-probability weighting to obtain unbiased estimates of the survival-weighted regression loss. Our contributions are as follows: • Acceptance survival. We characterize horizon selection through accepted-prefix survival and round cost for general causal proposals, showing how survival determines the expected number of committed tokens for each horizon (§ 3 ). • AMTP. We introduce a training-free online controller that chooses the MTP horizon before each round, by maximizing predicted tokens per second, learning from partial feedback of short horizons via randomized exploration and inverse-probability weighting (§ 4 ). • Prediction error to wall-clock time. We show that the prediction error of any online learner translates into throughput regret against the best horizon for each context, and in turn into a bound on expected completion time. With online gradient descent ( Zinkevich, 2003 ) under partial feedback, the regret is O ⁡ ( T 4 / 5 ​ ( 1 + P T ) 1 / 5 ) O(T^{4/5}(1+P_{T})^{1/5}) , which is sublinear (§ 5 ). • Experiments. Across five draft–target pairings and two reasoning benchmarks, AMTP decodes up to 4.1 × \times faster than standard decoding and matches or outperforms the fixed window in 8 of 10 settings, with throughput gains of up to 10% (§ 6 ). 2 Related Work Speculative decoding and multi-token proposals. Speculative decoding drafts tokens with a cheap proposal and verifies them in parallel with the target model, using an acceptance-and-correction rule that leaves the target distribution unchanged ( Leviathan et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023 ) . Most work uses a separate next-token draft model, or, as in EAGLE, a lightweight head that drafts autoregressively at the feature level ( Li et al., 2024b ) . Multi-token prediction (MTP) instead trains several future-token heads on a shared representation ( Gloeckle et al., 2024 ) ; Medusa adds such heads to an existing model and verifies candidate continuations with tree attention ( Cai et al., 2024 ) , and recent work obtains MTP models from pretrained next-token models by self-distillation ( Kirchenbauer et al., 2026 ) . Joint multi-token prediction studies how to learn representations that support predicting several tokens at once ( Ahn et al., 2025 ) . We keep the exact verifier and study a different question: given a fixed proposal, how many tokens should we draft in each round? Adaptive draft length for autoregressive drafters. A substantial line of work adapts the draft length of a next-token drafter. DISCO trains a classifier that decides after each drafted token whether to continue ( Mamou et al., 2024 ) ; SpecDec++ adds an acceptance-prediction head to the draft model and stops once the predicted probability of a rejection crosses a threshold ( Huang et al., 2024 ) ; AdaEDL stops when an entropy-based lower bound on the acceptance probability falls below a threshold ( Agrawal et al., 2024 ) ; and SVIP derives a similar entropy-based stopping policy for long-form generation ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) . EAGLE-2 instead grows a draft tree whose shape follows context-dependent confidence ( Li et al., 2024a ) , and Learning to Draft trains reinforcement-learning policies for draft depth and verification size with throughput rewards ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) . These methods share a structural assumption: drafting is sequential, so the decision to stop can be made token by token , after each drafted token is observed and before the next one is paid for. However, MTP removes this option. All heads fire in the same forward pass, so the cost of drafting is incurred up front and the horizon must be fixed before any draft token is sampled. Truncating a complete MTP draft afterwards saves verification cost but not drafting cost, and choosing the cut point after inspecting sampled tokens can break exactness (Appendix 3.1 ). AMTP is designed for this setting: it chooses the horizon from pre-draft information only, and our statistical and online-optimization analysis of horizon selection and acceptance survival applies to any causal proposal, including both independent and correlated heads. Online learning for speculative decoding. Verification feedback has also been used to adapt speculative decoding online. OnlineSpec updates an evolving draft model and relates its dynamic regret to accepted length at a fixed candidate length ( Qian et al., 2026 ) . Not-a-Bandit gives no-regret guarantees for selecting among draft models ( Liu et al., 2026 ) . BanditSpec treats speculative-decoding hyperparameters, including the speculation length, as bandit arms and bounds regret against the best fixed configuration ( Hou et al., 2025 ) . items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.28611 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics Authors: Jitendra Solanki , Anand Todkar , Ziran Min View a PDF of the paper titled Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics, by Jitendra Solanki and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability, an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, it bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building on this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We show conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. We also specify an open-source validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper on exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking. items.content: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics Jitendra Solanki Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Anand Todkar Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Ziran Min Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Abstract Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous, cognitively demanding task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), heavily bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across distinct monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability , an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, Semantic Observability bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building upon this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The structurally pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We demonstrate conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, substantially reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. Furthermore, we specify an open-source experimental validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the architectural groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper dedicated to exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking. Index Terms: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), Observability, Property Graph Database, Large Language Models, Multi-Agent Systems, Causal Inference, Root Cause Analysis (RCA). I Introduction The cloud-native paradigm shift has transformed software systems from monolithic units into distributed meshes of microservices, serverless tasks, and ephemeral container fleets. While this architecture provides horizontal elasticity and modularity, it complicates system observability. When a localized subsystem failure occurs—such as database disk saturation or network contention—it rarely manifests in isolation. Instead, it cascades downstream, producing service timeouts, connection-pool exhaustions, and anomalous HTTP 500 status codes across independent application tiers. In contemporary Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practice [ 1 ] , engineers triage incidents by correlating three primary telemetry pillars: metrics, distributed traces, and logs. Among these, logs provide the highest granularity of execution state. However, extracting causal insights during critical outages is hindered by three structural limitations: 1. Heterogeneity and Semantic Fragmentation: Log events originate from diverse entities (e.g., bare-metal hosts, Kubernetes pods, proxy gateways, and relational databases) and are emitted in disparate syntactic formats (e.g., unstructured text, Apache Common Log Format, Syslog, and arbitrary JSON). Existing centralized logging aggregators (e.g., Elasticsearch, ClickHouse) treat logs as indexable flat text or tabular documents, discarding relational topology and physical host context. 2. High Cognitive Overhead in Spatial-Temporal Correlation: Correlating events across independent machines requires an engineer to manually assemble a mental model of execution across multiple dimensions: Which container executed on this host? Which upstream endpoint invoked this downstream RPC? What log event transpired immediately preceding the database thread exhaustion? 3. Failure Modes of Standard LLM and Vector RAG Approaches: Direct application of Large Language Models (LLMs) via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over flat log files is ineffective for large-scale operations. Dense semantic vector spaces cannot capture strict graph topologies, causality, or microsecond-level chronological sequences. This leads to context window saturation, substantial API operational costs, and hallucinations where unrelated errors are erroneously diagnosed as causal antecedents. I-A Our Contributions To resolve these limitations, this paper proposes Semantic Observability , a framework unifying graph databases and autonomous multi-agent systems for enterprise diagnostics: • Unified Property Graph Telemetry Schema: We define a comprehensive graph data model that unifies physical infrastructure, service runtime topologies, and temporal event streams into an attributed Property Graph. • Dynamic Ingestion and Zero-Regex Parsing: We present an adaptive ingestion agent that utilizes localized semantic inference to parse heterogeneous log streams on the fly, eliminating brittle static regular expressions. • Deterministic Causal Subgraph Pruning: We formulate a graph traversal strategy combining temporal back-chaining ( NEXT_EVENT ) with dependency graph reachability, deterministically filtering ambient telemetry noise prior to LLM inference and drastically minimizing context window overhead. • End-to-End System Architecture: We present the complete multi-tier architectural blueprint—from zero-shot adaptive ingestion and dual-index property graph storage to stateful multi-agent orchestration and automated remediation. • Architectural Validation Methodology: We design a rigorous experimental protocol utilizing open-source benchmarks (LogHub and the Train-Ticket microservice suite) to evaluate MTTR reduction, token efficiency, and causal fidelity, establishing the foundation for extensive empirical benchmarking in follow-up work. II Problem Formulation and Mathematical Modeling Let a distributed computing environment be represented as a time-evolving Property Graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , 𝒯 ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{T}) , where 𝒱 \mathcal{V} denotes the set of attributed entities (nodes), ℰ \mathcal{E} denotes the set of typed directed edges, and 𝒯 \mathcal{T} represents the continuous time domain. II-A Entity Representation ( 𝒱 \mathcal{V} ) The vertex set 𝒱 \mathcal{V} is partitioned into three disjoint subsets: 𝒱 = 𝒱 infra ∪ 𝒱 soft ∪ 𝒱 event \mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{\text{infra}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\text{soft}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\text{event}} 1. Physical Infrastructure Nodes ( 𝒱 infra \mathcal{V}_{\text{infra}} ): v ∈ 𝒱 infra ⟹ Type ( v ) ∈ { \displaystyle v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{infra}}\implies\text{Type}(v)\in\{ Machine , Node , \displaystyle\text{Machine},\text{Node}, Container , StorageVolume } \displaystyle\text{Container},\text{StorageVolume}\} Properties include identifiers, network interfaces, IP addresses, OS types, and resource quotas: 𝐀𝐭𝐭𝐫 ⁡ ( v ) = { id , ip , region , … } \mathbf{Attr}(v)=\{\text{id},\text{ip},\text{region},\dots\} . 2. Logical Software Nodes ( 𝒱 soft \mathcal{V}_{\text{soft}} ): v ∈ 𝒱 soft ⟹ Type ( v ) ∈ { \displaystyle v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{soft}}\implies\text{Type}(v)\in\{ Service , Process , \displaystyle\text{Service},\text{Process}, Endpoint , DatabaseInstance } \displaystyle\text{Endpoint},\text{DatabaseInstance}\} Properties denote application names, versions, protocol metadata, and repository references. 3. Execution & Event Nodes ( 𝒱 event \mathcal{V}_{\text{event}} ): v ∈ 𝒱 event ⟹ Type ( v ) ∈ { \displaystyle v\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{event}}\implies\text{Type}(v)\in\{ Transaction , LogEntry , \displaystyle\text{Transaction},\text{LogEntry}, Exception , Span } \displaystyle\text{Exception},\text{Span}\} Each event node e ∈ 𝒱 event e\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{event}} has an assigned timestamp t ⁡ ( e ) ∈ 𝒯 t(e)\in\mathcal{T} , severity level σ ⁡ ( e ) ∈ { DEBUG , INFO , WARN , ERROR , FATAL } \sigma(e)\in\{\text{DEBUG},\allowbreak\text{INFO},\allowbreak\text{WARN},\allowbreak\text{ERROR},\allowbreak\text{FATAL}\} , and payload attributes. II-B Relational Topology ( ℰ \mathcal{E} ) The edge set ℰ \mathcal{E} defines spatial, administrative, and temporal relations, illustrated for a representative fault scenario in Figure 1 : • Spatial & Hosting: ( c , m ) ∈ ℰ HOSTS ⊆ 𝒱 container × 𝒱 machine (c,m)\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{HOSTS}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\text{container}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{machine}} • Logical Execution: ( s , c ) ∈ ℰ RUNS_IN ⊆ 𝒱 service × 𝒱 container (s,c)\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{RUNS\_IN}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\text{service}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{container}} • API Exposure: ( e , s ) ∈ ℰ EXPOSES ⊆ 𝒱 endpoint × 𝒱 service (e,s)\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{EXPOSES}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\text{endpoint}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{service}} • Provenance: ( l , s ) ∈ ℰ RAISED_BY ⊆ 𝒱 log × 𝒱 service (l,s)\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{RAISED\_BY}}\subseteq\mathcal{V}_{\text{log}}\times\mathcal{V}_{\text{service}} • Chronological Chain ( ℰ NEXT \mathcal{E}_{\text{NEXT}} ): Directed edges connecting adjacent log events within the same operational thread, transaction trace, or localized system component: ( l i , l i + 1 ) ∈ ℰ NEXT ⇔ \displaystyle(l_{i},l_{i+1})\in\mathcal{E}_{\text{NEXT}}\iff{} t ⁡ ( l i ) ≤ t ⁡ ( l i + 1 ) \displaystyle t(l_{i})\leq t(l_{i+1}) ∧ \displaystyle\land{} Scope ​ ( l i ) = Scope ​ ( l i + 1 ) \displaystyle\text{Scope}(l_{i})=\text{Scope}(l_{i+1}) where the edge contains an explicit weight attribute: w ⁡ ( l i , l i + 1 ) = Δ ​ t = t ⁡ ( l i + 1 ) − t ⁡ ( l i ) w(l_{i},l_{i+1})=\Delta t=t(l_{i+1})-t(l_{i}) ⬇ [ Machine : srv -04] | [: HOSTS ] v [ Container : pay -1] | [: RUNS ] v [ Service : Payment ] --[: EXPOSES ]--> [ Endpoint : / charge ] ^ [: RAISED_BY ] | [ Log : ERROR ] --[: CONTAINS ]--> [ Exception : Timeout ] ^ [: NEXT_EVENT { latency_ms : 14}] | [ Log : INFO ] ( DB connection checkout initiated ) Fig. 1: Illustrative property-graph fragment linking physical infrastructure, logical services, and a temporal event chain. II-C The Diagnostic Objective Given an anomaly symptom detected at node v ∗ ∈ 𝒱 event v^{*}\in\mathcal{V}_{\text{event}} where σ ⁡ ( v ∗ ) ≥ ERROR \sigma(v^{*})\geq\text{ERROR} at time t ∗ t^{*} , the diagnostic goal is to discover the minimal causal subgraph 𝒢 ∗ ⊂ 𝒢 \mathcal{G}^{*}\subset\mathcal{G} that contains the root cause entity v root v_{\text{root}} : 𝒢 ∗ = arg ⁡ min 𝒢 ′ ⊆ 𝒢 ​ | 𝒱 ⁡ ( 𝒢 ′ ) | s.t. ℙ ⁡ ( v root ∣ 𝒢 ′ , v ∗ ) ≥ 1 − ϵ \mathcal{G}^{*}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{G}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{G}}|\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{G}^{\prime})|\quad\text{s.t.}\quad\mathbb{P}(v_{\text{root}}\mid\mathcal{G}^{\prime},v^{*})\geq 1-\epsilon III System Architecture and Implementation Framework The Semantic Observability platform is architected as a distributed, four-tier reactive system designed to process heterogeneous, high-velocity telemetry streams, construct a unified topological graph model, and execute autonomous multi-agent diagnostic cycles upon anomaly detection. Figure 2 depicts the end-to-end platform topology across these tiers, and Table I summarizes the components and responsibilities of each tier. Fig. 2: Semantic Observability: end-to-end system architecture. TABLE I: Four-tier architecture of Semantic Observability. Architectural Tier Primary Components Operational Responsibilities Tier 1: Ingestion & Normalization eBPF Probes, OpenTelemetry DaemonSets, FluentBit, Kafka Buffer Streaming telemetry collection, signature hashing, zero-shot LLM regex induction, batch Cypher projection Tier 2: Property Graph Storage Neo4j / Memgraph Labeled Property Graph, Dual B-Tree / Lucene Indexes Structuring physical infrastructure, software topology, and temporal log sequences with [:NEXT_EVENT] edges Tier 3: Multi-Agent Reasoning Master Orchestrator, Graph Traversal Agent, Autonomous Codebase Agent, Diagnostic LLM Autonomous causal path back-tracing, blast-radius pruning, commit diff extraction, code-level root-cause synthesis Tier 4: Remediation & Integration GitHub/GitLab Repositories, Jira/ServiceNow APIs, Slack / PagerDuty webhooks Automated incident ticket creation, hotfix pull request generation, staged infrastructure remediation commands III-A Telemetry Ingestion & Adaptive Schema Induction Engine Enterprise environments run polyglot infrastructure in which log formats continually drift over time. Traditional log forwarders such as Logstash and Vector break when schemas diverge, degrading unparsed fields into raw, unstructured text. Semantic Observability addresses this limitation through an adaptive two-stage induction pipeline: 1. Signature Hashing & Fast-Path Matching: For each incoming raw log payload r r , an extractor derives its structural signature H ⁡ ( r ) H(r) based on delimiter distributions, key-value anchors, and token entropy. A thread-safe, high-concurrency LRU cache stores compiled extraction expressions: Signature ​ ( r ) → Φ regex \text{Signature}(r)\to\Phi_{\text{regex}} If H ⁡ ( r ) H(r) exists in the cache, the record is parsed natively via compiled C-extensions at high-throughput line rates per ingestion core. 2. LLM Zero-Shot Induction Cycle: When an unrecognized format appears ( H ⁡ ( r ) ∉ Cache H(r)\notin\text{Cache} ): • The record is routed to a specialized Schema Induction LLM with a system prompt specifying the Canonical Graph Schema: ⟨ \displaystyle\langle timestamp , machine_id , service , \displaystyle\text{timestamp},\text{machine\_id},\text{service}, severity , trace_id , message , payload ⟩ . \displaystyle\text{severity},\text{trace\_id},\text{message},\text{payload}\rangle. • The LLM produces a parameterized regular expression equipped with named capture groups and type-coercion semantics. • The newly synthesized parser is evaluated against a synthetic holdout batch. Upon validation, it is compiled into the cache under H ⁡ ( r ) H(r) , rendering subsequent log parsing overhead negligible (a design target of < 0.02 ​ ms <0.02\text{ ms} ). 3. High-Throughput Graph Projection: To prevent graph database lock contention, logs are not inserted individually. Instead, the Ingestion Engine stages parsed entries into micro-batches of 1,000 1{,}000 to 5,000 5{,}000 events, executed via parameterized Cypher statements using UNWIND semantics: Listing 1: Batch graph projection via parameterized UNWIND Cypher. ⬇ UNWIND $log_batch AS row MERGE ( m : Machine { id : row . machine_id }) MERGE ( s : Service { name : row . service_name }) MERGE ( s )-[: ON_MACHINE ]->( m ) CREATE ( l : Log { id : row . log_id , timestamp : row . timestamp , level : row . level , message : row . message }) CREATE ( l )-[: RAISED_BY ]->( s ) FOREACH ( _ IN CASE WHEN row . exception_type IS NOT NULL THEN [1] ELSE [] END | CREATE ( e : Exception { type : row . exception_type , stacktrace : row . stacktrace }) CREATE ( l )-[: CONTAINS ]->( e )); III-B Property Graph Knowledge Architecture & Indexing The storage subsystem represents the operational state as a Labeled Property Graph 𝒢 = ( 𝒱 , ℰ , 𝒯 ) \mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E},\mathcal{T}) [ 6 ] , partitioning entities into physical, logical, and temporal domains. Table II enumerates the core topological relationships of the schema. TABLE II: Core topological relationships of the property graph schema. Source Entity Relationship Edge Target Entity Topological Semantics :Machine :HOSTS :Container Physical host server executing container runtime :Container :RUNS :Service Container executing application microservice instance :Service :EXPOSES :Endpoint Microservice publishing routable API endpoint :Endpoint :TRIGGERS :Log Inbound transaction execution generating log event :Log :CONTAINS :Exception Log record capturing unhandled stack trace or fault :Log :NEXT_EVENT :Log Sequential temporal link with measured Δ ​ t \Delta t and trace ID III-B 1 Dual-Index Strategy Graph databases traditionally incur high traversal latency if the initial root node lookup requires a sequential scan. We implement a dual-index indexing hierarchy: • Composite Temporal B-Tree Indexes: Maintained over (:Log {service, timestamp}) and (:Log {trace_id, timestamp}) ensuring range lookups and starting-node resolutions in 𝒪 ⁡ ( log ⁡ | 𝒱 | ) \mathcal{O}(\log|\mathcal{V}|) time. • Full-Text Inverted Lucene Indexes: Maintained over Log.message and Exception.stacktrace enabling fuzzy signature lookups across unindexed contextual text.
