items.raw_text: Semantic Observability for Autonomous Systems Diagnostics Jitendra Solanki Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Anand Todkar Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Ziran Min Affiliation: Siemens Corporation Princeton, NJ, USA Abstract Modern distributed microservice deployments generate massive volumes of heterogeneous, multi-format observability logs across physically and logically partitioned infrastructure. Isolating root causes during cascading failures remains an arduous, cognitively demanding task for Site Reliability Engineers (SREs), heavily bottlenecked by manual keyword filtering and disjointed temporal correlation across distinct monitoring dashboards. We introduce Semantic Observability , an autonomous multi-agent framework that unifies disparate log streams into a dynamic, queryable Property Graph Database. By modeling physical infrastructure topologies, logical software dependencies, and chronological event sequences as attributed nodes and directed relations, Semantic Observability bridges the semantic gap inherent in flat, unstructured log repositories. Building upon this unified substrate, we deploy a stateful multi-agent system orchestrated through Directed Cyclic Graphs (DCGs). The system autonomously navigates the topology, applying causal graph algorithms and temporal back-traversal to isolate the precise blast radius of anomalies. The structurally pruned subgraph is then interpreted by a Large Language Model (LLM) reasoning engine to generate contextualized, code-level Root Cause Analyses (RCA) and actionable remediations. This paper establishes the foundational system architecture, formal relational ontology, and multi-agent control loops of Semantic Observability. We demonstrate conceptually how the framework eliminates ambient telemetry noise, substantially reduces Mean Time to Resolution (MTTR), compresses LLM token consumption, and prevents structural hallucinations. Furthermore, we specify an open-source experimental validation framework on standard benchmarks (LogHub and Train-Ticket), laying the architectural groundwork for a forthcoming companion paper dedicated to exhaustive quantitative evaluation and production benchmarking. Index Terms: Site Reliability Engineering (SRE), Observability, Property Graph Database, Large Language Models, Multi-Agent Systems, Causal Inference, Root Cause Analysis (RCA). I Introduction The cloud-native paradigm shift has transformed software systems from monolithic units into distributed meshes of microservices, serverless tasks, and ephemeral container fleets. While this architecture provides horizontal elasticity and modularity, it complicates system observability. When a localized subsystem failure occurs—such as database disk saturation or network contention—it rarely manifests in isolation. Instead, it cascades downstream, producing service timeouts, connection-pool exhaustions, and anomalous HTTP 500 status codes across independent application tiers. In contemporary Site Reliability Engineering (SRE) practice [ 1 ] , engineers triage incidents by correlating three primary telemetry pillars: metrics, distributed traces, and logs. Among these, logs provide the highest granularity of execution state. However, extracting causal insights during critical outages is hindered by three structural limitations: 1. Heterogeneity and Semantic Fragmentation: Log events originate from diverse entities (e.g., bare-metal hosts, Kubernetes pods, proxy gateways, and relational databases) and are emitted in disparate syntactic formats (e.g., unstructured text, Apache Common Log Format, Syslog, and arbitrary JSON). Existing centralized logging aggregators (e.g., Elasticsearch, ClickHouse) treat logs as indexable flat text or tabular documents, discarding relational topology and physical host context. 2. High Cognitive Overhead in Spatial-Temporal Correlation: Correlating events across independent machines requires an engineer to manually assemble a mental model of execution across multiple dimensions: Which container executed on this host? Which upstream endpoint invoked this downstream RPC? What log event transpired immediately preceding the database thread exhaustion? 3. Failure Modes of Standard LLM and Vector RAG Approaches: Direct application of Large Language Models (LLMs) via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over flat log files is ineffective for large-scale operations. Dense semantic vector spaces cannot capture strict graph topologies, causality, or microsecond-level chronological sequences. This leads to context window saturation, substantial API operational costs, and hallucinations where unrelated errors are erroneously diagnosed as causal antecedents. I-A Our Contributions To resolve these limitations, this paper proposes Semantic Observability , a framework unifying graph databases and autonomous multi-agent systems for enterprise diagnostics: • Unified Property Graph Telemetry Schema: We define a comprehensive graph data model that unifies physical infrastructure, service runtime topologies, and temporal event streams into an attributed Property Graph. • Dynamic Ingestion and Zero-Regex Parsing: We present an adaptive ingestion agent that utilizes localized semantic inference to parse heterogeneous log streams on the fly, eliminating brittle static regular expressions. • Deterministic Causal Subgraph Pruning: We formulate a graph traversal strategy combining temporal back-chaining ( NEXT_EVENT ) with dependency graph reachability, deterministically filtering ambient telemetry noise prior to LLM inference and drastically minimizing context window overhead. • End-to-End System Architecture: We present the complete multi-tier architectural blueprint—from zero-shot adaptive ingestion and dual-index property graph storage to stateful multi-agent orchestration and automated remediation. • Architectural Validation Methodology: We design a rigorous experimental protocol utilizing open-source benchmarks (LogHub and the Train-Ticket microservice suite) to evaluate MTTR reduction, token efficiency, and causal fidelity, establishing the foundation for extensive empirical benchmarking in follow-up work. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.28604 (cs) [Submitted on 20 Oct 2026] Title: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates Authors: Maoyuan Li , Haoyuan Li , Zhongsheng Wang , Jiamou Liu View a PDF of the paper titled Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates, by Maoyuan Li and 3 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression, the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization, how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz's Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at this https URL . items.content: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates Maoyuan Li Affiliation: Wuhan College of Communication Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: mli302@aucklanduni.ac.nz Haoyuan Li Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: hli962@aucklanduni.ac.nz Zhongsheng Wang Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: zhongsheng.wang@auckland.ac.nz Jiamou Liu † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: jiamou.liu@auckland.ac.nz Abstract Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression , the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization , how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz’s Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization . 1 Introduction Arguments gain much of their force from the values they bring into view. In debate, speakers do more than exchange claims and evidence: they reveal what they treat as fair, safe, free, dignified, or worth protecting. These value appeals shape why an argument feels compelling. Figure 1: Illustrative contrast between value expression and value organization. LLMs are increasingly able to generate fluent and persuasive debate utterances, and existing evaluation has largely focused on coherence, factuality, stance consistency, logical validity, and persuasiveness ( Liang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of value-oriented NLP has shown that human values can be identified in argumentative text, for example through Webis-ArgValues-22 and ValueEval ( Kiesel et al., 2022 ; Kiesel et al., 2023 ) . Yet the intersection remains underexplored: debate evaluation rarely asks how values are organized across turns, while value mining usually treats values as labels attached to isolated texts. We therefore ask how AI-generated debates compare with matched human debate references in value expression and value organization . As Figure 1 illustrates, a debate may be value-expressive by invoking recognizable value appeals, while differing in value organization: the AI-generated example spreads across a broader value range, whereas the human reference concentrates around a more compact core of Universalism and Benevolence. We frame value-based debate analysis as comparing distributions of value appeals across matched human-reference and AI-generated debates. This raises two challenges. First, values are rarely stated as explicit labels: a speaker may never name “security” or “autonomy,” while still embedding those values in the arguments. Second, values operate at multiple levels, from local argumentative units to utterances, stances, and full debates. We therefore adopt Schwartz’s Basic-10 theory as a theory-grounded value space ( Schwartz, 1992 ; Schwartz et al., 2012 ) . Following the claim–premise view of argument structure in Stab and Gurevych (2014) , we represent each argumentative unit as a stance-specific claim paired with a premise span extracted from the corresponding utterance. Each argumentative unit is assigned a soft distribution over the ten values, which is then aggregated at multiple levels. Figure 2: Conceptual framework. The shared Schwartz Basic-10 space (center) grounds two evaluation dimensions: value expression (breadth of value activation) and value organization (concentration and cross-turn dynamics). The right panel shows how paired differences are interpreted through surface controls, motion-type effects, and generation-system effects. Here, Human-TextOverlap denotes BLEU similarity between a generated debate and its matched human reference. This multi-level representation supports a diagnostic metric suite with two complementary components. For value expression, we measure how broadly a debate activates the Basic-10 value space and how closely its dominant values align with a paired human reference. For value organization, we define a family of metrics that treats debate values as both distributions and trajectories: entropy captures value diffusion, while stability, drift, and dominant-value persistence characterize how a stance carries its value profile across turns. These metrics shift attention from whether generated arguments mention human-recognizable values to how those values are structured and transformed within argumentative interaction. We instantiate the framework in a paired benchmark comparing general-purpose LLMs with R-Debater (Li et al., 2025). Results show a consistent separation: AI-generated debates activate as many or more Basic-10 values as human references while distributing value mass differently across utterances and stances. These patterns persist after surface-level controls and are supported by source-blind human evaluation. Our contributions are: (1) a diagnostic distinction between value expression and value organization; (2) a Schwartz-grounded multi-level framework representing debate values as distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates; (3) a metric family covering value coverage, alignment, local concentration, and cross-turn dynamics; and (4) a paired analysis showing that AI-generated debates activate broad value spaces while differing from human references in local concentration and cross-turn organization. 2 Related Work Automated debate generation and evaluation. Early automated debate studies focused on the components needed to build debating systems, such as evidence retrieval ( Rinott et al., 2015 ) , argument construction ( Gutfreund et al., 2016 ) , stance modeling ( Bar-Haim et al., 2017 ) , and argument quality assessment ( Bar-Haim et al., 2021 ; Toledo et al., 2019 ) . Project Debater later integrated retrieval, argument mining, and speech planning into an autonomous debating system ( Slonim et al., 2021 ) . Recent LLM-based work has shifted toward debate-like interaction, using simulated agents and multi-agent debate ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024b ) , retrieval-augmented debate generation ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and evaluation-guided optimization ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Debate evaluation has also expanded from winning-stance prediction ( Ruiz-Dolz et al., 2023 ) to multi-dimensional judging, chronological analysis ( Liang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , and LLM-as-judge benchmarking ( Sternlicht et al., 2025 ) . However, none measures how values are distributed and sustained across debate turns. Human values in argumentation. Values have long been central to argumentation theory. In value-based argumentation, argument acceptability depends not only on logical relations, but also on the values promoted by an argument and the audience’s value ordering ( Bench-Capon, 2003 ) . Early value-oriented argument mining focused on identifying implicit human values behind natural-language arguments ( Kiesel et al., 2022 ) . Later work expanded this line with larger and more diverse resources, including Touché23-ValueEval ( Mirzakhmedova et al., 2024 ) and the SemEval-2023 ValueEval shared task ( Kiesel et al., 2023 ) . Related value-modeling datasets also study human values in social scenarios, dialogue, or LLM outputs, such as ValueNet ( Qiu et al., 2022 ) and FULCRA ( Yao et al., 2024 ) . However, these studies treat values as labels for isolated texts. We instead study them as distributions in matched multi-turn debates. 3 Conceptual Framework This section introduces the conceptual framework used to analyze value expression and value organization in human-reference and AI-generated debates. Figure 2 summarizes the framework and its three layers: value representation, value-based measurement, and paired-difference interpretation. 3.1 Shared Value Space Value-based debate analysis requires a shared vocabulary for describing what values are invoked. We adopt Schwartz’s Basic-10 theory as this value space ( Schwartz, 1992 ; Schwartz et al., 2012 ) . Schwartz values are broad motivational goals guiding evaluations of actions and social arrangements, well suited to debate where arguments invoke safety, fairness, autonomy, or preservation. The Basic-10 level is broad enough to cover major motivational contrasts in debate. We use the framework to analyze textual value appeals expressed in debate discourse, not to infer the internal beliefs or moral commitments of a model. The same principle applies to human debate transcripts. Table 1 gives the acronyms used in Figure 2 and the debate-oriented interpretation of each value. The ten values define the value set 𝒱 \mathcal{V} used throughout the paper. Each value distribution in the framework is a probability distribution over this Basic-10 value space. Acr. Value Debate-oriented interpretation SD Self-Direction Autonomy, independent thought, freedom of choice. STM Stimulation Novelty, challenge, innovation, change. HED Hedonism Pleasure, comfort, enjoyment, quality of life. ACH Achievement Success, competence, merit, productivity. POW Power Authority, influence, status, control over resources. SEC Security Safety, stability, public order, risk reduction. CON Conformity Rule-following, responsibility, social norms. TRD Tradition Heritage, customs, continuity, cultural preservation. BEN Benevolence Care for close others, responsibility, loyalty. UNI Universalism Equality, justice, human rights, social or environmental welfare. Table 1: The Schwartz Basic-10 value space. 3.2 Debate as a Multi-level Value Structure We represent a debate formally as d = ( q , 𝒵 , 𝒞 , 𝒰 ) d=(q,\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{U}) , where q q is the topic, 𝒵 = { + , − } \mathcal{Z}=\{+,-\} denotes the pro and con stances, 𝒞 = { c + , c − } \mathcal{C}=\{c_{+},c_{-}\} contains the corresponding stance-specific claims, and 𝒰 = ( u 1 , … , u n ) \mathcal{U}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{n}) is the ordered utterance list. Each utterance u t u_{t} has text x t x_{t} , stance z t ∈ 𝒵 z_{t}\in\mathcal{Z} , and turn index t t . The two stances alternate in turn, i.e., z t ≠ z t + 1 z_{t}\neq z_{t+1} for any t t . Following the claim–premise view of argument structure in Stab and Gurevych (2014) , we adapt this structure to competitive debate, where the stance-specific claim is determined by the debate topic and the speaker’s stance. For an utterance u t u_{t} with stance z t z_{t} , SAPE-Agent extracts premise spans 𝒫 ⁡ ( u t ) = { p t , 1 , … , p t , k t } \mathcal{P}(u_{t})=\{p_{t,1},\ldots,p_{t,k_{t}}\} from the utterance text x t x_{t} . Accordingly, 𝒜 ⁡ ( u t ) = { a t , 1 , … , a t , k t } \mathcal{A}(u_{t})=\{a_{t,1},\ldots,a_{t,k_{t}}\} denotes the argumentative units in utterance u t u_{t} . These levels correspond to increasingly broader views of value expression. items.raw_text: Value-Rich, Differently Organized: Measuring Value Expression and Organization in AI-Generated Debates Maoyuan Li Affiliation: Wuhan College of Communication Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: mli302@aucklanduni.ac.nz Haoyuan Li Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: hli962@aucklanduni.ac.nz Zhongsheng Wang Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: zhongsheng.wang@auckland.ac.nz Jiamou Liu † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: University of Auckland Email: jiamou.liu@auckland.ac.nz Abstract Current evaluation of LLM-generated debate largely focuses on argumentative quality, leaving the value structure of generated arguments underexamined. We introduce a diagnostic metric framework for comparing how values are expressed and organized in human-reference and AI-generated debates. The framework separates value expression , the range of recognizable values a debate invokes, from value organization , how those values are distributed and sustained across turns. Grounded in Schwartz’s Basic-10 value theory, it represents debates as multi-level value distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates, enabling metrics for value coverage, alignment, diffusion, and cross-turn dynamics. Across multiple generation systems, AI-generated debates are broadly value-expressive, often activating as many or more value dimensions than matched human references, but they organize these values differently. Their utterances are more locally value-diffuse, and source-blind judges distinguish value clarity from value focus. These findings show that debate evaluation should consider not only value presence, but also value organization. Code and supplementary materials are available at https://github.com/Maoyuan-li/Value-Expression-and-Organization . 1 Introduction Arguments gain much of their force from the values they bring into view. In debate, speakers do more than exchange claims and evidence: they reveal what they treat as fair, safe, free, dignified, or worth protecting. These value appeals shape why an argument feels compelling. Figure 1: Illustrative contrast between value expression and value organization. LLMs are increasingly able to generate fluent and persuasive debate utterances, and existing evaluation has largely focused on coherence, factuality, stance consistency, logical validity, and persuasiveness ( Liang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . A separate line of value-oriented NLP has shown that human values can be identified in argumentative text, for example through Webis-ArgValues-22 and ValueEval ( Kiesel et al., 2022 ; Kiesel et al., 2023 ) . Yet the intersection remains underexplored: debate evaluation rarely asks how values are organized across turns, while value mining usually treats values as labels attached to isolated texts. We therefore ask how AI-generated debates compare with matched human debate references in value expression and value organization . As Figure 1 illustrates, a debate may be value-expressive by invoking recognizable value appeals, while differing in value organization: the AI-generated example spreads across a broader value range, whereas the human reference concentrates around a more compact core of Universalism and Benevolence. We frame value-based debate analysis as comparing distributions of value appeals across matched human-reference and AI-generated debates. This raises two challenges. First, values are rarely stated as explicit labels: a speaker may never name “security” or “autonomy,” while still embedding those values in the arguments. Second, values operate at multiple levels, from local argumentative units to utterances, stances, and full debates. We therefore adopt Schwartz’s Basic-10 theory as a theory-grounded value space ( Schwartz, 1992 ; Schwartz et al., 2012 ) . Following the claim–premise view of argument structure in Stab and Gurevych (2014) , we represent each argumentative unit as a stance-specific claim paired with a premise span extracted from the corresponding utterance. Each argumentative unit is assigned a soft distribution over the ten values, which is then aggregated at multiple levels. Figure 2: Conceptual framework. The shared Schwartz Basic-10 space (center) grounds two evaluation dimensions: value expression (breadth of value activation) and value organization (concentration and cross-turn dynamics). The right panel shows how paired differences are interpreted through surface controls, motion-type effects, and generation-system effects. Here, Human-TextOverlap denotes BLEU similarity between a generated debate and its matched human reference. This multi-level representation supports a diagnostic metric suite with two complementary components. For value expression, we measure how broadly a debate activates the Basic-10 value space and how closely its dominant values align with a paired human reference. For value organization, we define a family of metrics that treats debate values as both distributions and trajectories: entropy captures value diffusion, while stability, drift, and dominant-value persistence characterize how a stance carries its value profile across turns. These metrics shift attention from whether generated arguments mention human-recognizable values to how those values are structured and transformed within argumentative interaction. We instantiate the framework in a paired benchmark comparing general-purpose LLMs with R-Debater (Li et al., 2025). Results show a consistent separation: AI-generated debates activate as many or more Basic-10 values as human references while distributing value mass differently across utterances and stances. These patterns persist after surface-level controls and are supported by source-blind human evaluation. Our contributions are: (1) a diagnostic distinction between value expression and value organization; (2) a Schwartz-grounded multi-level framework representing debate values as distributions over argumentative units, utterances, stances, and full debates; (3) a metric family covering value coverage, alignment, local concentration, and cross-turn dynamics; and (4) a paired analysis showing that AI-generated debates activate broad value spaces while differing from human references in local concentration and cross-turn organization. 2 Related Work Automated debate generation and evaluation. Early automated debate studies focused on the components needed to build debating systems, such as evidence retrieval ( Rinott et al., 2015 ) , argument construction ( Gutfreund et al., 2016 ) , stance modeling ( Bar-Haim et al., 2017 ) , and argument quality assessment ( Bar-Haim et al., 2021 ; Toledo et al., 2019 ) . Project Debater later integrated retrieval, argument mining, and speech planning into an autonomous debating system ( Slonim et al., 2021 ) . Recent LLM-based work has shifted toward debate-like interaction, using simulated agents and multi-agent debate ( Du et al., 2024 ; Liang et al., 2024b ) , retrieval-augmented debate generation ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and evaluation-guided optimization ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Debate evaluation has also expanded from winning-stance prediction ( Ruiz-Dolz et al., 2023 ) to multi-dimensional judging, chronological analysis ( Liang et al., 2024a ; Wang et al., 2025 ) , and LLM-as-judge benchmarking ( Sternlicht et al., 2025 ) . However, none measures how values are distributed and sustained across debate turns. Human values in argumentation. Values have long been central to argumentation theory. In value-based argumentation, argument acceptability depends not only on logical relations, but also on the values promoted by an argument and the audience’s value ordering ( Bench-Capon, 2003 ) . Early value-oriented argument mining focused on identifying implicit human values behind natural-language arguments ( Kiesel et al., 2022 ) . Later work expanded this line with larger and more diverse resources, including Touché23-ValueEval ( Mirzakhmedova et al., 2024 ) and the SemEval-2023 ValueEval shared task ( Kiesel et al., 2023 ) . Related value-modeling datasets also study human values in social scenarios, dialogue, or LLM outputs, such as ValueNet ( Qiu et al., 2022 ) and FULCRA ( Yao et al., 2024 ) . However, these studies treat values as labels for isolated texts. We instead study them as distributions in matched multi-turn debates. 3 Conceptual Framework This section introduces the conceptual framework used to analyze value expression and value organization in human-reference and AI-generated debates. We use the framework to analyze textual value appeals expressed in debate discourse, not to infer the internal beliefs or moral commitments of a model. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. PODCAST SERIES The Shape of Things to Come Join Microsoft’s Doug Burger and guests as they dig into the fundamental truths about AI and how it will reshape the future. Listen now Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback.
